items.body: Felice Sciorilli first graced our pages last spring, appearing on Biodiversità Records’ 14 Soundcapes with the track “Breaths.” At the time, we recognized the unique nature of the piece, capturing the sound of “air pushed through the Etruscan sandstone cliffs by the incoming waves.” “Breaths” appears on Distant Places as well, a worthy inclusion. In a way, the album title is a misnomer. These places are not necessarily geographically distant; most come from the intertidal zone of the Tyrrhenian Sea. But as Sciorilli has a particular fascination with tide pools – some only centimeters deep – these sounds may be regarded as distant as most people seldom if ever encounter their nuances. When one hears that an album is recorded at the coast, one expects to hear a bevy of predictable material: wind and waves, gulls and other fair-weather fowls. These make appearances, but are not primary. Instead, Sciorilli concentrates on micro-sounds made macro. In “E,” water rushes into crevasses before spurting back out, powered by the force of the waves, although this is not technically the sound of the waves. Instead, this is the sound of waves in rocks, familiar to jetty walkers. As the angles of approach vary, so do the timbres. The tide pools first come into focus in the opening segment of “Cluster,” with a sound akin to the crackle of brine shrimp. The piece develops in movements, like the “Bohemian Rhapsody” of field recording. Soon there are crashing waves, then fizzes and pops, and finally the sound of pebbles tossing, turning, rolling back to the sea. “Bolle” and “Bubbles drift upward into the water” occupy different areas of the album while also being separated by tone. While hearing them, one recalls pablo diserens’ “The Shrinking Glacier” from last year’s ebbing ice lines, providing one with the opportunity to compare “healthy” bubbles with “unhealthy” bubbles, or bubbles that belong to a cycle with those escaping for the last time. The second piece is more effervescent, like alien birds swimming in soda; without hydrophones, one might never encounter such distant sounds. While listening, one is amazed by the number of musical parallels that can be found in nature: the quickening tempos of “From the Tidal Edge,” the glissandos of “Outflow.” Distant Places serves as a reminder that music imitates nature, not (save for starlings) the other way around. The set builds to the eighteen-minute centerpiece “Tiny Worlds,” a longer, reworked version of a piece that made the shortlist of The Radiophonic Broadcast’s Sounds of the Year 2025-26. Recorded in a tidal pool six centimeters deep (shown in the pdf that accompanies the download), the piece demonstrates just how rich, dense and diverse a micro-world can be, although to be fair, to the local Littorina snails there also exist micro-worlds within micro-worlds, from bacteria down to the smallest atom, each with a corresponding biophony. The “characters” that appear may be animate or inanimate, but each possesses a personality of its own: squeaking and whistling, popping and percolating. In the final piece, Sciorilli draws back from the water and embeds his microphone in the sand, muffling the sound of the nearby waves. “Under the Sand” operates as a parable. Sonic treasures are available everywhere, yet most of us never hear them; it is as if we too are buried in the sand, listening through wax and debris, treating micro-worlds as distant places although they are right beneath our feet. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Two newly reissued albums showcase the seismic psychedelia of George Clinton’s Funkadelic at its rawest and most disruptive, writes John Morrison in The Wire 512 Funkadelic Free Your Mind And Your Ass Will Follow Westbound/Org CD/DL/LP/2xLP/MC Maggot Brain Westbound/Org CD/DL/LP/2xLP/MC Released the summer before Jimi Hendrix tragically passed away in 1970, Free Your Mind And Your Ass Will Follow was not only the follow-up to Funkadelic’s promising self-titled debut of the same year; it signalled the arrival of George Clinton’s ensemble as the next great voice in Black rock and psychedelia. In his 2014 memoir Brothas Be, Yo Like George, Ain’t That Funkin’ Kinda Hard On You?, Clinton acknowledges this by contrasting the album’s release with Hendrix’s death, an event that he notes as “the end of an era”. During his brief but electrifying career, Hendrix moulded multiple aspects of the Black musical tradition – blues, rock, funk, R&B, jazz – into an electrifying corpus that opened up a new world of possibilities. With Hendrix dead and the psychedelic road map that he laid out for any adventurous soul to follow, Funkadelic went on to emerge as his mightiest descendents. While Funkadelic were recording Free Your Mind Clinton absorbed and pulled inspiration from underground comics, Black power/radical leftist theory and Erich von Däniken’s work theorising that aliens had made contact with and shaped the development of ancient human civilisations. Clinton took all the disparate cultural, historical, political and extraterrestrial influences swirling around in his head and drenched them in acid. The famously LSD soaked sessions produced an album that distilled the political, cultural and philosophical DNA of the 1960s into a new musical vision for the 70s. Built around Eddie Hazel’s gnarly blues and wah-wah drenched guitar, “Funky Dollar Bill” highlights the flipside of the concept of money as freedom explored on “Friday Night, August 14th”. With lyrics like "The pusher push, the fixer fix, the judge acquits, the junkie leads his life, for the dollar bill”, it's clear that here, money is less a vehicle for freedom than a tool for control. “Eulogy And Light” serves as the perfect album closer, with Clinton praying for strength in the face of temptation and moral degradation. In an innovative display of the band's willingness to experiment with sound and concepts, the music for “Eulogy And Light” is an earlier Funkadelic track called “Open Your Eyes” spun backwards. In doing this, Clinton and crew extract the source song's optimistic heart and repurpose its gospel-inspired tune into something stranger, more twisted. Free Your Mind opens with the epic ten minute title track. Amid a ghostly mass of distorted guitar, feedback and cosmic synthesizer bleeps, Clinton screams “Free your mind and your ass will follow/The kingdom of heaven is within!”. These simple yet spine-tingling chants formed something close to a succinct mission statement. More than just slogans, Clinton was directly addressing the intellectual, physical and spiritual demands of a new musical and ideological path. He has described “Friday Night, August 14th” as a “paycheck and party song” about how a little bit of money can buy a moment of joy and freedom. In that sense, the song feels like the spiritual heir to Louis Jordan's 1949 proto-rock ’n’ roll smash “Saturday Night Fish Fry”. By the time Funkadelic entered the United Sound Systems studio in Detroit to record the follow-up to Free Your Mind, the band were at once a formidable live unit and boundless experimenters in the studio. The result of those USS sessions was 1971’s Maggot Brain, one of the greatest psychedelic rock albums ever made and the crown jewel of Clinton’s extensive body of work. The album opens with a simple and ominous message that is both a continuation of the core theme examined throughout Free Your Mind and a harbinger of the band’s future: “I have tasted the maggots in the mind of the universe/I was not offended/For I knew I had to rise above it all/Or drown in my own shit”. Here the “maggots” are the corrosive forces of ignorance, self-doubt and control that infested Free Your Mind. To all intents and purposes, Maggot Brain is a trip through the other side of enlightenment, witnessed through the prism of life, death and the liberatory potential of madness. Famously, Clinton prompted guitarist Eddie Hazel to imagine that his mother had died before recording Maggot Brain’s almost ten minute long title track. Hazel transforms his guitar into a wailing and mourning instrument of grief. Beneath his solo, a dreamy, six note arpeggio acts as the bedrock to one of the greatest guitar performances ever captured on tape. “Can You Get To That” flips the energy from dark to light with its slick groove and doo-wop harmonies. A bright and joyous song at face value, the lyrics warn that even in death, no one escapes karma. “Hit It And Quit It” is a flamboyant acid rock tune with an odd metre that betrays Funkadelic's debt to both the church and the temple of Jimi Hendrix. For an outfit that proved so adept at conjuring colourful, funky images of utopia, it's curious that they chose to close out their greatest album with “Wars Of Armageddon”. Clocking in at over nine minutes long, the song is a minefield of explosions, screams and fuzzed-out guitars. The chants of “More power to the people/More pussy to the power” offer a reminder that Funkadelic’s psychedelic ideals and ambitions never strayed too far from the funky, carnal physicality of life on Earth. This review appears in The Wire 512 along with many other reviews of new and recent records, books, films, festivals and more. To read them all, pick up a copy of the magazine in our online shop. Wire subscribers can also read the issue in our online magazine library.

I understand that at the time all the rising musicians were trying to blend and incorporate their influences into their music but this album does not really work out. Some British psychedelia, some pop influences, some Greek folk elements, which does not blend well and the record is all over the place.Despite the respect I have for Demis Roussos, the best tracks here are sung by Claude Chauvet, "End of the world" & "Rain and tears". The two tracks that justify the two stars, otherwise I would have given this record one star. As I was writing this review I almost forgot to mention that "The shepherd and the moon" is easily one of the worst songs I have ever heard! Yikes!

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — More than a decade after releasing the fairly experimental 'Nocturniquet', The Mars Volta returnedwith a brand-new self-titled studio album, released by Clouds Hill in 2022. A brief hiatus and asecret 2019 reunion led to the formation of an updated lineup featuring the creative core of Omarand Cedric alongside bass player Eva Gardner, drummer Willy Rodriguez and synth player MarcelRodr�guez-L�pez. In what could only be interpreted as a creative reset for the band, 'The MarsVolta' represents a bold and spiritually moving art rock collection that sees the prog innovatorsplaying a warm and melodic combination of danceable Latin rock, neo-psychedelia with electronicundertones, and straightforward indie pop/rock. Undeniably this is the most radio-friendly versionof the band so far, whereas the writing of Omar Rodr�guez-L�pez sounds grounded, smooth, andconfident, and has little in resemblance with the unhinged experimentation that had marked The MarsVolta's earliest efforts.Catchy pop tunes and eerily atmospheric indie ballads prevail here, making this release aninteresting exercise in form and texture from a band known for its exaggerated rock-basedsoundscapes. Gentle Caribbean rhythms and layered ambient sounds provide an almost psychedelicbackdrop to the album, which is quite solid overall. What each musician is playing is clearlyidentifiable, and I find that clarity valuable in an experimentally inclined pop album, although I'mnot convinced that every part of the record works equally well. While you may find extravagant andexciting accessible tunes like 'Blacklight Shine', 'No Case Gain', 'The Requisition', or 'Que DiosTe Maldiga Mi Coraz�n', 'TMV' also features a good amount of watered down and forgettable trackswith an almost complete lack of rhythmic development like 'Cerulea', 'Shore Story', and 'CollapsibleShoulders', that for me add little to no substance to the record and on certain occasions seem to bemere tracklist placeholders. It is this disbalance between excellent and bland that must havestumped most listeners upon hearing this record for the first time, including myself. And while Iappreciate the uncompromising risk the band took with this album, I ultimately have to conclude thatthis is simply not their best work.

items.body: Review by Logan — There is a distinct emotional friction at the core of Music Has the Right to Children. The albumtriggers a strong sense of nostalgia in me, but it rarely feels entirely safe or comforting. Instead, my own experience with the record lands in a bittersweet, haunted territory where thedegraded educational samples and childhood imagery evoke memories that feel slightly wrong ordisplaced. When I listen to it, the music operates like a half-forgotten television broadcast fromyouth left to rot on a discarded VHS tape.A significant reason this atmosphere connects with me is the physical groove of the record. Unlikethe colder, more mechanical programming of their later electronic peers, the rhythm section herestrikes me as dusty and organic. My personal standout of this approach is "Aquarius". The trackanchors its counting-game vocal samples with a heavy, driving bassline and a hip-hop breakbeat thatcommands the room. To me, it represents the clear peak of the duo's ability to blend a functionalrhythmic pocket with an unsettling psychological undertone.That rhythmic focus carries right through what I consider the rest of the album's essentialhighlights. The deliberate, motorik propulsion of "Happy Cycling" provides a steady late-albumsurge, while the texturally complex beat on "An Eagle in Your Mind" showcases their mastery ofanalog tape manipulation. Even on a short, melodic pop vignette like "Roygbiv", which could easilyslide into saccharine territory, I find that the underlying groove ensures the track never dissolvesinto pure sentimentality. The brothers keep the entire project grounded in a heavy, physicalreality that I find myself returning to.The technical blueprint of the album confirms that this texture was never an accident. The Sandisonbrothers achieved this frayed quality through a deliberate process of analog degradation, treatingtheir studio like a laboratory for decaying magnetic tape. Instead of relying on the digitalprecision of late-nineties sequencing, the duo ran their synthesizers?frequently utilising the warm,unstable sub-bass of the Roland SH-101 and the gritty digital-to-analog character of the EnsoniqVFX-SD directly into decrepit tape machines. By bouncing audio onto consumer-grade Tascam four-track recorders and malfunctioning Grundig decks, they subjected clean melodies to physical wow-and-flutter, artificial dropouts, and tape saturation.This destructive production method transforms standard subtractive synthesis into a tactileexperience. On tracks like "An Eagle in Your Mind", the skittering rhythm section and heavilywarped vocal elements sound to my ears as though they are actively dissolving under the friction ofa sticking tape head. Similarly, the low-end thunk and swirling synths of "Aquarius" owe theirpresence to low bit-depth Akai S1000 samplers, which naturally crush the high frequencies and add adistinctive, dusty grit to the breakbeat. By leaning into the unpredictable quirks of old gearrather than flawless digital tracks, the duo built a soundscape where everything feels beautifullydecayed, matching how human memory blurs over time.This focus on unstable analog hardware explains why simpler pop vignettes like "Roygbiv" still hitme so hard. The track is built on a remarkably straightforward melodic hook, but the underlyingproduction ensures it never sounds cheap or overly sweet. The bassline carries a heavy, physicalthrum that balances out the drifting, sun-baked top melodies, proving to me that the duo could writean infectious pop tune without losing their signature sonic grit. It functions as my personalgateway into the album's stranger, more texturally complex spaces.By the time the record reaches "Happy Cycling", that playful energy has mutated into something farmore relentless. The track acts as a steady late-album surge, driving forward on a cyclical,motorik rhythm that feels both hypnotic and slightly ominous. The repetition does not tire me out;instead, it locks you into a specific, heavy-limbed trance that mirrors the physical exhaustion of along journey. By placing this sprawling, rhythmic marathon near the end of the tracklist, theSandison brothers solidify the album's broader structural arc, ensuring the listener finishes theexperience immersed in their strange, loop-based universe.Looking back at this debut from the vantage point of their broader discography reveals just howcrucial these early structural blueprints were. Music Has the Right to Children acted as thefoundational source code for every sonic mutation that followed across the next three decades. Thewarm, electro-acoustic infrastructure and acoustic guitar textures that defined The CampfireHeadphase find their genetic origin here in the brief, pastoral transitions of "The Color of theFire" and "Olson". The duo was already learning how to weaponise nostalgia, laying the groundworkfor a lighter, more organic detour before their mid-career pivot.Concurrently, the album contains the initial seeds of the cold, apocalyptic dread that eventuallyswallowed Tomorrow's Harvest and Inferno. The unsettling vocal mutations on "An Eagle in Your Mind"and the eerie, numeric counting games of "Aquarius" are early warning signs of the claustrophobic,paranoid environments that defined their later records. By balancing infectious hip-hop groovesagainst a deeply haunted psychological undertone, Music Has the Right to Children did not justlaunch the Sandison brothers' career; it established a timeless tension that they would spend thenext thirty years refining, dismantling, and rebuilding.Ultimately, Music Has the Right to Children remains a significant achievement because it refuses toage. While the late-nineties electronic scene largely chased hyper-polished digital futures, Boardsof Canada looked backward, constructing a sonic monument out of decaying magnetic tape andfragmented childhood ghosts. It is a record that demands you surrender your internal clock and sitwith the discomfort of its bittersweet, haunted landscapes. Nearly three decades after its release,its physical grooves and emotional friction continue to command authority, standing for me as thedefinitive masterpiece of a discography that has yet to be replicated.While I do consider this album to be a masterpiece, "Aquarius" in particular remains one of myfavourite Boards of Canada tracks, and this was one of my very favourite albums for years, aftergetting Inferno this does not appeal to me as much. Music has the Right to Children and Geogaddiwere my favourite BoC albums, but now those final three mean more to me. So this masterpiece willget a 4 at PA (I would go with 4.5 if we had the option as I did at RYM). Additionally, I primarily wanted to add BoC to Prog Archives for the final three albums.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Still Thick As A Brick? Of course, this title evokes that of Jethro Tull's masterpiece, *Thick As A Brick* (TAAB for those in the know or the lazy), to which Ian Anderson himself gave a sequel 40 years later: *Thick As A Brick 2* (2012). *Still Thick As A Brick* isn't Tull's *TAAB* Episode 3, but rather the album by a new band led by Berlin-based Lutz Meinert?who also fronts the psychedelic rock band Margin?supported on acoustic guitar and vocals by Englishman Paul Forrest, a member of the Jethro Tull Experience, Crystal Palace guitarist Nils Conrad, and American flutist Ulla Hartmuth, whose virtuosity on the instrument rivals that of Ian Anderson. Despite nearly identical track titles (of course, it's a joke?), *Still Thick As A Brick* is neither a sequel to *TAAB* nor a simple cover of that legendary album. Just as TAAB told the story of Gerald Bostock, Still Thick As A Brick aims to tell the story of an inspiring figure: the famous financial magnate Georges Boston. Personally, I'd never heard of him, but as Reflection Club points out, to learn more about him, all we have to do is read what Rellington Stone magazine has to say?an entire issue of which is included in the CD booklet. Ha! Ha!Musically, there are plenty of similarities to TAAB, the most striking being Paul Forrest's singing style, with a slightly nasal voice very similar to that of Ian Anderson from the '70s. On *Still Thick As A Brick*, we also find that same playful flute that pops up at any moment, that same sense of rhythmic disruption, that recurring acoustic guitar developing highly catchy folk-rock themes, that anachronistic yet electrifying harpsichord, that delightful Hammond organ?worthy of John Evan's?an instrument particularly showcased on the exhilarating "The Foray of the Sharks " (5:37) or the very Tull-esque rock track "The Great Dance Around the Golden Calf" (3:35).Reflection Club intentionally set out to make an album "in the style of" and has succeeded in creating a thrilling work, close in spirit to TAAB (not to mention the very obvious nods) but one that manages to stand on its own, with some tracks less tied to Jethro Tull's '70s style. For example, the jazzy tones of "Nervesoothers" (3:10) place it more firmly between Camel and The Tangent. Furthermore, the contributions of guest musicians on sitar and violin, as well as a few brass notes (likely played on a synthesizer), judiciously enrich the atmosphere. And Reflection Club doesn't hesitate to vary the moods, stepping away from the bouncy symphonic folk-prog typical of Tull to embrace a tender pop-rock sound on the aptly named "Sentimental Depreciation" (5:19). Thus, after a few listens?from the magnificently symphonic "Prelude" (2:00) to the closing "Look Across The Sea" (4:24), a sort of sea shanty dominated by bagpipes?STAAB manages to make us forget TAAB for 48 minutes.So I have to admit that Reflection Club skillfully showcases more personality and originality than its album title would suggest. While it doesn't quite reach the creative heights of its brilliant and unsurpassed?more or less acknowledged?role model, Still Thick As A Brick captures all of its timeless charm, making for an undeniably enjoyable listen that should appeal to a wide audience, not just longtime Jethro Tull fans. And if Ian Anderson's TAAB 2 didn't quite win them over, they can safely give this Still TAAB a listen to make up for it.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Formed in 1997 from the ashes of Violet District?making it one of the oldest active neo-prog bands today? RPWL started out as a simple Pink Floyd tribute band but quickly managed to branch out?without betraying that influence?finding, as early as the album *God Has Failed* (2000), a sound and style all its own that has endured to this day, with just a few stylistic variations. Musically, *Crime Scene* doesn't shake things up. To our great delight, we find Yogi Lang's hazy melodies sung languidly in his velvety voice, and Kalle Wallner's majestic guitar, as determined as ever to deliver his beautiful Floydian solos that soar and glide along a thread suspended in the sky. All of this has always played a major role in the addictive charm of this timeless music. The absence of keyboardist Markus Jehle is the only notable change in this regard, leaving the spotlight entirely to Yogi Lang and his synthesizers?which are a bit more subdued than usual, though he doesn't forget to treat us, toward the end of the album, to his unchanging and unmissable Mini-Moog solo in the purest spirit of Manfred Mann's MMEB era. Certain tracks on *Crime Scene*, however, offer some welcome surprises, such as the lively intro to the brilliant and powerful "Victim of Desire," which is closer in style to Yes than to Pink Floyd. And the touch of '60s psychedelia on "A Cold Spring Day in '22." The heavy, offbeat riff?bordering on stoner rock?in "Another Life Beyond Control" also stands out in an album that some might find a little too polished. "King of the World" (12:51) is the album's pi�ce de r�sistance, unusually long for the band, which allows it?without any lulls, on a rhythm section once again closer to Yes than to Pink Floyd?to traverse a whole range of musical emotions worthy of the golden age of '70s prog, against a backdrop of Mellotron evoking the gloomy moods of our youth, when we walked with our heads down and raised them only to implore the heavens to restore our childlike carefreeness. Where the Bavarians are most surprising is in the theme?anything but trivial?chosen for their eighth studio album. The memorable *Tales from Outer Space* (2019) imagined that salvation for our species would come from space. After the interstellar journey comes a plunge into the deep night of the human soul to shed light on its most violent aspects. As its title makes quite clear, *Crime Scene* doesn't offer a selection of fairy tales for young children but instead sets out to recount a series of edifying stories. Starting with the dark "Victim of Desire," a veritable encounter with a nightmare, A disturbing news item that might provoke a sense of unease in the most sensitive among us, as if certain symptoms of some kind of post-traumatic neurosis?one we might be suffering from without even knowing it?were resurfacing. Through a story as sad as the sun's permanent absence, the bluesy "Red Rose" attempts to show us just how far mad love can lead. The catchy and effective "A Cold Spring Day in '22" in turn tells us another deeply grim story of a decimated family. It's a masterclass in the art of contrast between music and lyrics. Violence in our society?violence committed by human beings against one another, self-destructive and unnatural?has it not been present since the dawn of time, ever since this species came to be called "human"? Violence is everywhere?all around us and within each of us. But above all, *Crime Scene*, as a mirror reflecting the sickening prevalence of all violence against women perpetrated by men, presents us with an image that leaves no one indifferent. We may feel very distant from the dramatic situations depicted here?more or less graphically?and yet at the same time feel entirely affected. Are we all potential victims? And are we all potential monsters? Through six disturbing stories, curiously set to pleasant, harmonious melodies?music that is relatively peaceful by comparison?RPWL attempts, with *Crime Scene*, to offer an objective perspective that sends a chill down your spine.

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — An unfortunate fate of some artists of the 1970s lies in the rapid evolution of "popular" music of that time. A band conceived in the early 1970s, formed in the mid 1970s, and finally committing their sound to new generations, even if mostly within their own family tree, in the late 1970s would be behind the times from the outset. In the case of Finnish chameleons KAAMOS, it might not have mattered since their sole release wouldn't have been original 5 years earlier, but in 1978 it was so distinctly undistinguished as to almost be innovative, but no. A pastiche of palettes from the late 1960s and early 1970s, mostly in a heavy rock vein with brushes of folk and blues, it recalls pretty much every band that was at least critically fashionable at that time, including WIGWAM which didn't sound particularly Finnish either. The playing is very competent, especially the lead guitars, organs and rhythm section, but, while they were clearly familiar with each other, I can't help feeling it's all a bit too democratic. Best deeds here would be the wildly but admirably mercurial "Strife" and the engaging instrumental "Barokki", but they can only save this one from complete ignominy.

items.body: Review by KansasForEver4 — Five years have passed since CASTANARC's rather mediocre *The Sea of ​​Broken Vows*, which featured eleven tracks ranging from three to five minutes in length?none of them particularly progressive in ambition. This time around, the approach is worlds apart from its predecessor: the album consists of just three tracks, with even the shortest one exceeding the length of the longest song on the 2021 release. One might well call this a "palace revolution"?a genuine surprise, as you can imagine.To appreciate CASTANARC, you first need to like Mark Holiday's somewhat distinctive voice?especially since the album is heavily vocal-driven, though the singing is superb. Yet CASTANARC is also defined by Mark Powell's multifaceted keyboards, which appear all over the album; there is plenty of piano, very little organ, and likely many sounds run through a Mellotron-style filter, with the smooth, fluid synthesizer work serving as the Doncaster band's trademark.We must also mention?lest anyone be overlooked?Neil Duty's excellent guitar work on the second track, "Ceasefire for the Innocent" (Duty previously appeared on the band's 1984 debut, *Journey to the East*, alongside Holiday and Powell); guest musician Dave Holley's contribution is equally impressive on the short "Cue Rain" (though at six minutes, "short" is relative); and the rhythm section?Peter Robinson on bass and Charlie Morgan on drums?delivers a solid, highly competent performance.While it doesn't break the mold with radical originality (remaining firmly within a very conventional neo-progressive vein), it is a fantastic surprise given the band's previous output.

items.body: Review by fuxi — The best album in the style of Yes since 2001, or even since 1977? Hmmm, it's a tricky question. I've always enjoyed DRAMA (1980) and I'm not sure if it surpasses THAT. I'm not fond of THE LADDER or MAGNIFICATION, but I only recently discovered FLY FROM HERE - RETURN TRIP and found it truly refreshing. I even thought MIRROR TO THE SKY (2023) had its moments, especially when Steve Howe takes flight, but I can't stand Jon Davison's emasculated vocals or the nonsense he's singing. And here we touch upon something essential, for is Jon Anderson's nonsense any better? I must admit I'd find TRUE ten times more enjoyable if we got to hear something more enlightening than 'Cup a sound now, chook around, chook around / Everything now, moving out, moving out / Once upon a time you were searching for / Dance around it, tiki-tai, tiki-tay'. But then, even at age eighty Anderson's voice undeniably has power, and that's something they can't take away. The melodies he (co-) wrote are pleasant, and the Band Geeks are blessed with keyboard players and a Yes-style rhythm section that's far superior to anything Yes's current incarnation have to offer. Besides, Steve Graziano on lead guitar isn't half bad either. I recently saw Jon Anderson & The Band Geeks live (admittedly with a different lead guitarist in tow) and their vitality greatly impressed me. Ever since that gig I try to let TRUE's buoyant spirit carry me away. It doesn't seem likely that Steve Howe and Jon Anderson will ever make up, which is tragic, because didn't they write most of CLOSE TO THE EDGE and TOPOGRAPHIC OCEANS together? But as things stand, dedicated Yes fans will probably get a lot of pleasure out of TRUE.

items.body: Review by DimitrisTheHead — Another really strong Procol Harum album, after their debut. Procol Harum is a great example of a less-is-more band, delivering strong music without being to complex or trying to be sophisticated. The music is piano/organ/vocal driven, the trademark Procol Harum sound, led by Gary Brooker and his warm, emotional voice. Matthew Fisher on the organ is again fantastic. The album is not loaded with guitar, but when Robin Trower comes in, he delivers some really tasty and artful sounds.I like all the songs here, and the highlight is the heavy psychedelic/progressive suite "In Held 'Twas In I" with classical and Eastern music influences.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — It is always good to blend humor with strong influences, and right from the opening track of their debut album, "Lambo No. 5," a play on the famous "Mambo", Rokost draws on inspirations ranging from Dave Douglas and his "ethnic" trumpet style to Miles Davis and the use of special effects to create unique sonic textures. At times, the music seems to venture into psychedelic territory without ever losing its infectious, frenetic rhythm. Later, Marta Winnitzki's Rhodes piano (she also plays synthesizers) introduces mid-tempo passages that shift the rhythm, though the original melody, driven by Michel Schroeder's trumpet, always returns. This Hamburg-based quartet plays with time signatures and reimagines them; we recognize the conventions of classic jazz-rock while sensing them being pushed beyond their limits, not to abandon the genre, but to "expand the battlefield," to borrow a phrase from Michel Houellebecq.Menschenfeind evokes a space-age atmosphere, yet in its own unique way, distinct from the past, though nods to that era remain. Synthesizers dart back and forth reminiscent of the 70s, while the trumpet and keyboards establish a more contemporary setting where the two elements collide. This is where the term "symphonic jazz" applies, not due to pomp or grandiosity, but because of the interplay between the keyboards and the bass-and-trumpet foundation, with the latter instruments taking their own solos."Trotz" is dissonant and syncopated until a driving rhythm, so electric it borders on electronic, builds in intensity; its staccato breaks are slightly reminiscent of Bill Bruford's Earthworks. At times, one gets the impression that if Miles Davis were still with us, he might be creating something akin to the track "Jazon Hunter Strikes Again!"; much like the brilliant Japanese pianist Hiromi Uehara, her admiration for the 1970s drives a fusion of contemporary avant-garde with classic progressive elements, dreamy synthesizers, sophisticated trumpet lines, and a floating groove. Here, the sounds of the 70s, 80s, and 90s, along with techno, blend into a pastiche that serves as both homage and a gateway to the dreamlike "Meloda," a piece where electronic music once again takes on a progressive character within a jazz context."Attitude Adjustment" has a full-on rock rhythm, guitars aren't needed; as Weather Report so aptly demonstrated, the timing comes from elsewhere. A distorted synthesizer creates just the right kind of confusion to scramble the senses, while the bass and drums hammer out their parts, underpinning solos that scale mountains and swim through rivers, pumping adrenaline into those greens and fruits, produce as organic as this musical concept itself, where the artificial element pulses with more life than ever."We Will Still Be Here Tomorrow" is split in two; a classical trumpet shifts into a Baroque style while something very modern emerges from the seemingly disjointed drum beats. Yet, just when there might be a moment of coherence and composure, "Lines & Crimes" introduces a disorder that nonetheless encompasses melody and meaning, for this instrumental music seems to tell a story. The keyboards go wild, while the trumpet wails in increasingly piercing, high-pitched tones. "The Machines That Walk At Midnight" is almost industrial in its mechanical rhythm, yet there is genuine feeling when the bass kicks in; the electronic element has permeated not just the sound but the composition itself. Amidst this, Michel Schroeder adds a warm, magical touch on the trumpet, playing with effortless class and style, to remind us that this spirit doesn't subtract or lose anything, but rather adds to and elevates the music.Continuing the metaphor linking Rokost's music to Houellebecq's literature, one could say that the elementary particles of the fusion are present here but developing independently; they continue to evolve, triggering the release of substances like serotonin, the neurotransmitter that relays messages between nerve cells and helps regulate various bodily functions.The map and the territory are already laid out on the table, exposed; now it is simply a matter of submission to the possibility of an island... where all these molecules arrive and rearrange themselves, ultimately altering matter.

items.body: “Dancing has its time, mourning has its time”, runs a line in “Gamachume”, the new single from Tbilisi artists Tamada and DillaNext, and a Georgian supra works exactly that way. The supra is the country’s traditional banquet, a long table of food and wine presided over by the tamada, who holds the room and proposes toast after toast, to peace, to family, to the homeland and to the dead. The guests drink after each one and often break into song. Singer and producer Lasha Chkhapelia named himself Tamada after that role, and across Dionysus vs Tamada and 2024’s 9 Deadly Sins for Tamada he has written his lyrics as toasts in ancient Georgian and set them over electronic beats. This time the glass is raised to Sukhumi, the main city of Abkhazia, a Georgian region on the Black Sea. Abkhaz separatist forces, backed by Russia, seized the region in the 1992–93 war, and most of the world still recognises it as part of Georgia. Chkhapelia and Zura Jishkariani, the novelist and poet who records as DillaNext, were among around 250,000 Georgians driven out as children. The lyric pictures a boy with a pistol and a rose, with Black Sea currents running down through his genes. The pair used the same image on last year’s “Sokhumeli Bichi” (“Sukhumian Boy”), where the sea ran through the veins of the boy of the title. In both songs the city passes down by blood, from parents who lived there to children who left too young to remember it. Another verse turns a burial into a planting: others dig the earth, he is the one laid in it, and the people who took him for dead find they have planted a tree of life. Thirty-three years after the war emptied Sukhumi of its Georgians, two of the children it drove out are putting the city into songs made in Tbilisi, and that is the tree the verse describes. “Gamachume” arrived with a video on 27 September on Deep Douqan, the label behind Tamada’s most recent singles. It closes on its title, Georgian for “silence me”, five times over, sung by the same voice that earlier claims it can “break armies apart”. At a supra, the tamada decides when the room falls quiet. Stream “Gamachume” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Tamada II DillaNext – GAMACHUME appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: La Feria returns to Liverpool this October for its eighth edition, spreading five days of Latin American music, theatre, dance, visual art and food from Hope Street down to Chinatown. The festival was launched in 2018 by Luma Creations, the Liverpool organisation led by Chilean-born songwriter Francisco Carrasco, to put artists from across Latin America and its British diaspora on the city’s stages. This year’s music starts in Chile, with songs built on the Andean rhythms of huayno and tinku and with folk tunes opened up through jazz improvisation. From there it moves to the brass-heavy mambo and salsa dura of a 13-piece Latin big band, to Afro-Colombian gaita flute set over electronic beats and deep bass, and to Brazilian forró and coco rhythms reworked as pop. Around the evening concerts and theatre performances, the week also brings a visual art exhibition, free workshops led by visiting artists, and two free family days to close the festival at the weekend. On Wednesday, Unity Theatre opens the festival with Manuelita, a one-woman show from Popelei in which Tamsin Hurtado Clarke takes on Manuela Sáenz. The Quito-born revolutionary fought through the independence wars at Simón Bolívar’s side, and in 1828 she helped him escape an attempt on his life in Bogotá. Hurtado Clarke tells her story through comedy and physical theatre to music by Colombian guitarist Camilo Menjura. Before the play, 18-year-old Argentine-British musician Eli Rowley plays Argentine and Andean tunes on the ronroco, a big-bodied, low-tuned relative of the charango, taking his cues from Gustavo Santaolalla and Jaime Torres. A short walk from Unity Theatre, the Music Room at Liverpool Philharmonic Hall takes over on Thursday, when Camila y Silvio return after selling out at La Feria in 2022. Camila Soria and Silvio Rozzi met during Chile’s student protests in 2011, and in 2015 they toured Argentina at length, learning the traditional styles of that country and the Andes. Their music moves between huayno, tinku, chacarera and vidala, with two voices over Rozzi’s guitar and charango and the deep thump of Soria’s bombo legüero. Fellow Chileans Peregrinos open the night. Guitarist Raimundo Santander and New York-based drummer Rodrigo Recabarren cut their first record together in Brooklyn in 2013, and they have used Chilean folk material as a starting point for improvisation ever since. By Friday the Music Room’s stage has to make space for thirteen musicians. Orchestra Mambo International came together in 2022 around Leeds salsa DJ Lubi Jovanovic and trombonist Jonny Enright to play the mambo of Tito Puente, Machito and Eddie Palmieri with a full big-band sound. Trumpets, trombone and baritone sax are stacked over piano, bass, vibraphone and a percussion section of bongos, congas and timbales. Since then they have written their own material, from mambos to cha-cha-chás, much of it gathered on their debut album Apúntalo. Up front, Venezuelan singer Carlos Peña, once a featured vocalist in Oscar D’León‘s orchestra, shares the vocals with Cuban singer Claritzel Miyares. It is the band’s first Liverpool show, and Cuban singer-songwriter George Peguero, returning to La Feria, opens the evening. Saturday night belongs to District, the club on Jordan Street in the Baltic Triangle, where Medellín producer Killabeatmaker sets Afro-Colombian and traditional Colombian rhythms over electronic beats and deep bass. His music keeps returning to the wildlife and landscapes of Colombia and the threats they face. On stage he beatboxes, raps and sings over live beats while Guadalupe Giraldo plays percussion and the gaita, the long, breathy duct flute of Colombia’s Caribbean coast. Opening the night, Mari Merenda plays her first ever UK show. The São Paulo singer/songwriter and producer built her name on videos of the asalato, a West African pair of seed-pod shakers knocked together on a cord. Her songs set forró and coco grooves against pop and R&B with electronic touches, most of them from her 2025 EP Reverbero. In Liverpool she switches between piano and asalato, with Guilherme Monteiro on bass, guitar and vocals, before moving on to Brighton and London. Before District opens its doors on Saturday night, World Museum on William Brown Street hands its galleries over to the festival for a free family day of music, dance, storytelling and workshops. The take-over is part of Cuerpos del Tiempo, a project with the museum’s Global Cultures Collections team to reimagine its Americas Gallery. Artists from eleven countries, from Argentina to Venezuela, perform among the displays. At midday Tamachij Chihuatl, a collective of more than 100 Indigenous Nahua women from Hueyapan in Puebla, Mexico, lead a food workshop. For forty years they have kept their village’s textile tradition alive, weaving wool and colouring it with natural dyes, and their name means “handmade”. La Feria’s free finale takes over The Black-E, the community arts centre on Great George Street, on Sunday. There, Orkney fiddler Catriona Price plays with El Guapo, a Buenos Aires duo on guitar, drums, percussion and vocals who mix Latin American roots with rock and funk. Together they run Routes to Roots, a project that brings musicians from different cultures together to write new music and rework traditional tunes, and which took them to the Edinburgh International Festival in August. Three dance companies share the day. London’s ArtPer UK bring Peruvian folk dances from the coast, the Andes and the Amazon, including the marinera norteña, a courtship dance in which couples circle each other waving handkerchiefs. Colibrí, a Manchester troupe of Mexican dancers led by Guerrero-born choreographer Magaly Flores, perform regional dances in traditional costume, from Veracruz and the Huasteca down to Oaxaca and Chiapas. Inti Tusuy, whose name is Quechua for “sun dance”, bring together dancers with roots in Bolivia, Mexico, Peru and the UK. Latin American food, DJs and dance workshops fill out the afternoon. Once the music stops at The Black-E on Sunday afternoon, the festival’s 2026 theme stays on the walls at Unity Theatre. Belonging, an exhibition by UK-based artists of Latin American heritage, runs there until 6th November, with work drawn from diaspora, ancestry and the places its makers call home.   Full programme and tickets are on the La Feria website The post Event Preview: La Feria 2026 (Liverpool; Wednesday 7th to Sunday 11th October 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Los Angeles duo Patriarchy released an official video for “Lilylicker” on 29 September 2026. The track is the second song on the EP “Appendices,” released 7 August 2026 as a companion to the band’s 2025 album “Manual for Dying.” Appendices by Patriarchy The track opens on a low synth line and a steady kick drum, with Huizenga’s vocals half-whispered through the verses. The arrangement hardens into an industrial-techno beat partway through, with distorted guitars entering on the chorus. Patriarchy describes its own sound as “snuff pop,” a mix of metal, synthpop, punk and dance music. “Appendices” runs five tracks: “Bite Marks,” “Lilylicker,” “Servile,” “Ode (to an Apprehensive Tyrant)” and “Hate Fuck.” Huizenga and English wrote, performed, produced and recorded all five themselves. AJ English mixed “Lilylicker” and Enyang Urbiks mastered it. Witch Club Satan adds backing vocals on “Servile.” The EP is also out as a limited 12-inch clear vinyl edition of 300 copies, shipping around 1 November 2026, alongside digital formats on Bandcamp and streaming services. Patriarchy’s video for ‘Lilylicker’ Patriarchy directed the “Lilylicker” video itself, with cinematography by Hazel Hill McCarthy. Huizenga appears in a white gown holding lilies, then in a pink dress with chains and a metallic corset with gold wings; AJ English, also known as The Drummer, holds a skull and wears white wings. Huizenga’s son also appears in the video. The crew had to relocate the shoot outdoors to the hills above Los Angeles after the original studio balked at the concept and at having a child on set. Huizenga said the move improved the result: “A lot of the things that went ‘wrong’ ultimately added to the beauty of it, like having to shoot outside, where moths kept flying in front of our lenses.” On the project’s name and intent, Huizenga commented: “Patriarchy has never been about perfection, it’s about realizing we are the last remnants of human existence before AI enslaves us all; that’s why the project is called Patriarchy after all.” About Patriarchy Patriarchy formed in Los Angeles as a collaboration between Actually Huizenga and Andrew Means, who met when his band 3TEETH played a show at Das Bunker and offered to work with her in the studio between tour dates. Huizenga had been focused on filmmaking after a prior solo album, “Predator Romantic,” but the sessions with Means led the two to release the songs and build a band around them. Patriarchy released its debut album, “Asking for It,” on 8 November 2019 through Dero Arcade. The band built on that start with “The Unself,” released 26 August 2022, and “Manual for Dying,” out 19 September 2025 and trailed by the singles “Boy on a Leash,” “New Way” and “Die Like Everyone Else.” Patriarchy’s current lineup pairs Huizenga with AJ English, known as The Drummer. The band’s videos, including the earlier live performance clip “No Touch Torture,” are staged and directed largely by Huizenga herself. “Appendices,” the band’s companion EP to “Manual for Dying,” draws on Oscar Wilde, the Marchesa Luisa Casati, the emperor Tiberius and the Manson family as reference points. “Lilylicker” is the second single pulled from that EP, following “Servile,” and its video is Patriarchy’s newest visual release.

items.body: Canadian electronic duo Delerium release their 16th studio album, “Exaudire”, on 22 January 2027 via Metropolis Records. The album arrives on regular CD and as a limited edition double vinyl pressed on oxblood-colored vinyl in a deluxe gatefold sleeve. The title “Exaudire” is Latin for listening, hearing and being heard. Metropolis Records describes the album as moving between the tangible and the dreamlike, built from electronic textures, expansive atmospheres and guest vocal performances. Side-Line previously reported on the album’s lead single, Into the Light, which embeds portions of Diamanda Galás’s 1986 recording “Deliver Me from Mine Enemies: IV. Ε Ξελόυ Mε (Deliver Me)” from her album “The Divine Punishment”. Exaudire by Delerium ‘Exaudire’ tracklist and guest vocalists The 12-track “Exaudire” features five different guest vocalists across its running order, confirmed via the album’s Bandcamp listing: “Higher Power” (feat. Mimi Page), “Into the Light” (feat. Diamanda Galás), “Dream Palace” (feat. Magic Wands), “Buried Light” (feat. Mimi Page), “Apocalypse” (feat. Inna Walters), “Stolen” (feat. Phildel), “Into the Unknown” (feat. Jaël), “Multiplying Zero” (feat. Inna Walters), “Chasing the Wind” (feat. Mimi Page), “Exaudire”, “Had to Go” (feat. Jaël) and “Litany” (feat. Mimi Page). Mimi Page is an American singer-songwriter and composer who has released four full-length albums since 2011. Magic Wands, a dream pop trio from Los Angeles, are also signed to Metropolis Records, with the albums “Switch” (2023) and “Cascades” (2025). Jaël, a Swiss singer, previously collaborated with Delerium on the 2003 EP “After All” and the album “Chimera”. Inna Walters, based in Nashville, already appeared on Delerium’s 2023 album “Signs”. Phildel is a classically trained English singer, pianist and songwriter from London. Delerium songs have previously appeared in the films “Brokedown Palace” and “Lara Croft: Tomb Raider”. “Silence”, the duo’s 2000 collaboration with Sarah McLachlan, was more recently heard in the BBC drama “Industry”. Side-Line also covered Peter Murphy and Boy George’s 2026 Delerium remix of “Let the Flowers Grow” and Restless Mosaic’s tribute track referencing the project. About Delerium Delerium was founded in Vancouver, Canada, in 1987 by Bill Leeb and original collaborator Michael Balch. Rhys Fulber later joined as Leeb’s main songwriting partner. Both Leeb and Fulber built their reputation in the electro-industrial group Front Line Assembly, and Delerium initially served as an outlet for dark, cinematic ambient soundscapes distinct from that project’s harder industrial sound. Early albums “Faces, Forms & Illusions” and “Morpheus” appeared in 1989. Through the 1990s, Delerium’s sound evolved from industrial electronics and ambient trance toward song-based electronic pop built around guest vocalists, a shift marked by 1994’s “Semantic Spaces”, which introduced a rotating cast of female singers on largely downtempo songs, a format the duo has used on every album since. “Karma” (1997) established Delerium’s more danceable side, and “Poem” (2000), produced with Chris Peterson, included “Silence” featuring Sarah McLachlan, which reached worldwide chart success and won a Juno Award in 2000. After the Leeb-Fulber reunion album “Chimera” (2003), Delerium continued through “Nuages du Monde” (2006), “Music Box Opera” (2012), the atmospheric “Mythologie” (2016) and “Signs” (2023), the latter featuring Inna Walters among other vocalists. “Exaudire” is Delerium’s 16th studio album and its first collaboration with Diamanda Galás.

items.body: Belgian electronic dance act Lords Of Acid release their new album “Mundo Bizarro” digitally on 15 October 2026 via Metropolis Records. LP and CD formats follow on 9 November. The album is the group’s first collection of new material since 2018’s “Pretty in Kink”. “Mundo Bizarro” gathers the four singles Lords Of Acid have issued since April 2026, Karaoke Superstar (featuring Princess Superstar), Dream Boy (featuring Carla Harvey), “El Mundo Está Loco” (featuring Tony & The Kiki) and Ich Will Nur Dass (featuring Mari Kattman), alongside seven further new songs. The full tracklist, confirmed via the band’s Bandcamp page, runs: “Dreamboy”, “Dancing on the Flames”, “El Mundo Está Loco”, “Dopamine War”, “Maximo Roboto”, “Ich Will Nur Dass”, “City of Angels”, “So Stoned Today”, “Karaoke Superstar”, “You’re Obscene” and “A Viking’s Heart”. Mundo Bizarro by Lords Of Acid Carla Harvey, formerly co-lead vocalist of the American heavy rock band Butcher Babies, joined Lords Of Acid in January 2025, succeeding the late Ruth McArdle. The digital release of “Mundo Bizarro” coincides with the second leg of Lords Of Acid’s Cheeky Freaky North American tour, first announced in February 2026. At that time, the album carried the working title “Acid Reign”. The September 2026 press release from Metropolis Records confirms the final title as “Mundo Bizarro”. Specific October and November tour dates were not included in the current press materials. About Lords Of Acid Lords Of Acid formed in Antwerp, Belgium, in 1988, founded by Praga Khan together with Oliver Adams and Jade 4U. The group emerged from the hard-edged electronic dance scene of that era, blending techno, acid house and industrial music with lyrics centered on sexuality, drug use and hedonism. The band debuted with the New Beat single “I Sit on Acid”. Its first album, “Lust”, followed in 1991. “Voodoo-U”, with Ruth McArdle on vocals, arrived in 1994 and brought a heavier industrial dance sound along with the band’s best-known US club hits. “Our Little Secret” appeared in 1997. The B-side compilation “Heaven Is an Orgasm” (1998) and the remix album “Expand Your Head” (1999) came next. The rock-influenced “Farstucker”, featuring Deborah Ostrega, arrived in 2000. After a long gap, “Deep Chills” (2012) introduced Mea Fisher on vocals, and the Kickstarter-funded “Pretty in Kink” (2018) introduced Marieke Bresseleers. Metropolis Records remastered and reissued the band’s catalog from 2017 onward. Ruth McArdle died in 2024. Carla Harvey, previously of Butcher Babies, was announced as the band’s new lead vocalist in January 2025 and has since toured extensively with the group, including the 2025 “Praise The Lords” tour and the 2026 “Cheeky Freaky” tour. “Mundo Bizarro” is Harvey’s first full studio album with Lords Of Acid.

items.body: Ministry‘s “Moral Hygiene” turns 5 on 1 October. The industrial metal band released its fifteenth studio album through Nuclear Blast on 1 October 2021, produced by Al Jourgensen. The record runs ten tracks and 47 minutes, and it marked the first Ministry album since 2012’s “Relapse” to include a cover song. “Moral Hygiene” was recorded over roughly three years following 2018’s “AmeriKKKant” and is the first Ministry album to feature bassist Paul D’Amour, formerly of Tool, who joined the band in 2019. It is also the first record since 2006’s “Rio Grande Blood” without guitarist Sin Quirin, who left Ministry in March 2021. The album’s cover of Iggy Pop and James Williamson’s “Search and Destroy” was released as a single on 20 August 2021, alongside “Alert Level” (24 April 2020) and “Good Trouble” (8 July 2021), the latter accompanied by a “Unity Mix” the band put out to honor civil rights leader John Lewis. Guest musicians on “Moral Hygiene” include guitarist Billy Morrison, former Megadeth bassist David Ellefson, former N.W.A member Arabian Prince, and Jello Biafra, Jourgensen’s former bandmate in Lard, who takes lead vocals on “Sabotage Is Sex.” The album was engineered by Michael Rozon and mastered by Dave Donnelly. It was released on CD, vinyl, cassette and digital formats via Nuclear Blast. Moral Hygiene by Ministry About Ministry Ministry formed in Chicago in 1981 as the synthpop project of Al Jourgensen. The band’s 1983 debut, “With Sympathy,” was released through Arista Records and leaned toward the synth-driven sound of the era, a direction Jourgensen later disowned as label-imposed. Ministry’s sound shifted toward the aggressive, guitar-driven industrial style that would define the band starting with 1986’s “Twitch,” produced with Adrian Sherwood, and continuing through 1988’s “The Land of Rape and Honey” and 1989’s “The Mind Is a Terrible Thing to Taste,” both released on Sire Records. The band’s commercial breakthrough came with 1992’s “Psalm 69: The Way to Succeed and the Way to Suck Eggs,” which went platinum in the United States and included the single “Jesus Built My Hotrod” featuring Gibby Haynes of the Butthole Surfers. Ministry continued through the 1990s with “Filth Pig” (1996) and “Dark Side of the Spoon” (1999), then released “Animositisomina” (2003), the final album to feature longtime bassist Paul Barker, before Jourgensen turned to a trilogy of albums aimed at the George W. Bush administration: “Houses of the Molé” (2004), “Rio Grande Blood” (2006) and “The Last Sucker” (2007). Jourgensen announced Ministry’s retirement after “The Last Sucker,” then reactivated the band with 2012’s “Relapse,” recorded after he survived a near-fatal ruptured ulcer. Ministry has released albums steadily since, including “From Beer to Eternity” (2013), featuring posthumous contributions from guitarist Mike Scaccia, “AmeriKKKant” (2018), “Moral Hygiene” (2021) and “Hopiumforthemasses” (2024), each addressing the political landscape of its release year. Jourgensen remains the band’s sole constant member, working alongside a rotating cast of musicians including longtime guitarist Cesar Soto and, since 2019, bassist Paul D’Amour. “Moral Hygiene” extended that run five years ago this October, arriving as Ministry’s fifteenth studio album.

items.body: Lacrimosa released their seventh studio album, “Fassade,” through Hall of Sermon and Nuclear Blast on 1 October 2001. The gothic metal record turns 25 this year. The Swiss duo, Tilo Wolff and Anne Nurmi, recorded and mixed “Fassade” between January and June 2001 at Impuls Musicproductions in Hamburg, with orchestral parts performed by the Deutsches Filmorchester Babelsberg recorded in March 2001 at the Scoring Stage in Berlin. JP Genkel recorded and mixed the album, and Helge Halvé handled mastering in July 2001. Wolff arranged, produced and sang on the record; Nurmi wrote and sang the album’s English-language track, “Senses,” while Wolff wrote the remaining seven songs. The eight-track album is built around the title piece “Fassade,” a three-part composition split across tracks one, five and eight, with the remaining songs, “Der Morgen danach,” “Senses,” “Warum so tief?,” “Liebesspiel” and “Stumme Worte,” filling out a 52-minute run time. “Fassade” reached number 20 on the German Albums Chart and number 31 in Switzerland, following 1999’s “Elodia,” which had marked the band’s commercial breakthrough with the London Symphony Orchestra. “Fassade” streams on Spotify. About Lacrimosa Tilo Wolff founded Lacrimosa in Frankfurt, Germany, in 1990, recording a demo tape titled “Clamor” before launching his own label, Hall of Sermon, in 1991 to release the debut album “Angst.” A harlequin has appeared on every Lacrimosa album cover since, becoming the band’s logo. Wolff released “Einsamkeit” (1992) and “Satura” (1993) as the project’s sole member before Finnish musician Anne Nurmi, formerly of the gothic rock band Two Witches, joined as a permanent second member in 1994. Nurmi has contributed her own compositions in Finnish and English on every album since “Inferno” (1995), which became the band’s first charting release in Germany. “Stille” (1997) introduced the heavier, symphonic metal direction that defined the band’s sound going forward. “Elodia” (1999) became Lacrimosa’s commercial breakthrough, reaching number 12 in Germany with orchestral parts recorded by the London Symphony Orchestra at Abbey Road Studios. “Fassade” followed on 1 October 2001, continuing the orchestral approach with the Deutsches Filmorchester Babelsberg, an arrangement repeated on “Echos” (2003). In 2008, Hall of Sermon reclaimed the rights to the band’s back catalogue from Nuclear Blast, restoring full independence over the discography. Lacrimosa continued to release albums through the 2000s and 2010s, including “Lichtgestalt” (2005), “Sehnsucht” (2009), “Revolution” (2012), “Hoffnung” (2015) and “Testimonium” (2017), the latter a requiem in four acts dedicated to musicians who died in 2016. Side-Line marked the band’s 25th anniversary in 2015 with the announcement of a new studio album, and reported on the band’s 2021 return with “Leidenschaft,” delayed at the time by a worldwide paper shortage. Side-Line also covered the 2023 release of the double live CD “Nachts” on Hall of Sermon. “Lament,” released in 2025, completed a stylistic trilogy begun with “Testimonium” and debuted at number 7 in Germany, the band’s highest chart position since “Elodia.” Lacrimosa remains one of the longest-running self-released acts in the gothic metal scene, operating continuously through Wolff’s own label since 1991. “Fassade” turns 25 this year, marking a quarter century since the band’s most explicit engagement with themes of individuality and societal conformity.

items.body: De/Vision, the German synth-pop duo of Steffen Keth and Thomas Adam, released their sixth studio album “Two” on 1 October 2001 through E-Wave Records, a division of Drakkar Entertainment GmbH distributed by BMG. The De/Vision “Two” album turns 25 this year. It was the first De/Vision studio album recorded as a duo, following Markus Ganssert’s departure from the band in 2000. De/Vision ‘Two’ tracklist and credits The ten-track CD runs “All I Ever Do,” “Silent Moan,” “Drowning Soul,” “Heroine,” “Blindness,” “Heart-Shaped Tumor,” “State of Mind,” “Escape the World,” “Uncaring Machine” and “Lonely Day.” Georg Kaleve produced and mixed the album, with Keth handling pre-production; Stefan Ulrich engineered the sessions, recorded across Pizza Hat and Mikrokosmos-Studio in Berlin and Palais Aux Etoiles in Bremen, and Michael Schwabe mastered the record at Skyline Tonfabrik in Düsseldorf. Achim Färber played drums, Josef Bach added piano, and Kaleve, Bach and Lars Baumgardt contributed guitar; vocalist Sandrine appears on “State of Mind” and Clara Hill supplies additional vocals elsewhere on the album. Dirk Rudolph designed the sleeve around cover photography by Christof Schulte and band photography by Harald Hoffmann. “Two” peaked at number 42 on the German album chart. Lead single “Heart-Shaped Tumor” reached number 89 in Germany that September, De/Vision’s first charting single since “We Fly… Tonight” in 1998. A Different Drum issued a separate US edition of the album in 2004, and Popgefahr Records released a 17-track deluxe reissue of “Two” in 2016, adding instrumental and remix material to the original ten songs. About De/Vision De/Vision formed in July 1988 in Bensheim, near Darmstadt, Germany, as a quartet of Steffen Keth, Thomas Adam, Markus Ganssert and Stefan Blender. Blender left in 1991. The band self-released the single “Your Hands on My Skin” in 1990 and issued “Boy on the Street” in 1992 through Synthetic Product Records, before the 1993 maxi single “Try to Forget” brought them to Strange Ways Records. The debut album “World Without End” followed in January 1994, and “Unversed in Love” arrived in January 1995, both on Strange Ways. “Fairyland?” followed in August 1996 and became the band’s first German chart entry, and “Monosex” moved the band to WEA Records in 1998, reaching number 30. Ganssert left the group in 2000, the same year “Void” reached number 34 on WEA. Keth and Adam, now a duo, signed to E-Wave Records for “Two,” released on 1 October 2001 and distributed internationally through BMG. The duo continued on E-Wave through “Devolution” (2003), “6 Feet Underground” (2004), “Subkutan” (2006) and “NOOB” (2007), before founding their own label, Popgefahr Records, in 2009. Later albums “Popgefahr” (2010), “Rockets and Swords” (2012), “13” (2016) and “Citybeats” (2018) all appeared on Popgefahr, alongside the 2016 deluxe reissue of “Two.” Keth also records with Daniel Myer of Haujobb as Devision Redux, and De/Vision themselves toured with Lakeside X and Empathy Test in 2025. Twenty-five years on, “Two” marks the album that opened the Keth/Adam duo era of the band.

items.body: Wumpscut’s eighth studio album, “Wreath of Barbs,” turns 25 this year. The German electro-industrial project released the record on 1 October 2001 through Beton Kopf Media in Germany, with Metropolis Records issuing the US edition on 9 October 2001. Wumpscut is the recording name of Bavarian musician Rudy Ratzinger, who wrote, arranged, performed, mixed and mastered the album himself. “Wreath of Barbs” runs eleven tracks: “Opening the Gates of Hell,” “Deliverance (Album Mix),” “Wreath of Barbs (Album Mix),” “Dr. Thodt,” “Mankind’s Disease,” “Christfuck,” “Troops Under Fire,” “Line of Corpses,” “Hate Is Mine,” “Bleed in Silence” and a remix of Kirlian Camera’s “Eclipse,” titled “Eclipse (Kaelte Container Remix).” Aleta Welling contributes female vocals and wrote the lyrics for “Wreath of Barbs” and “Dr. Thodt.” The album peaked at #13 on the CMJ RPM Chart in the US. Exclaim! described it as “a celebration of darkness and foreboding” and praised “Ratzinger’s talent for writing a catchy song.” Concurrent with the release, Ratzinger ran a remix contest for the title track, providing samples through his website and inviting any musician to submit a version for a chance at inclusion on the subsequent “Wreath of Barbs” MCD. The album has since seen multiple reissues, including a 2017 “Concentrated Camp Edition” and a DAT edition, and Wumpscut announced vinyl reissues of “Wreath of Barbs” and “Body Census” in December 2021. About Wumpscut Wumpscut, stylised as :wumpscut:, is a gothic-influenced electro-industrial project founded in Munich, Bavaria, in May 1991 by DJ Rudy Ratzinger, born Rudolf Ratzinger in 1966 in Gangkofen, West Germany. Ratzinger has remained the project’s sole member throughout its history, occasionally bringing in guest contributors such as vocalist Aleta Welling. He has cited the early work of Leæther Strip as his reason for moving from DJing to recording, saying in a 1997 interview that he “was a DJ for several years and was tired of offering the audience only alien stuff.” Wumpscut’s first release was the demo cassette “Defcon” in late 1991, followed by the project’s first full-length album, “Music for a Slaughtering Tribe,” in 1993. That album’s track “Soylent Green” drew early attention in goth and industrial club circuits in Germany, the UK and the US. Wumpscut released “Bunkertor 7” in 1995 and “Embryodead” in 1997, the latter reaching #20 on the CMJ RPM chart. The 1999 album “Boeses Junges Fleisch,” built around the life of German serial killer Fritz Haarmann, reached #25 on the CMJ RPM chart and #17 on the German Alternative Charts. The 2000 EP “Blutkind” followed, reaching #5 on the DAC Top 50 Albums of 2000 in Germany and #17 on the CMJ RPM chart in the US. Ratzinger started his own label, Beton Kopf Media, in 1995 to release Wumpscut material to the European market, and later ran the label Mental Ulcer Forges. “Wreath of Barbs,” released in 2001 through Beton Kopf Media in Germany and Metropolis Records in the US, reached #13 on the CMJ RPM Chart, the project’s highest US chart placement to date. Wumpscut has continued releasing albums since, including “Wüterich” (2016), “Fledermavs 303” (2021), “Schlossgheist” (2024) and “Chew Chew Chew” (2025), while remaining a studio-only project that has never toured. Twenty-five years on, “Wreath of Barbs” remains one of the project’s most commercially successful releases.

items.body: This new album by Alessandro Tedeschi—better known by his sonic alter ego, Netherworld—is a remarkable work. Quite by chance, thanks to his young daughter, he stumbled upon old recordings dating back more than twenty years. These were recordings he had all but forgotten. Upon rediscovering them and realizing that their atmosphere perfectly matched the dark, sombre period he had been going through in recent months, he decided to revisit and rework material that no one had ever heard before. You could quite rightly call these Netherworld’s earliest experiments. Seven tracks were salvaged and restored. They fit seamlessly into the concept of Glacial Movements—Alessandro’s own label—leaving a profound, icy impression through their Ambient and Cinematic sound. We discover a Soundscape created—and, above all, inspired—by early expeditions to the North Pole. Distinctive field recordings echo through the metallic tones. You sense the imaginary presence of malevolent forces watching you, potentially pushing you towards a state of paranoia; you experience a sense of evil and an invisible presence that relentlessly pursues you. This effect is achieved simply through the power of the compositions, which, in my opinion, might well be hailed as Netherworld’s finest work. The sound is authentic and archaic, with deep, dominating tones that hit their mark with undeniable impact. It is hardly surprising, then, that the only track that failed to fully captivate me was the most ethereal one on the album. When music becomes an expression of dark thoughts, an artist is often at their most inspired—a fact perfectly embodied by the evocative title, “The Hermit”. (Rating:8). Listen to “Loneliness”: Loneliness by Netherworld About Netherworld Netherworld is the moniker of Alessandro Tedeschi, an Italian ambient and dark ambient composer based in Rome. The project is released through Tedeschi’s own label Glacial Movements, which he founded in 2006; “The Hermit” marks the label’s 20th anniversary. Netherworld’s music draws on manipulated fragments of classical music and field recordings, including ice masses, aurora-related material and Arctic wind recordings. Before focusing on Glacial Movements, the project released music through labels including Fario, Angle Rec, Umbra and Taalem. “Eternal Frost”, recorded in 2004, was originally issued by Umbra in a hand-numbered edition of 99 copies and later appeared on Bandcamp in February 2022. The Glacial Movements catalogue includes “Mørketid” (2007), “Over The Summit” (2011) and “Alchemy Of Ice” (2013, Tedeschi’s tenth full-length release). In 2017, Netherworld collaborated with Eraldo Bernocchi on “Himuro” for the label’s Iceberg Series. “Algida Bellezza” followed in 2019, and Side-Line’s interview with Netherworld was built around that release. “Vanishing Lands” appeared in 2022 and the Bvdub collaboration “Equilibrium” in 2023. “The Hermit” returns to material recorded before Glacial Movements existed: seven tracks salvaged from deteriorated CD-Rs and Minidiscs recorded in 2004.

items.body: Halcyon eyes, kind of gloomy in-between (If not now, then when we gonna do it, baby?) Holy pledge, Nostradamus said we’re clean (If not you, then who is gonna teach it to me?) PONS have somehow made a song that sounds as though a demon discovered stimulants, bought an expensive string section, read half a book about Roman emperors, and immediately decided he ought to run for king of hell. IF NOT NOW… is five-plus minutes of Brooklyn dance-punk delirium built around repetition as both engine and psychological hazard. Jack Parker and company plant a krautrock riff in the floorboards, then proceed to furnish the room with strings, horns, electronic abrasion, post-punk angles, and enough manic forward motion to make stopping seem medically inadvisable. Somewhere between Suicide, Brainiac, Liars, Sextile, and Ecce Schnak, after several catastrophic decisions, PONS turn excess into an organizing principle. Parker admits that excess comes naturally. “I have a really maximalist impulse when I’m writing music that I’ve recently been trying to get away from.” You can hear him losing that argument in spectacular fashion. The Eclectica String Quartet enters the picture alongside arrangements refined with Steve La Rosa, and suddenly the song has the air of an espionage film whose secret agent has misplaced the microfilm and joined a Dionysian cult instead. The repetition is crucial. PONS keep worrying the central figure until familiarity starts producing strange side effects, with each return carrying another detail, another escalation, another reason to suspect somebody has slipped something questionable into the punch. Parker wanted “something as repetitive and hypnotic as possible,” and the band stretches that idea toward absurdity without losing its grip on the dance floor. Lyrically, appetite keeps mutating. Sex, ambition, prophecy, intoxication, history, conquest, divine entitlement, and cultural memory pile together until the speaker begins sounding less like a romantic opportunist than somebody preparing to annex a small republic before breakfast. Desire becomes destiny; destiny develops an ego problem. By the closing stretch, bravery, brutality, providence, and personal mythology have become indistinguishable enough to suggest that civilization may have been a clerical error. Animator Arturo Baston pushes the same madness into the accompanying video. “Arturo had the idea of animating some sort of nightmare carnival bumper car ride filled with freaks and ghouls,” says Parker. From there, Parker becomes a Ghost Rider-like figure traveling through the underworld on his way toward infernal royalty, because apparently ordinary professional advancement was unavailable. Watch the video for If NOT NOW… below: IF NOT NOW… belongs to the forthcoming RACECAR, out November 5 via Casa Gogol Records, Eugene Hütz’s new label. If this single represents the album’s governing philosophy, PONS have built themselves a machine whose accelerator has been welded permanently to the floor. Normies should probably stand clear. Listen to IF NOT NOW… below and order the single here. You can pre-order RACECAR here.
