VOICE』等カルチャー誌に執筆... 詳しく見る 2026年10月1日～10月31日の運勢 牡羊座（3/21～4/20） 牡牛座（4/21～5/21） 双子座（5/22～6/21） 蟹座（6/22~7/23） 獅子座（7/24~8/23） 乙女座（8/24~9/22） 天秤座（9/23~10/23） 蠍座（10/24~11/22） 射手座（11/23~12/21） 山羊座（12/22~1/19） 水瓶座（1/20~2/18） 魚座（2/19~3/20）   2026年下半期の運勢《総括》と12星座別の運勢はこちら 牡羊座（3月21日～4月20日） 支配星・火星がクリエイティブのハウスを通過中。太陽は対人関係のハウスにあり、他人と力を合わせて創造していくことに大きな幸運が。牡羊座の若々しい精神、永遠の青春時代を生きているような心の瑞々しさが、理解してくれる人との語らいのなかで「目に見える何か」に発展していきそう。 夢を表す海王星と、エネルギーを表す火星を結ぶラインの頂点には、天才星の天王星が輝いています。あなたが封印していた才能を、今こそ発揮するタイミングです。 10月11日は対人関係のハウスで新月となり、新しい場所に出向くことで建設的な人脈が築けるとき。カルチャースクールや講演会に参加するのも大吉。オンラインよりも実際にライブで学ぶのがおすすめです。メディアから得られる知識や情報は便利なものですが、あなたが持っている経験は何よりの宝です。昔話としてではなく、あなたの見てきた「時代」を知りたいと思っている後輩は多いようです。 今月の牡羊座におすすめのラッキー・アルバム：『ジョン・ウィリアムズ レガシー』 牡羊座の2026下半期の運勢 牡牛座（4月21日～5月21日） 対人関係のハウスで、支配星・金星が長期的な逆行を続けています。火星も難しい配置にあり、組織や集団の中で自分のポジションを確保するのに、いつもの倍の努力が求められそう。牡牛座の素直さ、こじれないストレートな言葉が難局を打破していくでしょう。 過去に想いが引き戻され「あの頃はよかった」という感傷にふけることも。今は強引に何かを動かそうとするより、便利になったものを有効に使ったり、年下世代がすすめてくるものに少しだけ関心を持ったりして、自分に穏やかな変化を課して。ごく親しい相手に対しては、頑固な面が表れやすく、少しばかり注意が必要。100%わかり合うことは無理でも、補い合うことでベストな着地点が見つかります。 10月26日はあなたの星座で満月。種をまいてきたことを刈り取るタイミングで、長年の活動にスポットライトが当たったり、育てた人材から恩返しのサプライズがあったり。 金運は倹約第一で。買いだめはしないほうが◎。 今月の牡牛座におすすめのラッキー・アルバム：HIMARI『Debut』 牡牛座の2026年下半期の運勢 双子座（5月22日～6月21日） パワフル。あなたの存在感が増します。長年、上が詰まっていたという人も、世代交代でようやく双子座に主導権が回ってきそう。あなたを新しいボスに迎えたいというグループも出てくるようです。 キーワードは「深い絆」。広く浅く、のスタイルが得意な双子座ですが、今求めているのは軽いポジションではないはず。また、リーダーシップをとるためにも、普段から品行方正な態度で日々を過ごすことです。新しい人材をスカウトしたり、昔一緒に働いた人をキャスティングしてメンバーに加えたりなど◎。他人に煩わされない自由なライフスタイルを送っている双子座は、ここで少し人にもまれたほうが成長するかも。短期契約での就職もおすすめ。 プライベートは、親友や恋人との二人旅が楽しいとき。秋の景色が美しいスポットを探してみて。 今月の双子座におすすめのラッキー・アルバム：アンドラーシュ・シフが弾く『ブラームス：ピアノ小品集』 双子座の2026年下半期の運勢 蟹座（6月22日～7月23日） これまで成功してきたパターンが、周囲の変化によって通用しなくなってくることがあるかもしれません。2020年以降、蟹座は現実的にものを見て、計画を立て、緻密に計算をして実行に移すことで、手堅い評価と富を得てきましたが、木星が導いていたピーク期を終え、現在は新しいやり方がトレンドに上がってきています。 どちらかというと「個性」のようなものを暑苦しく思っていた蟹座は、多くの現場で「クセの強い個人主義者」が優遇されているのを目にすることが増えるでしょう。 具体的な対処策としては、とにかく他人に対するキャパシティを拡げ、自分の「肝を強くする」こと。仕事面でも、楽しそうに集中して取り組む人が好まれるので、「義務のため苦役に耐える」心構えでは、先細りに。 いつもより目立つファッションを取り入れる、女性ならメイクを濃くしたりヘアカットしたりする、というアクションは吉と出るはず。ネットの知識に頼りすぎず、実際にレッスンに通ったり、生身の人間からのアドバイスを受けると、得るものが大きいでしょう。 今月の蟹座におすすめのラッキー・アルバム：小澤征爾＆ボストン・フィル『チャイコフスキー：交響曲第6番《悲愴》』 蟹座の2026年下半期の運勢 獅子座（7月24日～8月23日） 待望の火星を約2年ぶりに迎え、マルス（火星）とジュピター（木星）が近づき合って遊ぶ獅子座という星座は、12星座で一番にぎやかで楽しいムードに包まれます。青春時代に好きだったものを再び引っぱり出して観たり、聴いたり、ライブや上映会を催したりと、イベントの中心となって同志と楽しんでみては？ 年下世代と価値観が合わず、窮屈な思いをしていたという獅子座は、自分と同じジェネレーションが似た葛藤を抱えていることに気づくはずです。ぽつぽつとエンタメ作品のリバイバルも浮上してくるこの秋、初めて触れるオーディエンスに向けて「このアルバムが出た当時は」「映画が最初封切になったときは」という興奮をアピールし、貴重な時代の伝道師になって。 プライベートはグルメツアーが楽しめるとき。秋の実りを五感で味わい尽くしたいものです。 今月の獅子座におすすめのラッキー・アルバム：ニコラウス・アーノンクール＆ロイヤル・コンセルトヘボウ管弦楽団『美しく青きドナウ～シュトラウス管弦楽曲集』 獅子座の2026年下半期の運勢 乙女座（8月24日～9月22日） 浮き沈みの激しい日々は続きますが、仕事や人間関係はまずまず安定路線。少し前のような鬱々とした気分や、「同じことを繰り返して無意味に感じる」ということも減ってきそう。シリアスになりすぎず、現状でのポジションをキープしていくことで生活は回っていくでしょう。 トラブル星・火星は「無意識と見えない敵」のハウスにいて、不自然に急接近してくる相手や、イージーなビジネスに誘ってくる相手には警戒を。穏やかだった「あの人物」が牙を剥いてくるケースも。あなたの優しい心が餌食にならないよう、ボディガード的な人物に側についてもらうのも良案です。 10月23日以降、仕事面で発展的な展開がありそう。海外や、広い市場への進出も視野に入れて。第一報はメールで届きそうです。 お酒はワインが◎。香り高いものを少しずつ仲間と楽しんで。飲みすぎはタブーです。 今月のあなたにおすすめのラッキー・アルバム：メータ指揮 ニューヨーク・フィル ホルスト『惑星』 乙女座の2026年下半期の運勢 天秤座（9月23日～10月23日） 久々に主役としてセンターで活躍できるシーズン。火星・木星もコミュニティのハウスから天秤座の太陽を応援し、これまでの努力や取り組みに、まとまった評価が与えられるタイミングです。 2026年に入って、あなたの優雅な社交性や、相手を思いやる上品なマナーが、以前よりよいリアクションを得られなくなっていたかもしれません。周囲の殺伐としたムードに染まらず、自分のスタイルを保ってきたあなたに、格別のチャンスを与えてくれる人が現れるかも。 仕事面では、平均的な進め方に満足せず、あなたが特別に評価されるようなプラスαを、普段から盛り込んで。人として誠実であること、相手にとって何が不足しているのかを察する心が功を奏するでしょう。 10月25日からは逆行していた支配星・金星が再びあなたの星座に入り、12月4日まで滞在。豊かさと喜びを供給してくれます。愛情面での収穫も。 今月の天秤座におすすめのラッキーアルバム：チェリストのカミーユ・トマによるフィリップ・グラス『FOR CELLO』 天秤座の2026年下半期の運勢 蠍座（10月24日～11月22日） 水星・金星が蠍座を通過中。金星は10月3日から逆行しはじめ、11月14日まで逆行が続きます。水星は10月24日から逆行。秘めた想いを閉じ込めて、一心不乱に何かに没頭する季節になりそうです。 無理に「他者と交流しよう」と駆り立てなくても大丈夫。今あなたがやるべきことは、たったひとつの目標に辿り着くために、無駄を排して生活を整えていくことです。 経済面で不安があるのなら、自分を甘やかさず無駄をとことんカットして。不必要な社交もカットして問題ないでしょう。10月26日には対人関係のハウスで満月となり、「この人との縁はここまででいいかも」と区切りがつくタイミング。相手に宣言する必要はなく、あなたが心に決めた瞬間、さまざまなことが好転していきます。 10月23日には太陽が蠍座入りし、表舞台に立つことも多くなりそう。ありのままのあなたが、神々しく輝く季節です。 今月の蠍座におすすめのラッキー・アルバム：アカデミー賞俳優で画家のアンソニー・ホプキンスが88歳にして作曲家としてデビューした『Life Is A Dream』 蠍座の2026年下半期の運勢 射手座（11月23日～12月21日）   安定感のある運勢。しばらく音沙汰がなかったあなたの信奉者たちから支援の声が上がり、自然体で実力を見せていく季節です。あなたは決して休んでいたわけではなく、人目につかない場所で淡々とライフワークを継続していたはず。時代の流れと本格的にシンクロしていくこの秋から、「やはり凄い人だった」と再評価され、望むような仕事のオファーが続くでしょう。2020年以降、縮小傾向にあったことも、ここを起点として拡大傾向に。 内なる自信はあなたに魅力を与え、次々と人が寄ってきそう。アドバイスを請う相手には、あなたの経験からくる実感を語ってあげると感謝されそう。小粒なライバルたちは影をひそめ、再びあなたに覇権を譲ることになるでしょう。 プライベートでは、自然の力強さに触れて。温泉や鉱泉からは、地熱のパワーが得られます。 今月の射手座におすすめのラッキー・アルバム：アンドレアス・オッテンザマー『New Era~18世紀のクラリネット作品集』 射手座の2026年下半期の運勢 山羊座（12月22日～1月19日） キャリアと重責のハウスに太陽が昇り、リーダーとしての正念場を迎えることになりそう。あなたが率いているグループの規模の大小に関わらず、これまでの教育・指導に判定が下されます。おおむね、高い評価となるでしょう。 厳しく後進たちを鍛えてきた山羊座は、彼らの意見も聞き入れてみるタイミング。予想外のやり方で、彼らは自分磨きをしているかもしれません。 土星と海王星は引き続き安息のハウスで逆行し、山羊座にとっては「本当の安らぎとは何か」「安心できる居場所はどこ？」という試行錯誤が続きます。自宅のリフォームにとりかかる前に、条件によっては移転もありと選択肢を広げてみては？ 家族と暮らしている人は、家族のライフステージの変化も吟味して。 自由な暮らしを満喫している山羊座は、健康面でのケアを怠らずに。オフィシャル面が緊張続きで、その反動でリラックスのために過剰な気晴らしを続けてきた人は、今後の体調が不安定になるケースも。検査など健康のための出費は惜しまずに。 今月の山羊座におすすめのラッキー・アルバム：オルフェウス・チェンバー・オーケストラによるストラヴィンスキー集『Shadow Dances』   山羊座の2026年下半期の運勢 水瓶座（1月20日～2月18日） 太陽が調和的な配置にあり、秋の実りの季節を満喫できそう。長期的に、周囲との摩擦が大きかった人も、回り道をせずに戦ってきた成果がここで出るようです。 しぶきを上げる波間から顔を出す岩のように、水瓶座は不動のポジションで自らを鍛え上げてきました。年下世代からは、自分たちの知らない時代を知っている先輩として尊敬され、年上世代からは気骨ある仕事人として評価されそう。同世代とは、共闘して何かを始めるのも◎。あなた一人でもパワーは十分ですが、パートナーシップのハウスに幸運星がいる2027年7月までは、協力者を見つけることでゴールへの到達が早まります。 この季節で一番あなたをほっとさせるのは、財政面での雪解け。正当な評価が与えられることで窮状から脱出でき、もとから経済面で恵まれてきた人は、さらに昇給が期待できます。 今月の水瓶座におすすめのラッキーアルバム：ヤン・リシエツキが弾くモーツァルト『ピアノ協奏曲第20番&第21番』 水瓶座の2026年下半期の運勢 魚座（2月19日～3月20日） 周囲の人間関係は張り詰めていますが、魚座の存在がムードメーカーとして有り難がられるときです。あなた自身、自分の人生にまったく不安がないわけではないのですが、これまでさまざまな工夫と「ウルトラC」によってサバイブしてきた経験は、他の人にはない余裕のオーラを与えています。 異性が多いグループでは、男女問わずに魚座がアイドル的存在に。理詰めで物事を解決するのではなく、人の心を「溶かす」スタイルで進めていって。射手座の先輩はよきアドバイザーに。彼らのもつ善良さと道徳性は、魚座に大きな好影響を与えるでしょう。 プライベートはフットワーク軽く、人と会う機会を増やしてみてください。しばらく会うことのなかった親戚を訪ねてみるのもおすすめ。 10月23日以降、新しい免許を取ることがさらなる発展につながりそう。いざというときの武器になってくれます。車の免許も大吉。 今月の魚座におすすめのラッキーアルバム：ギタリストのパク・キュヒによる『The Live』 魚座の2026年下半期の運勢 【2026年後半《総括》】2026年下半期は誰もが「主役」！

items.body: ジャズ・ピアニストの海野雅威が、10月16日（金）に東京・有楽町の I’M A SHOWでライブ「Tribute to OSCAR PETERSON “We Get Requests revisited” presented by 海野雅威」を開催。楠井五月（b）、後藤龍太郎（ds）とのトリオで、オスカー・ピーターソンが1964年に発表した名盤『We Get Requests』（邦題：プリーズ・リクエスト）をテーマにステージを繰り広げる。 海野にとってピーターソンは、音楽人生の原点といえる存在だ。9歳の時に来日公演で聴いた、圧倒的なスウィング感にあふれる演奏に魅了されたことが、ジャズ・ピアニストを志す大きなきっかけになったという。本公演では、オリジナル・アルバムへの敬意を込めながら、海野ならではの解釈で名盤の魅力を新たな形で表現する。 公演に向けて海野は「9歳の頃にライブで聴いたオスカー・ピーターソン。今でも心に残るあたたかなライブでジャズの魅力に目覚め人生が変わりました」とコメント。さらに、その公演でピーターソンのドラマーを務めていたのがジェフ・ハミルトンだったことに触れ、35年を経て自身がハミルトンのトリオで世界を巡っている現在を「これもきっとオスカーが繋いでくれた縁でしょう」と語る。誕生日がピーターソンと同じであることも、子供の頃からの自慢だという。 当日は、海野がピーターソンを好きになった当時からよく聴いていた『We Get Requests』の楽曲を中心に披露する予定。昨年、生誕100周年を迎えた巨匠に想いを馳せる一夜となりそうだ。 【公演情報】 Tribute to OSCAR PETERSON “We Get Requests revisited” presented by 海野雅威 日時：2026年10月16日（金）開場18:15／開演19:00 会場：I’M A SHOW（東京都千代田区有楽町2-5-1 有楽町マリオン別館7F） 出演：海野雅威トリオ／海野雅威（p）、楠井五月（b）、後藤龍太郎（ds） 料金：全席指定8,200円（税込）※入場時ドリンク代600円別途必要／未就学児入場不可 チケット：チケットぴあ（Pコード：333-678）、イープラス、ローソンチケット（Lコード：75035）、チケットサンライズ（0570-077-020）ほかで発売中 投稿 海野雅威がオスカー・ピーターソンの名盤『We Get Requests』に捧げるトリビュート公演を開催 は ARBAN に最初に表示されました。

items.album: 塚田優｜さらに新たなるイメージ論へ向かって──前川修、佐藤守弘、増田展大編『イメージ論の冒険者たち』（前編）

items.excerpt: 発行日：2026/08/26 発行：東京大学出版会 発行元ウェブサイト：https://www.utp.or.jp/book/b10170978.html イメージにまつわる理論的言説は数多い。そもそも視覚表象を生み出す制作手法はさまざまだし、心に浮かぶ像を指してイメージという言葉が使われたりもする。それゆえ、これについて考えるアプローチも多様な実践が積み重ねられてきた。 『イメージ論の冒険者たち』は「美学芸術学や美術史、写真／映像論、人類学」★といった専門領域において、イメージを論じ成果を上げてきた海外の主要な論者24名について概説された書物である。掲載順は歴史的な通時性を意識しつつも、各部は時代や主題のグラデーションによって編まれている。このことは結果的に、社会やメディアが変化するなかで、同時多発的かつある種の必然をもって方法論が更新されてきたことを窺わせる。しかし同書で飛び交うテクニカルタームは先に挙げた研究領域に加え、哲学・思想領域も含み多岐にわたる。そこで、ここでは美術史、写真／映像論の論者に絞って簡単な系列化を示し、読者の助けとしたい。 まず美術史の方から整理しよう。例えば

items.body: So much has been written about John Coltrane and he's such a widely acknowledged and worshiped figure - one of jazz's top two most iconic artists, along with his once employer Miles Davis - that I don't feel I have anything new to bring to the table. Asked to comment on a favorite Coltrane album, however, I comply, for what it's worth. The first Coltrane album I purchased - a secondhand 1987 CD release - was Live at the Village Vanguard Again , recorded May 28, 1966. Prior to this, I had only heard Coltrane on Miles Davis' Kind of Blue . Village Vanguard Again was a punch in the gut, a puzzle for the mind and the record that won me over to free jazz for good, although it didn't happen overnight. I initially didn't understand what was going on, what to make of it. But was soon repeatedly attracted by the unhinged, torrential sounds unleashed on lengthy versions of "Naima" (a tender ballad with exquisite chords, here exuding rage and sorrow) and "My Favorite Things" (a distinctly lighthearted song from the movie "The Sound of Music", here given a terminally outrageous, or wonderfully out there treatment, according to your inclinations) interspersed with a six-minutes Jimmy Garrison bass solo. Each time I pressed the play button, I was unable to stop listening until the end of the total running time. The album held some arcane truth I couldn't live without anymore. It was music I had to sort out for myself, keep to myself, not music I could share with friends or relatives, let alone spin at parties... The line up had Alice Coltrane on piano, Pharoah Sanders on tenor sax and flute, Rashied Ali on drums, with Coltrane on tenor, soprano and bass clarinet. I was unaware there was a much-loved Coltrane "classic quartet" then, and that this was not it! Some of the Impulse! catalogue was being reissued at that time (the mid-90s), Sanders' "Tauhid" and "Karma" among the batch, both also expanding my musical outlook. Coltrane's albums and archival releases were dropping in quick succession, each new one a mandatory listen. I stumbled on small-priced, worn out LP copies of "Transition" and "Kulu Se Mama" (both recorded in 1965). I was hooked, although none of those albums, and no other Coltrane record I heard after the 1966 live set, had the same definitive, life-altering effect, or reached the same high as that first exposure to the work. Could it be that I had started with a peak, a logical conclusion to what had come before? The music was equal parts perplexing, intimidating, meaningful, dark, luminous, an unrelenting war machine yet brimming with sensitivity, not quite inviting if you were not ready to surrender to its revolutionary approach, but fully uplifting and cleansing if you were. items.body: Label: Endectomorph Records, 2026 Personnel - Kenny Warren: trumpet; Adam Schneit: alto saxophone, clarinet; JP Schlegelmilch: organ; Andrew Dow: electric bass; Nathan Ellman-Bell: drums. Slow Tiger—the jazz quintet of trumpeter Kenny Warren, saxophonist and clarinetist Adam Schneit, organist JP Schlegelmilch, electric bassist Andrew Dow, and drummer Nathan Ellman-Bell—releases its debut album, pointing in many directions with an impeccable flow and assured tones. All its members, with the exception of Ellman-Bell, contribute compositions, filtering influences through the lens of this cohesive collective ensemble. Melodies stick on the ear as the band, whose prior successful collaborations led to the album, leans toward a pop/rock style that easily accommodates jazz-leaning improvisation. Warren's " Powerpuff Backpack " is a tribute to late trumpeter Ron Miles, revealing traces of folk and funk woven into the framework of pop and psychedelic rock infusions. Occasionally, bands like Inspiral Carpets and Jethro Tull come to mind, and Schneit's clarinet explores with effortless inside/outside agility, followed by Warren, who also brings in " Eleven Six ”. Its title comes from the fact that Ellman-Bell plays a cymbal pulsation in eleven while Dow shapes an upbeat six-beat bass figure that provides solid ground for the horn players to interact. They exchange ideas with grip and avant-garde stance, while Schlegelmilch makes the piece soar via hypnotic organ waves and ostinato-leaning textures that add dimension to the music. Schneit, who was born in Portland, Maine, named " Wharf Street " after the street where he grew up. This is a pop tune permeated with a strong 60's vibe, with the composer and Warren intersecting phrases with insouciant power, precision, but also freedom. They also bring this strategy to Schlegelmilch's time-shifting " Maritime Studies ”, which is buttressed by a sluggish beat and cautiously measured unisons. The organist's response to the pandemic's forced pause comes with " Mending the Nets ”, a gentle waltzing ballad moved by sizzling brushes, melancholic melody, and church-like organ sustains. The quintet aligns in relaxed sounds on the title track, " Slow Tiger ", a soulful, melodically seductive piece romanticized by warm R&B colors. It contrasts with Dow's " Funhouse ", whose groove in nine defines the tempo. With the organ illuminating the scenario with crested ripples of sound, the piece morphs into openly avant-garde territory as the horns criss-cross atop the rhythmic net laced by bass and drums. Slow Tiger shows potential, and its debut is a tantalizing promise of more albums to come. Favorite Tracks: 02 - Maritime Studies ► 05 - Eleven in Six ► 07 - Funhouse ► 09 - Slow Tiger

items.body:
IVE are giving DIVE an early look at their next era. Ahead of the release of their new EP Looks Can Kill on 26 October, the K-pop group are teaming up with Spotify for Spotify DIVE ACADEMY, a three-day fan experience taking place at Ark Gangnam, Seoul, from 17 to 19 October.

The event will kick off on 17 and 18 October with an immersive experience inspired by IVE's return as "Girl Heroes". Fans will be able to explore interactive zones, complete special missions, and step into the visuals, energy, and storytelling behind Looks Can Kill.

On 19 October, DIVE ACADEMY will transform into a concert space for a one-night-only live show featuring ANYUJIN, GAEUL, REI, JANGWONYOUNG, LIZ, and LEESEO.

The group will perform fan favourites alongside brand-new material, including the first-ever live performance of the Looks Can Kill title track, which will be released on the same day. Another song from the forthcoming EP will also be performed ahead of its full release on 26 October.

The evening will also feature a talk segment, giving the members an opportunity to share more about their new era and the making of Looks Can Kill.

"We're so grateful to DIVE for always showing up for us on Spotify," shared IVE. "Spotify DIVE ACADEMY is our way of returning that love, and we're thrilled to be working with Spotify to make this happen. We can't wait for DIVE to experience Looks Can Kill with us, and look forward to spending this time together."

For fans unable to attend in Seoul, videos of all performances from the event will subsequently be released exclusively on Spotify. A special video podcast featuring the talk segment will also be made available on the platform.

items.body:
CLOSE YOUR EYES have dropped their fourth mini album, 256th Note, alongside a music video for ‘Drop That!’.

Released on 30 September, the seven-track project follows the K-pop boy group’s 2025 EP blackout and sees them expand their sound through jazz-inspired improvisation, hip-hop, R&B, electropop, bossa nova, and more.

Taking inspiration from the spontaneity of jazz, 256th Note centres on capturing emotions as they occur rather than containing them within conventional forms. Its title references the 256th note, one of the shortest possible moments in music, as a reflection of the fleeting and unfiltered emotions found in everyday life. The album's seven tracks also mirror the seven-note musical scale.

The record opens with ‘Open Your Eyes’, an experimental meeting of jazz improvisation, hip-hop, and R&B featuring pianist Yohan Kim and saxophonist Jacob Scesney. ‘Drop That!’, meanwhile, reinterprets Yoon Si-nae’s ‘이 밤을 즐겁게’, described as an early example of Korean jazz funk, through 1990s street hip-hop and sampling. Its accompanying music video was released alongside the album.

Elsewhere, ‘Vibe Check’ pairs piano, restrained bass, and groovy drums with the members’ vocals and rap, while ‘Slowly Bleed’ moves between contemporary pop, electropop, and alternative R&B. ‘Fool For You’ leans into vintage-inspired R&B and lo-fi textures, while ‘Baby Bossa Nova’, featuring rising R&B artist Joo Hyerin, draws from traditional Brazilian bossa nova.

The album closes with ‘Eternity’, a pop ballad featuring lyrics written with participation from all seven members. Built around acoustic piano and vocals, the song expresses the group’s feelings towards their fans, CLOSER.

Formed through PROJECT7, CLOSE YOUR EYES comprise JEON MINWOOK, MA JINGXIANG, JANG YEOJUN, KIM SUNGMIN, SONG SEUNGHO, KENSHIN, and SEO KYOUNGBAE. Since debuting in April 2025, the group’s debut mini album ETERNALT sold 316,000 copies in its first week, while follow-up Snowy Summer surpassed 200,000 copies on its first day. Their debut focus track, ‘All My Poetry’, also earned the group their first music show win nine days after debut.

Led creatively by executive producer and creative director Lee Haein, CLOSE YOUR EYES continue to broaden their musical palette on 256th Note, turning brief moments of emotion into a seven-track snapshot of the group’s evolving sound.

items.album: Tegh & Adel Poursamadi ~ Bayal بیل
items.excerpt: Gholam-Hossein Sa’edi’s The Mourners of Bayal (1964) remains one of the defining works of modern Iranian literature. Across eight interconnected stories set in the fictional village of Bayal, Sa’edi explores poverty, famine, superstition, grief and death through a world where collective anxiety gradually erodes the distinction between reality and hallucination. items.body: Gholam-Hossein Sa’edi’s The Mourners of Bayal (1964) remains one of the defining works of modern Iranian literature. Across eight interconnected stories set in the fictional village of Bayal, Sa’edi explores poverty, famine, superstition, grief and death through a world where collective anxiety gradually erodes the distinction between reality and hallucination. Equally striking is his attention to sound. The village first announces itself acoustically: dogs bark across rooftops, a bell drifts through the darkness, voices pass from window to window, footsteps punctuate long stretches of silence. Bayal is heard before it is fully seen. Tegh & Adel Poursamadi respond directly to this sonic imagination, drawing not on the individual plots of the stories but on their atmosphere and, above all, on the way Sa’edi constructs the village through listening as much as through sight. Like Ima and After You Left, Bayal بیل grew out of extended improvisational dialogues between Tegh’s electronics and Adel Poursamadi’s violin, viola and traditional Iranian instruments before being carefully sculpted into finished compositions. Yet this third collaboration feels markedly more concentrated than its predecessors. The earlier records moved through broader dynamic contrasts, opening onto expansive drones. Bayal بیل occupies a narrower emotional register, maintaining an almost continuous state of subdued tension lending the album a quiet claustrophobia entirely in keeping with Sa’edi’s village, where lives unfold beneath the weight of forces that remain largely unseen. The opening “Black Stone” establishes that landscape from the outset. Electronics and bowed strings emerge from a dense greyscale haze where instrumental identities remain deliberately obscured. Sounds appear like distant outlines. “The Cow” deepens this sense of collective but undefined presence. Throughout the piece, faint layers of indistinct voices drift through the mix like fragments of overheard conversation, suggesting the murmur of Bayal’s unseen inhabitants as they move through alleys and courtyards beyond the listener’s field of perception. These ghostly traces repeatedly dissolve into silence before returning once more, punctuated by resonant strikes that resemble a ritual gong, briefly gathering the surrounding sounds before allowing them to disperse again. The effect closely recalls Sa’edi’s opening pages, where barking dogs, distant bells and whispered exchanges establish the village long before individual characters emerge. “Toward the Vast Mountain” broadens the perspective without abandoning the prevailing sense of enclosure. Percussive markers recur throughout the piece, functioning almost like ritual or processional signals that quietly propel the music forward through its suspended atmosphere. The composition advances with measured inevitability, each percussive gesture subtly reorienting the listener while strings dissolve into electronic residue. “Pāpākh” is the shortest track on the album and refers to the village dog in Sa’edi’s stories, whose barking, pacing and sudden silences are interpreted by Bayal’s deeply superstitious inhabitants as signs of looming disaster. The music mirrors that heightened state of alertness without becoming illustrative. “Zanguleh” occupies a distinctive place within the album. Whereas much of Bayal treats the strings as part of a larger electroacoustic fabric, here Adel Poursamadi’s playing comes decisively to the foreground. Long, lyrical violin lines unfold over a restrained electronic backdrop whose role is less to obscure than to sustain the instrument’s resonance. The piece carries the emotional weight of a lament, offering the album’s clearest expression of grief without disturbing its overall restraint. After the denser first half, its relative transparency feels almost startling. The closing “Under the Willow Tree” follows naturally, letting suspended harmonics, slowly decaying resonance and carefully measured silences carry the emotional weight long after the final sounds have disappeared. The artwork by Atoosa Pourhosseini extends this vision with remarkable coherence. Anonymous figures occupy the margins of a blurred architectural landscape whose contours dissolve beneath mist, grain and diffuse light. The image perfectly reflects Tegh’s description in the liner notes of approaching Sa’edi’s village from the crest of a hill, where movements remain visible but faces, conversations and individual lives disappear into distance. Like the music itself, it withholds detail in favour of atmosphere, inviting the viewer to contemplate Bayal from the same remove that shapes the album’s entire aesthetic. The affinity between Sa’edi’s prose and Tegh and Poursamadi’s music extends beyond mood. The Mourners of Bayal rarely explains events directly, allowing rumour, fragments of dialogue and sensory details to shape the reader’s understanding. Bayal follows the same logic. Voices remain indistinct, instrumental identities blur, and meaning accumulates through resonance, silence and suggestion rather than narrative illustration. Slow, and foreboding, the album faithfully captures the psychological climate of Sa’edi’s fictional village, translating one of the great works of Iranian literature into an electroacoustic language of emotional depth. photo by Aram Tahmasebi To find out more we reached out directly to Tegh and Poursamadi. Unfortuantely, due to the current situation in Iran, only Tegh was available to answer. Ima ایما imagined post-human communication through a dialogue between acoustic instruments, Iranian traditional music and electronics, while After You Left revolved around memory and uncertainty. With Bayal, the starting point is much more concrete: Gholam-Hossein Sa’edi’s The Mourners of Bayal. Yet the new album also feels more restrained and claustrophobic than the previous two, remaining within a remarkably narrow emotional and dynamic range. Did the world of Sa’edi’s book lead you towards this concentration, or was this already a direction your musical dialogue was taking after After You Left? TEGH: Yes, exactly. The atmosphere of the book had a very strong influence on the sound of the album. IMA was supposed to be the first chapter of a larger project. The idea was to continue the project by working with other musicians from different backgrounds and bring different worldviews into the kind of world-building I had in mind. Unfortunately, this part of the project has not really worked out so far. But after the first album, both of us wanted to continue working together. We wanted to keep the colours, contrasts and freedom that we found in the making of IMA, but develop them further and make them more mature. We felt that this could give us a lot of potential for different kinds of experiments, both in terms of meaning and technique. This led to After You Left, and I think it will also be present in some of the work we release in the future. But Bayal follows a different path. I see it as a completely different chapter. As you said, the album stays within the space it presents initially, and to me, the pieces have very simple forms of storytelling, and these qualities came from our personal reading of the atmosphere of the book. In The Mourners of Bayal, it was not so much the events themselves that affected us, but the atmosphere of the book. I feel that this atmosphere does not change very much throughout the book and stays with you. The political and social uncertainty in the stories, the way everything is unreal and yet it becomes believable, and the fact that the stories seem to be made up of people who feel isolated from each other, maybe strangers to one another, and sometimes even strangers to themselves, all affected us. This idea of alienation is present throughout the book. Even in that small fictional village, society itself can hurt and oppress people. The village is surrounded by poverty, death, illness and hunger. All of these things pushed us towards creating a more claustrophobic and oppressive atmosphere in the album. Maybe “post-defeat” is the right word for it. That is my own personal way of describing it. What struck me while reading The Mourners of Bayal is how much of the village Sa’edi constructs through sound: barking dogs, bells, footsteps, voices travelling between houses, and long stretches of silence often precede any clear understanding of what is happening. Your description of approaching Bayal “from the top of a hill”, hearing cries and other sounds without being able to make out their details, seems closely related to this. Were you consciously responding to Sa’edi’s use of sound and listening as literary devices, and how did you translate that sense of hearing a community at a distance into pieces such as “The Cow” and “Pāpākh”? TEGH: I think that is exactly spot on. Sa’edi’s use of sounds, and the way he created the atmosphere of the book through them, was one of the reasons we chose this specific work. It was not really a conscious decision to respond to this aspect of the book. We never really sat down and talked about choosing this direction. I think we were simply influenced by it to such an extent that it found its way into the album naturally. For example, there is the sound of the bell attached to the empty carriage, coming from far away in the desert. It is mentioned several times throughout the book, often in connection with moments where there is death. The character of this sound, and the meaning it carries, had a strong effect on us and led us towards making “Zanguleh,” which means “bell” in Farsi. It might sound strange or unrelated, but this carriage and its bell also remind me of the cart in Béla Tarr’s The Turin Horse. It creates a very heavy image like that in my mind. The idea of looking at the events from a distance, as if we were standing on top of a hill looking at the village, came from our wish not to create a direct sonic retelling of the book. This perspective allowed us to stay away from simply recreating the events and focus more on what we personally felt from the atmosphere of the book and do our own thing based on that. We wanted to make music based on the effect the book had on both of us, rather than trying to represent the story itself. That is also why we left quite a lot of time between reading the book and starting to make the music. We wanted to forget as many details of the stories as possible and work only with what had remained in our minds, and of course it helped us avoid using the sounds from the book in a more literal way. For example, Papākh, the village dog, is one of the most important characters in the book for me. He has a strong presence, and in a way he observes everything while remaining silent and the villagers have a strange relationship with him. In general, the villagers have very close relationships with animals. The relationship between Mashdi Hassan and his cow, Islam and his goat, Papākh and the villagers, all stayed in my mind. The fact that this is a village suffering from famine, where some people have to go from one village to another to beg or steal food, but they still do not kill their animals for food, was particularly striking to me. The two tracks came out of this. We were more interested in making music out of the feeling we got from the presence of these characters in the story, rather than directly referring to the sound of Papākh or Mashdi Hassan’s cow. You describe the recording process as a series of improvisational dialogues that were subsequently processed and structured, with responding to the concept taking precedence over conventional musical rules. From your perspective, how does that process work? When Adel produces a sound, are you responding to it electronically in real time, or do the more radical transformations happen later during editing and processing? And at what point, for you, does an improvisation cease to be the documentation of a performance and become a composed piece? TEGH: Naturally, this way of working was not something new for Adel and me. We worked in an almost similar way on the two previous albums as well. We talked a lot about the effect the atmosphere of the book had on us. We both knew what elements of it made us hear things, and what kind of feelings we wanted to communicate. But we never really talked about what the tracks should sound like, what their structure should be, or what we should or should not do. The process usually started with one of us doing something, and the other responding to it. This would continue through different sessions, and then we would listen back to the recordings. Sometimes, from a one-hour recording, only one melody and one beat would come out, like in “Toward the Vast Mountain.” We felt that they were close to the concept we had in mind, and then we developed them into a track at a later stage. “Zanguleh” and “The Black Stone,” for example, both came out of the recording of a single session. A lot of the changes and processing happened afterwards, especially the processing of the sounds and shaping the forms. This was important for bringing the different sounds together and making them feel like they belonged to the same world. One of the main reasons for this is that I am honestly not a very good improviser. In many of the sessions, instead of being able to immediately reach the sound I had in mind, I was more often just leaving some kind of indication of what I wanted to reach later. For example going back to “Toward the Vast Mountain,” I had already written a beat for the melody in the improvisation, but the sounds and the pattern were quite different from what you hear on the final track. As for the last part of your question, it is a little difficult to explain. There is a point during the process when you suddenly think, “Ah, we found it. This is becoming something.” It is a moment when you find each other, everything starts to work together, and you feel that you have reached something. For me, that is the point where I can change the way I look at the material. I can stop thinking only about finding sounds or making the improvisation work, and start looking at what we have from the perspective of storytelling and how the idea can develop, where it can go, and how it can become a composition. artwork by Atoosa Pour Hosseini One of the most affecting moments for me is “Zanguleh”, because Adel’s violin suddenly becomes much more exposed and lyrical after spending much of the record partially submerged within the electroacoustic texture; it almost functions as a lament before “Under the Willow Tree” carries the record towards silence. Across Ima ایما , After You Left and now Bayal بیل, has your understanding of the relationship between strings and electronics changed? Are you increasingly interested in making it difficult to tell where one ends and the other begins, and what made you choose to break that ambiguity so strikingly on “Zanguleh”? TEGH: Absolutely. One of the things I personally question now after several years of working with Adel is exactly this. In IMA, and to some extent in After You Left, there is still quite a clear distance between the sound of the instruments and the electronics. Maybe you could say that the meeting between my world and Adel’s world did not always become a third world, something that was neither completely mine nor completely his. I think this improved in After You Left, and we got even closer to it with Bayal. I would not necessarily say that I am trying to make it difficult to tell the sounds apart. What is more important to me is that, in the composition, sound design and all the different stages of the process, I do not treat the instruments and electronics as separate things. I also try not to let the source of a sound decide how I treat it. I want to reach a point where by the end of the process there is a kind of continuity between the sounds, and they feel like they belong to the same family. It does not matter whether you can recognise where each sound comes from, what matters is that when these different sonic characters are put together, they do not feel like they have been taken from completely different worlds and simply placed next to each other like a collage. As for “Zanguleh,” as I mentioned earlier, the track was influenced by the sound of the bell coming from far away in the story. In my personal interpretation, I connect this sound with death, not as an ending, but as something that has been staying with you. As you said, that section was meant to work almost like a lament. It is actually a mourning. Our idea was for the track to reach a point where it could finally break out and mourn freely, and that is where the track ended up. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.album: The Fall Reveal Final Studio Album, ‘Post Script’

items.body: The LP has been built from archival vocal recordings of late frontman Mark E Smith dating from 2001 to 2014 The Fall are releasing their "definitive" final studio album, Post Script. Coming nine years on from 2017's New Facts Emerge, the band's 32nd studio LP was built from archival vocal recordings of late frontman Mark E Smith dating from 2001 to 2014. The musical backing was completed by long-time collaborators and former manager / producers Ed Blaney and Simon Archer. The nine-track record brings together garage rock and spoken word pieces, according to a press release. It will be released on CD and vinyl formats. Cog Sinister will release Post Script on 2 October 2026. ... The post The Fall Reveal Final Studio Album, ‘Post Script’ appeared first on The Quietus.

That, for me, is the first seconds of Pugnello, and it hardly relents from there. Dara Kiely comes in screaming on ‘The Angelus’, all scalded shriek, hollering about Bananas in Pyjamas and Gary Lineker as crisp maniac. The track pitches somewhere between Lightning Bolt and a ten-thousand-mile thundercloud, Adam Faulkner’s rolls hurtling underneath like Swans at triple speed. The title rewires the Angelus, RTÉ’s evening bell, into a street preacher bawling in tongues. That opener alone would underline everything they’ve been since France 98... items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — "All-Bumm" is a title that doesn't quite speak for itself; it is worth clarifying, then, that Achtzehn Karat Gold has little to nothing to do with Krautrock. To begin with, the lineup, Lothar Meid (bass and vocals), J�rg Evers and Klaus Ebert (guitars), and Keith Forsey, served as the backing band for pop and country-tinged singer Peter Maffay on his album Omen (1973). Confusion may have arisen because the members of Achtzehn Karat Gold also participated in Amon D��l II's Vive La Trance!. As for the album itself, it leans toward ballads and glam rock reminiscent of Udo Lindenberg, which is by no means a bad thing; it is well-crafted, though the track "Flying" does take off a bit and could arguably be linked to the aforementioned Krautrock genre.The same could be said of "Goldrush": the interplay between the two guitars and the bass creates an aura of intrigue, mystery, and danger. However, "Star-Eyed" features vocals reminiscent of Marc Bolan and a sound akin to T. Rex, while "Dr. Stein" and "I Am Just a Man" venture into country and rhythm and blues territory, recalling the stylistic shift of another band, Improved Sound Limited, which briefly flirted with Krautrock before changing direction in 1973. The album encompasses everything from solid German-style rock 'n' roll (in the vein of Udo Lindenberg) and glam to distinctly pop-oriented tracks like "If My Guru Would Know" and the jazzy, Lou Reed-esque "Cool"; it is a well-crafted, eclectic record, though it falls short of achieving true Krautrock status.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Leviathan, an Italian outsider on the neo-prog scene who emerged in the late 1980s in the shadow of the genre's leading acts (Marillion, IQ, Pendragon, Pallas?), returns today in top form and highly motivated with *Heartquake/Redux*, a re-recorded version of their debut album, *Heartquake* (1988), while also planning the upcoming release of a brand-new album titled *Testudo*, which we'll be sure to discuss further when the time comes.A true manifesto of hyper-melodic, sensitive, and energetic neo-prog?with its sights set on the best of Genesis from the '78?'80 period?*Heartquake* is a resounding success, despite having been recorded under precarious conditions (in barely a week and on a shoestring budget). Andrea Amici, the keyboardist and principal composer of the current Leviathan lineup, didn't join the band until their second album, *Bee Yourself* (1990)?a record that's nearly impossible to find these days and deserves at least a reissue. Amici quickly became the principal composer alongside singer-songwriter Alex Brunori and longtime drummer (who also plays bass) Andrea Monetta. In this role, Amici appears to be the architect of the band's musical shift, moving from the English-flavored neo-prog of *Heartquake* to the more personal RPI sound of the third album, *Volume* (1997), with Paolo Antinori replacing Brunori on vocals. Since the album failed to achieve commercial or critical success?which, in my opinion, is regrettable and unfair (Volume deserves to be revisited and vindicated if necessary), Amici and Monetta then put the "monster" to sleep.It wasn't until the mid-2000s that Leviathan resurfaced, with two dazzling, lengthy suites composed by Amici in the vein of modern symphonic RPI, which were incorporated into projects by the Finnish collective Colossus: "Un Pensiero e Sempre Libero" (26:34) in 2005 and "Vecchi Giochi" (21:00) in 2008. These two grandiose pieces, sung in Italian (by Paolo Antinori on the first, then Pierfrancesco Drago and Rossella Salvucci on the second), are teeming with a succession of haunting melodic themes linked together with disconcerting brilliance, evoking the enchanting power of Samurai of Prog's finest moments; they likely represent Leviathan's most remarkable work to date.Since then, we've heard nothing more from Leviathan, but we've been able to console ourselves by following the career of Andrea Amici, who has never stopped composing and producing albums of primarily instrumental music, spanning genres as varied as classical piano (Romantic or Baroque) and electro, without ever completely severing ties with his love for progressive rock. Electronica was very much on the agenda last year with his latest solo album, *The Eye of the Storm*, performed entirely on keyboards?a result quite close to the best and most memorable recent work by Rick Wakeman and Tangerine Dream, enhanced with an irresistible touch of sunny RPI.Probably?and quite legitimately?capitalizing on the current resurgence in popularity and interest in neo-prog among prog fans, Amici and Monetta?this time with the return of singer Brunori?have managed to resurrect Leviathan from its still-hot ashes. But before presenting us with their brand-new compositions, the Roman band chose to remind us of their legacy with *Heartquake/Redux*, a reinterpretation of *Heartquake* that benefits from a bit more recording time and modern technological resources, designed to amplify the album's original qualities. The original compositions thus take on the luster they deserved, stripped of the overly 80s-style sound of the original. With the help of two other heavyweights of Italian prog?guitarist-producer Fabio Serra, leader of R�senkre�tz, and bassist Andrea Castelli, currently involved in the comeback of Il Rovescio Della Medaglia?Leviathan showcases one of its strongest sides: the guitars, as lyrical as ever, have become sharper; the keyboard sound has gained in clarity and maturity; Monetta's playing is more subtle yet just as powerful; and Brunori's voice hasn't suffered too much from the passage of time. One can only regret the absence of the last two tracks from *Heartquake*. Indeed, the very Hackett-esque instrumental "There's Only Watershade", and "In the Dream of Up We Quake!," a studio live recording (featuring Amici on keyboards) from the *Bee Yourself* sessions in '89, which was later included as a bonus track on the CD edition of *Heartquake*.But is this little facelift enough to make *Heartquake/Redux* a must-have for those who own and appreciate the original version? I'll leave it to the readers concerned to come up with an answer. For everyone else, *Heartquake/Redux* is an excellent opportunity to discover one of the jewels of Italian symphonic neo-prog?a band with undeniable potential and obvious artistic qualities, but one that history and a lack of commercial success have not sufficiently brought to light.For my part, I hope that Testudo, their next studio album, will combine the technical prowess of *Heartquake/Redux* with the inventiveness and melodic exuberance of the two suites Leviathan released in the 2000s.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Since its inception in 2015, the ESP musical project of Tony Lowe has released almost one album a year. In 2023, we had discovered the symphonic Reverie (in French but without accent) where contrary to his habit, the english multi instrumentalist was in the stand alone position, including vocals. Obviously, the inspiration failure is not for now. In 2024, in partnership with the singer-songwriter Louise Browne and her soft voice, Lowe has offered us Silver Waves ~ Astral Dreams, his ninth album under this band name, always illustrated by the essential Cheryl Stringall (she also holds the keyboard - strings on two tracks while dealing with the Sunn Creative label).From "Curious Dreamer - The Dreaming Field", Tony Lowe takes up business where he left off in 2020 after the excellent Phenomena: a mix of bright and languid pop-prog ("Curious Dreamer") and elegant instrumental jazzy prog ("The Dreaming Field"), the combination of two styles in the same piece seems a bit artificial here, comments that had already been noted on the previous record. "Silver Waves" (7:39) is most convincing, especially for its sensitive melody and its mesmerizing recitative set on a slow tempo that eventually accelerates in bizarre technoid rhythmic, the transition between the two parts being once again obvious. Sung in angelic voice by the Londoner Louise on a slow rhythm, �Glorious Persuasion� (7:40) begins once again with a beautiful relaxing melody, Tony being an example in this field.And for the third time in a row, which is becoming a formula, almost a gimmick, the rhythm suddenly accelerates, always so abrupt, to give way to a kind of irresistible electro discoid rock that brings us in the atmosphere of the 80s at the time of the band Propaganda. To put it more clearly, it seems that "Glorious Persuasion" is made of two separate pieces without really hurting the listener's enjoyment. �High Inspiration - It Wasn't a Dream� is the same mixed formula but this time in reverse. There are two distinct parts and no apparent connection in the same piece but the part of the song is placed before the staccato allegro, illuminated by discreet interventions of a Tony Banks-like synthetizer, followed by a dreamy ballad full of feeling. �The Brightest Star� (5:55), pretty country-pop feel good, with a soft and light atmosphere, enjoys a floydian guitar solo on a Hammond organ background that takes it into a whole other dimension. On "Life Pod" (4:34), a dynamic instrumental that would not have disavowed Alan Parson, the organ is found in a more important jazzy role, supported by an overflowing bass, mixed with love, played by Steve Gee as an exceptional guest. Silver Waves ~ Astral Dreams has reserved his best part for the end: �Love Returns� (5:45), a ravaging slow as in the most beautiful days of the most romantic Barclay James Harvest. Perhaps the most beautiful melody ever composed by Tony, who was never stingy, a positive music of the kind to send us back to the infinite in which our mind is lost while listening to it, daughter of the spiritual world, illuminated by the day of heaven, animated by a divine breath. Silver Waves ~ Astral Dreams is not the most progressive album of ESP Project but it's one of the most enchanting and sophisticated, sublimated by a Louise Browne in weightlessness. And we are already hoping for the next one to come in 2025, a promise of soothing melodic pleasures, if Tony Lowe's magical creativity does not falter.(previously published in Big Bang # 127 (prog french magazine))

items.body: Review by ChuChu — One of my favourite albums of all time and, in my opinion everyone who likes the later more proggy Floyd stuff should give it a listen. The album mostly written by Syd Barrett, features tons of experimental and psychedelic stuff that no other album by Pink Floyd and any other band replicates. Astronomy Domine is a great opener track with a great instrumental part in the middle, Flaming and Matilda Mother evoke in me the feeling of childhood, Interstellar Overdrive and Lucifer Sam are really catchy psychedelic tracks and The Gnome feels like reading "Lord Of The Rings" and "Hobbit" all over again.I love this album, it has a great selection of tracks and a really fun vibe to it, would recommend this album to someone who wants to get into Pink Floyd but only knows "The Dark Side Of The Moon" and "Wish You Were Here"

items.body: Review by yarstruly — TAKEN FROM MY REVIEW ON MY BLOG "SCOTT'S SONG BY SONG SPOTLIGHTS" Which has links for purchasing, and more.Clicked 5, but really a 4.75The prolific UK composer and keyboardist Clive Nolan may be best known as the keyboardist in Pendragon and Arena (see my spotlight on Arena on this blog), but he has really done so much more! He is also part of the bands Shadowland and (formerly) Strangers on a Train. Furthermore, he has a bachelors and masters degree from the London College of Music, and has written, produced and staged musical theater productions with his Caamora Theatre Company. He has also been a part of numerous collaborations, including three albums with Oliver Wakeman. The man is a musical mastermind. His latest solo project "Song of the Winter Throne", due to be released on Friday October 2, is a massive undertaking. It consists of a main CD and a Bonus CD totaling approximately 2 hours in length. The subject of this concept album is H�kon H�konarson, aka Hakon IV, or Hakon the Old. He was a Norwegian King born in 1204, and reigning between 1217-1263, a whopping 46 years! (Interestingly, a Norwegian musician, whose band The Windmill also has been given a Spotlight, Morten L. Clason assisted Clive Nolan in engineering the album.) As H�kon H�konarson ascended to the crown at the age of 13, he was initially King in name only and regent Earl Skule B�rdsson pulled the strings until H�kon reached adulthood. However, B�rdsson would later declare himself king even as H�kon was still on the throne. The true king would have the usurper executed in 1240 and continued his reign. This execution put a close to the long Norwegian Civil War into which H�kon himself was born. His reign is considered to be the zenith of medieval Norwegian civilization.There are a large number of people involved in bringing Clive's musical vision to life. The primary instrumentalists are: Clive Nolan - Keyboards, Orchestration and ProgrammingMirko Sangrigoli - Drums and GuitarsStig Andre' Clason - GuitarsMorten L. Clason - FluteHennie Hagen Johnsen - GuitarsArnfinn Isaksen - BassMeanwhile, the main cast members are:Gemma Ashley - SolveigRyan Morgan - H�kon H�konarsonChristina Booth - TyraClive Nolan - Music & LyricsNatalie Barnett - Freja Ross Andrews - The StorytellerAdditionally, there are 38 members of the chorus, so I will include a picture of that page of the CD booklet, so they get the credit they deserve. (Scroll to the bottom.)Many readers will surely notice the name of Christina Booth, the amazing vocalist of the Band Magenta. Stig Andre' Clason is the son of the aforementioned Morten Clason, who also plays with The Windmill.The album comes courtesy of Anne-Claire of Bad Dog Promotions. As always, I am free to call it as I hear it, and I receive no additional compensation. As per my usual method, this is a cold listen.Obviously, this is a massive production, so let me get on with it and dive into the music!Track 1 - Born in Shadow (3:14)This begins with some sound effects and the narration from Ross Andrews, in dramatic style. Equally dramatic music follows, creating an overture for what is to come. The massive chorus is put to use on this, yet the drums and underlying rhythm keep a rock feel in the music, despite how symphonic it is. A massive opener!Track 2 - The Woman from Varteig (4:34)This begins without a pause from the opener, but the music drops to a drone. Ross Andrews continues the story, discussing the circumstances of H�kon H�konarson's birth. Christina Booth as Tyra sings first, and is joined by both of the other women in their characters. They sing of how they will protect the boy to ensure the safety of the would-be king. Being born "illegitimately" during a civil war was a great danger to the boy. The vocals are flawless and set the tone magnificently. Track 3 - Wolves Gather (3:03)A traditional drum and sound effects accompany Ross Andrews' narration, then foreboding music with chanting enters and then Gemma Ashley and Natalie Barnett sing beautifully in harmony. Power chords from the guitars help to accent the mood of the music.Track 4 - Flight of the Birkebeiners (3:27)The Storyteller continues the saga, then the dramatic music takes over. The string parts are somewhat reminiscent of the piano part on "The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway" (Genesis). The chorus joins in making the scene even more dramatic. Fantastic piece of classical-level music.Track 5 - The Hidden Prince (4:12)The Storyteller continues, then H�kon (Ryan Morgan) joins in for the first time. He sings of the circumstances of his upbringing in the woodlands. A very engaging song!Track 6 - Ritual of Faith (4:29)Ross continues the story, telling of the "Trial by Ordeal" that his mother underwent to prove the boy's lineage and suitableness to become the King. The chorus, along with Tyra and Freja bring the tale to life. A powerful song, fantastically delivered by the amazing cast of musicians Nolan has assembled. Track 7 - The Puppet Crown (4:22)The Storyteller tells us how H�kon was King in Name Only, ruled over by Regents. H�kon sings that it is "The Puppet Crown" along with Solveig. The chorus tells us:This is the puppet Crown,I wear the gold, I wear the gown,But another wields the power,A hand on the hilt of a sword unbound?However, the last line of the song is:"But one day?I'll cut the strings!"The song is probably the catchiest one so far, with lots of power.Track 8 - Fractured Throne (3:40)This song tells of how even after H�kon was King in his own right, his former Regent, Skule B�rdsson, even after being given the title of Duke (the first Duke in Norway), still tried to usurp the Crown and declared himself King?spoilers, It didn't end well for Skule. All of the main characters participate in this song. The song has an air of darkness about it, but H�kon is resolute in saying "I am King, I rule alone!"Track 9 - The Sword and the Fire (6:04)Of course the storyteller starts this one off, and then H�kon and the Chorus perform together on this one. This one describes the civil war battles that finally unified H�kon's power as Skule is executed. Musically there are some odd meters here. Ryan Morgan hits a fantastic sustained high note about halfway through that is fantastic. The resolution portion of the song is so powerful! At the end of this track is the first full stop in the music.Track 10 - A Kingdom Rejoices (3:23)The storyteller describes the full coronation of H�kon as recognized by The Pope, and Norway's rejoicing, and H�kon's successes. There is some joyous music between narrative sections in a quick 6-8. Fun track!Track 11 - Frost Upon the Longships (4:38)Now that H�kon has cemented his position as King, he led Norway to become the most powerful nation in the Northern Seas. The refrains of the song are sung with only H�kon and the male members of the chorus, giving a very masculine sound. The tempo is moderately slow. There are big power chords and heavy drumming along with the orchestrations.Track 12 - Storms and Wrecks (3:51)This one describes the conflict over certain islands that broke out with rival Scotland. Mid-tempo, with some flute-like interludes. This one features Gemma Ashley's beautiful voice as Solveig. Wonderful performance!Track 13 - The King in the Mist (4:52)This is a mid-tempo bittersweet ballad, based on acoustic guitar, with H�kon describing his final days in the Orkney Islands during the Scottish Expedition. "Raise up the King in the mist, I'm ready to go home?"Track 14 - The Winter ThroneAfter the opening from the Storyteller, this one goes into a riff that sounds like a Symphonic Power Metal song. The chorus performs in Norse. It closes out the story harkening us to always remember the great reign of H�kon H�konarson!Bonus CD [Note- I have no real information about these tracks as to how they fit into the saga.]:Track 1 - We Are the Storm and The Iron (6:05)This seems to be an alternate version of "The Sword and the Fire". The lyrics are a bit different. The refrains are in English as opposed to Norse. Track 2 - Back to Varteig (4:40)One of the ladies is speaking in Norse, as opposed to The Storyteller with dramatic music accompanying. She then sings what appears to be a lullaby, in English. The other female leads join in harmony.Track 3 - Strings and Necks (3:20)I think the title refers to the guitar solo in this track. Well actually both electric and acoustic guitar solos. An outstanding (almost) instrumental track that lets the guitarists stretch out and be featured. There is a bit of a chant from one of the ladies near the end of the track. Track 4 - Crowns Across Time (4:31)This seems to be an alternate version of "The Puppet Crown". This one seems to be a little more basic in the arrangement/production; more stripped down.Track 5 - In the Mist (4:51)Once again, one of the ladies is speaking in Norse at the beginning. After that it is an alternate version of "The King in the Mist" in a more basic form, but it's sung from the perspective of one of the female characters. It seems that Clive changed his mind in regards to the point of view on some parts of the story. She speaks in Norse again at the end of the track.Track 6 - The First Prince (4:00)This is an alternate version of "The Hidden Prince" without The Storyteller at the beginning. Also a more stripped down version. I am thinking that many of these are demos/early versions. The harmonies are wonderful, only accompanied by a drumbeat at one point.Track 7 - Ritual of Faith Ceremonial Mix (3:36)No Storyteller at the beginning. There is only a basic drum accompaniment, so the vocals really pop out! The vocals are absolutely pristine!Track 8 - More Wreckage (3:50)It begins in Norse with one of the ladies speaking, as some of the others have. An alternate version of "Storms and Wrecks".Track 9 - Purely Instrumental Flight (3:33)Despite the title, I hear some "throat singing" as this begins. There are gothic choir sounds as well. This is the backing track from "Flight of the Birkebeiners" without the lead vocals. It's an impressive piece of music either way!Track 10 - Puppet Frets (4:32)The guitarists get the spotlight on this version of "The Puppet Crown".Track 11 - Frost Upon the Longships - Backing Track (4:01)The title tells you all you need to know!Track 12 - The Narration Fireside Mix (8:13)This is all of the "Storyteller" narration combined into one track. It recapitulates the opening stanza at the end, to give it a sense of completion.OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:This is begging to be staged! If anyone is capable of doing that, it is certainly Clive Nolan! With his experience in leading Caamora Theatre Company, I would not be surprised if that is already the plan. This is grand musical storytelling at its finest! The arrangements, performances, playing, singing and production are all flawless! If you are a fan of "Jeff Wayne's Musical Version of The War of the Worlds", then this is right up your alley! Three years ago, in September of 2023, I gave that album a 4 out of 5 Stars (80%). I like this one even better than that, but it is not quite one of my absolute favorites of 2026. Don't get me wrong, this is a production on an absolutely epic scale and it is achieved magnificently! Many kudos to Clive Nolan for what he and his massive cast of collaborators have accomplished here! However, I am giving it a near perfect 4.75 out of 5 (95%) as there are a few albums out there that appeal to my tastes a little more in 2026. I am certain that some will unabashedly give it a perfect score, and I certainly wouldn't fault them for it! Again, as I keep saying, 2026 has been an amazing year and prog, and almost on a daily basis, I get offered even more potentially amazing albums to review. This album certainly reinforces my assertion that 2026 will go down as one of the most amazing years in the modern prog era.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Lucro Sucio; Los Ojos del Vacio' is the unexpected, overly mysterious, and definitely dream-likeninth studio album by The Mars Volta, released in April of 2025 through Clouds Hill, serving as thefollow-up to 2022's self-titled LP and its acoustic follow-up from the following year. The reformedband features an interesting lineup that sees masterminds Omar Rodriguez Lopez and Cedric Bixler-Zavala joined by Omar's brother Marcel, who plays some keyboards and is involved in the engineeringof the album, versatile female drummer Philo Tsoungui, keyboardist-saxophonist Leo Genovese, andbass player Josh Moreau, a session player with some serious experiences in well-known rock andalternative bands. As for the album in question, 'Lucro Sucio' is an 18-track labyrinth of hazy andethereal synth soundscapes, indulgent jazzy interludes, and meditative psychedelic melodies,elevated by the iconic voice of Bixler-Zavala, who sounds as solid as ever on this LP.What I really like about this record is how the gently protruding latin rock elements from the twoprevious albums have been preserved on 'Lucro Sucio', but with an artsy, cryptic undercurrent. Thereis also a very generous interpolation of various synths that allows the pristine production to shinethrough, while the tranquil, ambient tones that prevail give the collection a somewhat ominous, hazyfeel. Leaning more towards trippy art rock than prog, 'Lucro Sucio' is not necessarily the mostsubstantial Mars Volta album, especially when compared to some of the band's intimidating andmaximalist early classics. It almost feels as if Omar and Cedric are attempting to capture theopposite of what their early releases had represented, and to be honest, there is something daringand novel in such a risky experiment. The album is innovative yet accessible, with an abundance ofbeautifully composed electronic-laden psychedelic pieces like 'Reina Tormenta/Enlazan lasTinieblas', 'Cue the Sun/Alba del Orate', 'Poseedora de Mi Sombra', 'Vocifer�', and 'Un Disparo alVac�o'.The finale is a little too monotonous for my taste (that would be last five tracks), but the factthat the entire work weaves through like one continuous piece makes it more diverse and immersivethan the band's 2022 self-titled release. Nevertheless, 'Lucro Sucio' is tame and ethereal, whichfor longtime listeners of the band represents just one side of The Mars Volta's expansive studiosound.

items.body: Review by martindavey87 — 'Pulse For a Graveheart' is the second studio album by Italian progressive metal band Mind Key. Released in 2009, the group has shown a significant improvement over the four years that had passed since their debut, with stronger writing and a better-sounding production, a high quality is consistently maintained throughout the album. One major change in the bands line-up is the addition of new vocalist Aurelio Fierro. Former singer Marco Basile had a fantastic range, but at times his voice seemed quite tinny, whereas Fierro's powerful voice fits more comfortably with the music, adapting for soft, melodic sections or heavier, more aggressive parts. As expected with this genre, the musicianship is fantastic as always, featuring plenty of great interplay between all the instruments, with particular praise going to guitarist Emanuele Colella and keyboardist Dario De Cicco. There's also guest appearances by the likes of keyboard maestro Derek Sherinian, Tom Englund (of Everygrey fame), and Winger's Reb Beach.With highlights including 'Sunset Highway', 'Dead Fame Hunter', 'The Seventh Seal', 'Citizen of Greed' and 'Graveheart', this is a solid progressive metal album and sure to please all fans of the genre.

items.body: “Curandera” opens Bestiaria with a healer giving instructions. “Niña / Escucha cómo tu cuerpo te habla,” sings Ana Karen G. Barajas of Karen y Los Remedios: girl, listen to how your body talks to you. The song comes from Karen’s own illness and from the women in her family who saw her through it with advice, recipes and limpias, the cleansing rituals Mexican grandmothers pass down. The curandera in the lyric hands the work back to the girl, telling her to listen to her body and to how her soul breathes, and warns her that “Cuando callas te guardas / Lo malo / Y lo bueno”: stay silent and you keep the bad in with the good. Karen, guitarist Guillermo Berbeyer and Mexico City producer Jiony set it as a dark cumbia over a low bass and a steady beat. Trombone and cowbell sit around her voice, an organ hangs at the back of the mix, and in the instrumental breaks synth and guitar lines take over. She lives in Hong Kong now, a long way from the Mexico City she was born in and the Guanajuato she grew up in. Bestiaria, the follow-up to 2023’s Silencio, builds its twelve songs around twelve figures, among them the agave goddess Mayahuel and the Fates of “Las Moiras”. “Curandera” is the fourth single from it. Listen to “Curandera” HERE and pre-order Bestiaria, out on 9 October via ZZK Records, following THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Karen y los Remedios – Curandera appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: A Rammstein producer, a string section and a major label: Covenant made their fifth album under different conditions from the four before it. Ka2 Music, a division of Sony Music, released “Northern Light” in Europe on 30 September 2002, and Metropolis Records followed in the United States on 8 October 2002. The Swedish futurepop trio from Helsingborg had spent its previous albums on the independents Memento Materia, Off Beat and Dependent Records. The album turns 24 this year. Jacob Hellner, who had produced Rammstein’s first three albums, produced “Northern Light” after pre-production by the band. Stefan Glaumann mixed “Call the Ships to Port”, “Bullet”, “Invisible & Silent” and “Prometheus”, Ulf Kruckenberg mixed the other seven tracks, and Björn Engelmann mastered. Axwell added programming, Ricard Nettermalm played live drums and Lizzie Zachrisson sang backing vocals on “Bullet”, “Scared” and “Atlas”. The Stockholm Session Orchestra, arranged and conducted by Joakim Milder, played the strings on “Invisible & Silent”, and Ulf Ivarsson played bass on “Atlas”. Joakim Montelius wrote the lyrics for seven tracks and Eskil Simonsson for five. “Rising Sun” carries a co-writing credit for American techno producer Steve Stoll and uses elements of his tracks “Reciproheat” and “Falling Down”. The eleven tracks run 58 minutes and 39 seconds: “Monochrome”, “Call the Ships to Port”, “Bullet”, “Invisible & Silent”, “Prometheus”, “We Stand Alone”, “Rising Sun”, “Winter Comes”, “We Want Revolution”, “Scared” and “Atlas”. Ka2 issued the album as a standard CD, a limited digipak CD and a numbered gatefold double vinyl of 1,000 copies. The vinyl added four tracks not on the CD: club versions of “Bullet” and “Call the Ships to Port”, “Bullet (Funky Indian)” and “Don’t Go”. The Sony CDs carried copy protection and a label reading “Auf PC/Mac nicht abspielbar”, and early copies came with a sticker listing the “Northern Light” tour dates. Metropolis pressed its US edition as an HDCD. Two singles bracketed the release. “Call the Ships to Port” came out on 12 August 2002 as a CD maxi with remixes by Oliver Klitzing, Christian Morgenstern, Kaylab and Thomas P. Heckmann, and reached number 93 on the German singles chart. “Bullet” followed on 9 December 2002 with an Ellen Allien “Flow Mix”, a Le Dust Sucker mix and the otherwise unreleased “Atom Heart”. A “Bullet” DVD with the video and making-of footage appeared in January 2003. About Covenant Eskil Simonsson, Joakim Montelius and Clas Nachmanson, three school friends from Helsingborg in southern Sweden, started making music together in 1986 after seeing Front 242’s first Scandinavian show, and took the name Covenant in 1988. They built a studio in Nachmanson’s bedroom while studying in Lund. Their first released track, “The Replicant”, appeared on a Memento Materia compilation in 1992, and the label issued the debut album “Dreams of a Cryotank” in December 1994. Off Beat signed the trio in 1995 after a German festival appearance. “Sequencer” followed in May 1996, with the “Stalker” single and a tour alongside Haujobb and Steril later that year. San Francisco label 21st Circuitry handled the United States, where the “Theremin” EP appeared in 1997. “Europa” came out in April 1998. When Off Beat closed in 1999, Covenant moved to the newly formed Dependent Records in Germany and SubSpace Communications in Sweden, while Metropolis Records took over the American catalogue. “United States of Mind” appeared in February 2000, with the “Der Leiermann” single, and the live album “Synergy” followed in November 2000. “Northern Light” moved the band to Sony’s Ka2 division in 2002. By then Montelius lived in Barcelona and Simonsson in Berlin, with Nachmanson still in Helsingborg. “Skyshaper” arrived in March 2006, and in March 2007 the band announced that Nachmanson would no longer tour, with Daniel Myer of Haujobb taking his place on stage. The tour film “In Transit” came out on DVD in October 2007 and confirmed Nachmanson’s departure. “Modern Ruin” followed in January 2011, the first album with Myer as a full member, and Daniel Jonasson joined the live line-up that year. Andreas Catjar joined in 2013 on keyboards and guitar, playing on “Leaving Babylon” in September 2013 and on “The Blinding Dark”, released on 4 November 2016 after the “Sound Mirrors” single. Montelius told Side-Line at the time that the line-up had grown to five, and that “Covenant’s basic principle is to always evolve: change is the only constant.” The band handed out the “Fieldworks: Exkursion” EP on its German tour in February 2019 and released a cover of Yazoo’s “Winter Kills” in December 2020. Andreas Catjar-Danielsson died on 29 July 2024 after a long illness, and the charity “Andreas EP”, recorded with Simonsson, came out on Dependent Records on 17 October 2025. Twenty-four years after Ka2 pressed it, “Northern Light” remains the album that brought “Call the Ships to Port” and “Bullet” into the Covenant catalogue.

items.body: The Mission’s tenth studio album, “Another Fall from Grace,” turns 10 this year. The English gothic rock band released the record on 30 September 2016 through Eyes Wide Shut Recordings. Wayne Hussey has described the album as a link between The Sisters of Mercy’s “First and Last and Always” and The Mission’s own debut, “God’s Own Medicine,” citing his return to 12-string guitar as part of that connection. “Another Fall from Grace” runs just over an hour across twelve tracks and was produced by Wayne Hussey and Tim Palmer, with Palmer also mixing at ’62 Studios in Austin, Texas, and mastering by James Bacon. All songs were written by Hussey, except “Another Fall From Grace,” “Can’t See the Ocean for the Rain” and “Valaam,” co-written with Simon Hinkler. The album features a run of guest vocalists: Julianne Regan on the title track and closer “Phantom Pain,” Ville Valo of HIM on “Met-Amor-Phosis,” Gary Numan on “Within the Deepest Darkness (Fearful),” Evi Vine on “Can’t See the Ocean for the Rain” and “Never’s Longer Than Forever,” and Martin Gore of Depeche Mode on backing vocals for “Only You & You Alone.” Duke Garwood contributes alto clarinet and saxophone on “Phantom Pain.” The tracklist runs “Another Fall From Grace,” “Met-Amor-Phosis,” “Within the Deepest Darkness (Fearful),” “Blood on the Road,” “Can’t See the Ocean for the Rain,” “Tyranny of Secrets,” “Never’s Longer Than Forever,” “Bullets & Bayonets,” “Valaam,” “Jade,” “Only You & You Alone” and “Phantom Pain.” The album peaked at number 38 on the UK Albums Chart, number 2 on the UK Rock & Metal Albums Chart and number 49 in Germany. A deluxe edition followed in 2017 under the title “The Complete Another Fall From Grace,” adding a bonus disc and DVD. About The Mission The Mission formed in Leeds, England, in 1986 after Wayne Hussey and Craig Adams left The Sisters of Mercy. The pair recruited guitarist Simon Hinkler and drummer Mick Brown, initially performing as The Sisterhood before settling on The Mission. The band signed to Mercury/Phonogram’s Chapter 22 offshoot and released its debut single, “Serpent’s Kiss,” in 1986, followed by the debut album “God’s Own Medicine” in 1986, which reached the UK top ten. Through the late 1980s and 1990s, The Mission released a run of albums including “Children” (1988), “Carved in Sand” (1990), “Masque” (1992) and “Neverland” (1995), with several lineup changes affecting the rhythm section while Hussey remained the constant frontman. The band went on hiatus multiple times before reconvening for later studio work, including “God Is a Bullet” (2007), “The Brightest Light” (2013) and “Another Fall from Grace” in 2016, the latter recorded with Craig Adams back on bass and Mike Kelly on drums alongside Hussey and Hinkler. “Another Fall from Grace” brought together guest contributions from Gary Numan, Martin Gore, Ville Valo and Julianne Regan, produced by Tim Palmer and released through Eyes Wide Shut Recordings. Ten years on, the album stands as one of the band’s most complete studio statements of its post-2000s period.

items.album: Nitzer Ebb’s ‘Ebbhead’ turns 35 on 30 September
items.excerpt: British EBM group Nitzer Ebb released their fourth studio album, “Ebbhead,” on 30 September 1991 through Mute Records in the UK, with Geffen handling the release in the US. The album turns 35 this year. Nitzer Ebb recorded “Ebbhead” between May and July 1991 at Konk Studios in London, following writing and programming sessions at Sync City earlier that year. Depeche Mode’s Alan Wilder and Flood produced the album together, with Steve Lyon engineering and co-mixing.
items.body: British EBM group Nitzer Ebb released their fourth studio album, “Ebbhead,” on 30 September 1991 through Mute Records in the UK, with Geffen handling the release in the US. The album turns 35 this year. Nitzer Ebb recorded “Ebbhead” between May and July 1991 at Konk Studios in London, following writing and programming sessions at Sync City earlier that year. Depeche Mode’s Alan Wilder and Flood produced the album together, with Steve Lyon engineering and co-mixing. The ten-track record introduced sampled metal guitar to the band’s sound for the first time, most audibly on the single “Godhead,” and brought in a fourteen-piece string and bass section arranged by Andrew Poppy on “I Give to You.” Issued on CD, vinyl LP and cassette, the album runs 44 minutes across “Reasons,” “Lakeside Drive,” “I Give to You,” “Sugar Sweet,” “DJVD,” “Time,” “Ascend,” “Godhead,” “Trigger Happy” and a remix of “Family Man.” Mute lifted three singles from the album: “I Give to You” (27 August 1991), “Godhead” (30 December 1991) and “Ascend” (30 March 1992), while the “As Is” EP, issued in June 1991 ahead of the album, previewed the “Family Man” remix later included on the tracklist. “Ebbhead” streams in full on Spotify. About Nitzer Ebb Nitzer Ebb formed in 1982 in Chelmsford, Essex, England, when school friends Vaughan “Bon” Harris, Douglas McCarthy and David Gooday started the group, first as La Comedie De La Mort before adopting the Nitzer Ebb name. The trio self-released the demo “Basic Pain Procedure” in 1983 and met producer Phil Harding two years later, who produced their 1985 debut single “Isn’t It Funny How Your Body Works?” and helped them launch their own label, Power Of Voice Communications. Three further singles, “Warsaw Ghetto” (1985), “Warsaw Ghetto Remixes” (1986) and “Let Your Body Learn” (1986), followed before the band signed to Mute Records in 1986. “Murderous” (1986) and a re-released “Let Your Body Learn” (1987) built the band’s reputation in the EBM and industrial rock scenes, and “Join in the Chant” (1987) crossed into the emerging Balearic and UK acid house scenes. Nitzer Ebb released their debut album, “That Total Age,” in 1987, and Depeche Mode invited them to open the European leg of the Music for the Masses tour that year. Gooday left after the tour, and McCarthy and Harris completed the duo’s second album, “Belief,” in 1989 as a two-piece with Mark “Flood” Ellis producing. Julian Beeston joined as a touring drummer and became a regular contributor. In 1989 the band also teamed with German EBM act Die Krupps to re-record “Wahre Arbeit – Wahrer Lohn” as “The Machineries of Joy.” The third album, “Showtime” (1990), moved toward a less confrontational sound, and its single “Fun to Be Had” reached the US dance chart in a George Clinton remix. For their fourth album, “Ebbhead,” released on 30 September 1991, Nitzer Ebb brought in Depeche Mode’s Alan Wilder alongside Flood to co-produce, introducing sampled guitars and orchestral arrangement to their sound for the first time. The band promoted the album with a global tour that ran from the southern United States to Barnaul in Siberia. Their fifth album, “Big Hit” (1995), leaned further into live instrumentation, with Jason Payne joining on percussion and John Napier added on guitar for touring, and it remained the band’s final release for close to fifteen years. McCarthy went on to record and tour with Alan Wilder’s Recoil project and later formed Fixmer/McCarthy with French producer Terence Fixmer, while Harris relocated to Los Angeles and produced under the names 13mg and Maven. Nitzer Ebb reconvened in Los Angeles in 2007 and, with Flood back on production, completed “Industrial Complex,” released in 2010 and reissued on double vinyl in 2015 with an Alan Wilder remix. The band toured through the 2010s, including dates opening for Depeche Mode’s Tour of the Universe, and continued to tour with Front 242 on the Join The Forces tour into 2023, with founding members David Gooday and Simon Granger back in the lineup from 2019. McCarthy died in June 2025 at age 58, and Harris has continued Nitzer Ebb with Gooday and Granger, discussing the band’s 2026 European tour and a new album in a recent interview. “Ebbhead,” the album that introduced guitars and orchestration to the band’s EBM sound, turns 35 this year.

items.body: This release is essentially a concept piece comprising a substantial 120-page book and an accompanying Soundtrack. Merciful Nuns needs no introduction by now, and their driving force, Artaud Seth, has found the perfect vehicle here to further flesh out his “Kvltan” universe. The book serves as a guide to the ancient civilization known as Kvltan, which predates known human civilization by a vast margin. It suggests that humanity’s origins lie much further back in space and time than we realize. It is a mythological narrative in which ancient gods, lost knowledge and rituals, portals to other dimensions, dream worlds, and much more converge. Central to this are the ‘Oneironauts’—individuals capable of entering other realms of consciousness through their dreams. The book constantly straddles the boundary between dream and reality, life and death, past and future. It acts as a narrative guide to which Merciful Nuns have composed the accompanying music. The release features a 33-minute-and-33-second track divided into four parts, followed by a second track. The first piece is particularly intriguing, sounding like a genuine film score—a departure from the German band’s usual style. It is entirely Cinematic in nature, defined by an omnipresent ritualistic atmosphere that gradually evolves. Spoken-word elements are incorporated alongside deep, rumbling vocals, while the use of strings further reinforces the Soundtrack aesthetic. To my ears, this piece complements the book perfectly. The second track feels more familiar, offering a blend of Metal guitar and Gothic atmosphere, topped off by Artaud Seth’s deep, charismatic vocals. Beyond the power of the guitars, the track is further enriched by piano passages. Fans of Merciful Nuns may find themselves faced with a somewhat atypical work here, but it fits perfectly within the band’s ritualistic dynamic. Moreover, the book itself is a relatively quick read, making the entire release an intriguing and immersive experience for anyone willing to step into the mysterious world of Kvltan. (Rating:7½). Watch the clip for “Black Monoliths”: About Merciful Nuns Merciful Nuns is the vehicle of German multi-instrumentalist Artaud Seth, formed in 2010 after the disbandment of his earlier band The Garden Of Delight. Seth also records as Near Earth Orbit and runs the Solar Lodge label, through which Merciful Nuns’ own catalogue is released. The project’s 2010 debut album, “Lib. I”, drew heavily on The Sisters Of Mercy; by 2022 Seth counted “Kvltan” as the band’s eleventh album, a fusion of industrial, gothic and psychedelic elements built around the mythology of the ancient civilisation Kvltan, as he explained in a Side-Line interview. “Liber Kvltanae” continues that story and the “Liber” naming convention set by the band’s debut.
