items.body: Her secret lies behind his broken eyes. You carry her all alone inside of you. And you’re still searching for some validation. Why only find frustration? Well, I don’t know. Sometimes the body gets treated like evidence. People inspect it, name it, assign meaning to it, and then act surprised when the person living inside has a different account of who they are. When a person spends enough years absorbing that scrutiny, it can become difficult to tell where somebody else’s judgment ends and their own voice begins. That confusion can be especially brutal for a trans person, because acceptance may require untangling identity from shame that was handed to them before they had the language to reject it. Novelí’s debut single, Mind or Body, begins from inside that argument. The longtime underground DJ, who describes her hybrid of darkwave, synthpop, old-school EBM, Latin freestyle, and related electronic strains as “Maximal Wave,” builds the track from stern machine rhythms, synthetic bass pressure, and melodies that carry the extravagant romanticism of early electronic pop. You can hear traces of Dead or Alive and Depeche Mode in its architecture, alongside the severe physicality of Anhalt EBM and the strange emotional immediacy of a forgotten 1990s game soundtrack playing through cheap speakers in an empty room. Then Novelí opens her mouth. Her register brings Andrew Eldritch and Peter Murphy immediately to mind, though the visual contradiction is part of the pleasure. Novelí embraces femme-fatale glamour while singing in a bass voice she once regarded as incompatible with womanhood. Her own explanation says everything: “I used to think my voice was too deep for a woman, but I’ve grown to think there’s something kind of sickening about being a bass singer who looks like a femme fatale,” Mind or Body gets its emotional voltage through lyrics that move through secrecy, frustration, loneliness, scrutiny, and the weary confusion that comes from being forced to interrogate your own existence over and over. The physical body and social expectation become tangled until even the source of pain becomes hard to locate. Novelí leaves room for uncertainty, but she also introduces a far more dangerous possibility: what if the part of yourself you were taught to hate could become beloved? “Not everyone can relate to the trans experience, but I think almost everyone can relate to feeling like something about you is socially unacceptable, so you feel like you have to carry it alone,” she says. “And ideally, you eventually figure out how to live with it and even embrace it. It’s about entertaining even the tiniest possibility that you can fall in love with the parts of yourself you’ve been hating for a long time.” Daniel Foerste’s accompanying video pushes that idea into religious horror. Novelí appears as a sacrificial figure who eventually becomes a living altar, drawing on Bauhaus, Siouxsie Sioux, Sopor Aeternus, Giallo, Butoh, religious imagery, and vaporwave unreality. “Society sees trans bodies as something horrific, and I wanted to capture that. We’re so often scapegoated, but I also wanted to show that there can be something divine in us, something sacred.” Watch the video for Mind or Body below: Released on the Autumn Equinox and destined for the forthcoming album Transfigure, “Mind or Body” makes transformation feel messy, theatrical, frightening, sensual, and spiritually charged. Novelí has begun her recording career by turning the courtroom inside her head into a nightclub, then placing the accused behind the microphone. Novelí says the sales will support her gender-affirming care and sustain her artistic practice. Listen to Mind or Body below and order the single here. items.body: Daydreaming, lost and found Daydreaming, nowhere bound Falling deeper, falling down, it took me over And I can’t get out The life inside your head has certain advantages: better dialogue, revised endings, people who finally say what you needed to hear. Spend enough time there, though, and the ordinary world begins to feel like an interruption. Somewhere between rehearsing a happier life and forgetting to participate in your own, the imagination acquires a troubling degree of authority. Minsk-based artist Tomorrows Letters traces that retreat on *Daydreaming*, a troubled synthpop lullaby set against a stark, black-and-white DIY video. The solo project of Kiryl Karotki, Tomorrows Letters gives the song an especially compelling frame: music that draws you close as its singer searches for a way out. A deep snare and a looping bassline establish a measured, insistent rhythm, with a low metallic synth figure moving beneath high, resonant chimes. The bells lend the opening a fragile sweetness, soon complicated by Karotki’s voice. Drenched in reverb, his baritone carries regret and despondency with considerable poise, allowing dread to gather beneath the melody. Certain phrases soften toward a tender whisper without losing their weight. There is a strong affinity with Dave Gahan here, particularly the sensual unease of Depeche Mode around Violator and Songs of Faith and Devotion. High harmonies brush the edges of the lead vocal, while a gentle acoustic jangle and deeper string tones add movement beneath it. Karotki gives these familiar pleasures a distinct arrangement: the bass keeps circling, the bells retain their nursery-room delicacy, and the voice seems increasingly conscious of how far it has drifted from safety. “The track was originally titled ‘Maladaptive Daydreaming’, and that’s the core of it,” Karotki explains. “It’s about that state where your inner world becomes so consuming that it starts to replace reality. It’s about how escapism can turn into a trap.” The lyrics trace that loss of control through thoughts taking flight in swirling formations, gathering a momentum their owner cannot arrest. A second voice has apparently dismissed the habit as a way to cope; the singer answers by describing the grip it has taken on him. The chorus keeps returning to the same admission, “And I can’t get out.” By the outro, the private entertainment has exhausted itself: the curtain falls, the screen goes silent, and an empty chair remains. Even then, the imagined story keeps calling. Karotki built the recording around sampled bass guitar and bells, producing it on two vintage hardware samplers running from floppy disks. His intention was to keep the sound firmly within 1980s synthpop, with the equipment lending its own worn texture to the arrangement. He then mixed the track with Andrei Bobrovka, known for his work with Molchat Doma and Nürnberg, and completed the cover artwork himself. The self-filmed video extends Karotki’s affection for classic Depeche Mode imagery into stark black-and-white rural scenes. He sits blindfolded on a chair in an open field; elsewhere, he performs with a guitar or peers through a screen of leaves. Flocks of birds fold and turn across the sky, giving the opening lyric’s murmuration a visual counterpart. The field offers room in every direction, yet the blindfold makes that freedom inaccessible. Images of the chair picked out by light against darkness bring the song’s final sense of vacancy into view. Watch the video for Daydreaming below: Working with a hardware-only approach, Tomorrows Letters draws on New Romantic pop and minimal synth to examine isolation, compulsive creation, and the less hospitable corners of the self. On Up Against the Wall, Karotki cast self-judgment as a trial with no prospect of acquittal. Daydreaming approaches that inward confinement through the comforts that gradually become dependencies, extending his interest in the mind’s capacity to make captivity feel familiar. The single also includes a remix by Farforovyekoty, the side project of Nürnberg’s vocalist, which gives the song a more aggressive, post-punk treatment. Besides the original’s uneasy lullaby, it offers another route into Karotki’s fixation. The invitation is gentle enough; the difficulty comes when you try to leave. Listen to Daydreaming via Apple Music or Spotify below: The single is also available for purchase on Bandcamp. items.body: My sins are all forgiven. I might be desperate, but I won’t let you forget. I know you will give in to me. I am dead set. I am dead set. She 1 • Him 2 have built their latest single Obsessed around one of pop music’s most reliable bad ideas: somebody confusing romantic destiny with a complete inability to take no for an answer. The Cleveland duo of Evan Nave and Cassie Bishop bring years of Lestat and Shy Moon behind them, though Obsessed feels leaner and brighter than that résumé might suggest. The synths skip forward in sharp little patterns, Bishop keeps her vocal airy and cool, and underneath it all sits an electroclash streak that brings to mind the clipped attitude and wiry pop economy of Elastica fed through a rack of 80s electronics. There is plenty of Human League, Yazoo, Soft Cell, and Ladytron in the bloodstream, but the guitars give the track an extra shove. Producer Michael Seifert threads in parts with a distinctly Fixx-like character, adding just enough bite to keep the arrangement from becoming too polished for its own good. “This song has been amazing to put together,” says Nave. “An 80s vibe with a very modern spin. And our producer, Michael Seifert, dropped some very Fixx-like guitars on it. Love the dark lyrical tone versus the upbeat music dichotomy.” That contrast is where Obsessed starts getting funny in a slightly alarming way. The music suggests somebody having a marvelous time under bright club lights; the lyrics suggest that somebody has already memorized your commute. Bishop drew inspiration from the horror film Obsession and its character Nikki, played by Inde Navarrette. “I wrote the lyrics to this song based off the movie Obsession, which I loved and thought was a unique and fun idea for a horror movie,” says Bishop. “I wanted to capture some of the elements and mood of the film in this piece.” She certainly found the right emotional neighborhood. The character at the center of the song barrels through pleading, certainty, possession, and total romantic entitlement while treating every objection as a temporary inconvenience. Love becomes less a mutual arrangement than a hostile takeover conducted in excellent makeup. Bishop wisely keeps her delivery light. She never overplays the menace, and that restraint makes the character more convincing. The voice remains smooth, composed, almost sweet, even as the lyrics tighten their grip. It gives Obsessed the unnerving quality of someone smiling pleasantly while explaining why the two of you are obviously meant to spend eternity together. The electroclash edge helps, too. Those angular guitars and bright electronics give the song a brisk, fashionable nastiness, somewhere between synthpop precision and the kind of deadpan cool Elastica once made look effortless. Obsessed is catchy enough to dance to and unhinged enough to make you reconsider sharing your location. Romance, apparently, remains a dangerous hobby. The charming video channels that same bubbly sycophancy inside the studio, where eager autograph and selfie seekers chase the performers around, hoping for — and eventually fighting over — a moment with their idols. There is something wonderfully silly about the escalation, and visually it brings to mind Toni Basil’s Mickey, with its bright, performative enthusiasm and choreographed fan frenzy. The joke fits the song neatly: admiration is only one bad decision away from fixation. Watch the video for Obsessed below: Listen to Obsessed below and order the single here. items.body: The Future arrived Tuesday No one knew, however A girl packing her suitcase saying, “Maybe now or never” There is a bassline in Ganser’s Futuretripping that seems to know the economy is fake, the clocks are lying, and somebody somewhere is trying to sell you another subscription to tomorrow. Around it, Brian Cundiff’s guitars jab and veer while Alicia Gaines sings with the cool composure of someone watching the machinery malfunction exactly as expected. The result lands somewhere between Bikini Kill, The Breeders, and DEVO, all wired together by a song obsessed with time, delay, and the peculiar modern habit of waiting for permission to panic. Futuretripping is a wiry, nervy post-punk offering built from elastic bass, restless guitar, and the kind of lyrical absurdity that makes modern life sound only slightly more ridiculous than it already is. Somewhere between The Breeders, Bikini Kill, and DEVO, the song turns anxiety about time, media, and collective hesitation into something sharp enough to dance to. The track picks up the rhythmic intelligence that ran through Animal Hospital, the band’s third LP, while pushing the tension into a tighter frame. The bassline keeps the song in motion with a thick, spring-loaded bounce, while the guitar scratches and darts around it with nervous energy. Alicia Gaines sings with a dry, controlled delivery that gives the song’s stranger images room to land without forcing the joke. The lyrics revolve around a world trapped in endless anticipation. Screens insist that everything is going according to plan, people wait for the next signal, and tomorrow becomes something they can apparently borrow from a shady acquaintance with the right connections. Ganser turns that uncertainty into deadpan comedy, presenting the future as another dubious commodity sold to people who have already spent too much of the present waiting around. The image of someone selling umbrellas beneath a clear sky gets at the song’s humor perfectly. It is ridiculous, vaguely ominous, and just believable enough. “Ahead of going on the road with Bikini Kill, I was interested in the concept of cheating time, where one could go for just a little more of it,” says Gaines. “After coming back from Europe earlier this year, we found our personal senses of time were distorted as we were dropped back into life in Chicago, mixing the mundane with the fantastical. Reaching into tomorrow for a little more of today became an inside joke, now Futuretripping.” Cundiff frames that temporal confusion as something closer to collective agitation. “Everybody’s waiting for the sign to change,” he says. “People tend to wait around to be fed what they should react to these days, what to do, and I suppose there’s a bit of that restlessness in the music and lyrics as well. It’s an agitation that it’s not tomorrow while also wanting more time today, right now.” Gaines also directs the accompanying video, which leans into a loose ’90s montage aesthetic, cutting random footage against the band performing beneath a bright blue sky. The editing has the same sideways humor as the song, constantly shifting between ordinary images and mildly surreal interruptions. Ganser leave us with a world where everybody is waiting for the sign to change while the sign itself appears to have wandered off. Watch the video for Futuretripping below: Chicago’s Ganser have spent the years since their 2018 debut Odd Talk developing an increasingly restless conversation between post-punk, noise rock, and art-school absurdity. Just Look At That Sky followed in 2020, while the 2022 EP Nothing You Do Matters brought Liars’ Angus Andrew into the producer’s chair. Bassist and vocalist Alicia Gaines and drummer Brian Cundiff remain central to the band’s writing, balancing physical rhythms with dry humor and an eye for the contradictions of everyday life. Their third album, Animal Hospital, was released through Felte on August 29, 2025, with production shared by Ganser and Andrew. A deluxe edition followed on April 22, 2026, adding five alternate versions of songs from the record. Touring with IDLES, Mclusky, and Ted Leo has helped sharpen their live attack; this September, Ganser joined Bikini Kill for shows in Milwaukee, Chicago, Royal Oak, and Cleveland. Futuretripping, released September 10, extends that momentum with a new song written and arranged by Gaines and Cundiff. For future live announcements and ticket links, visit Ganser’s official shows page. Listen to Ganser’s Future Tripping below, and order the single here. items.body: With autumn extending its chilly tendrils and release season in full swing, I found myself in the welcome but somewhat overwhelming company of three album promo’s clamoring for review. Fortunately we have a perfect if seldom used format for this that may be dredged up from the blog’s murky depths when needed. Here we go...Brymir – What We Leave BehindIf you know Brymir, you know what they do. That may be one of my least inspired opening lines ever, but I stand by it. These Finnish purveyors of melodic death metal embellish the well-established style of Finnish melodeath with sweeping orchestral arrangements, mostly resulting in a predictable but no less exhilarating couple of absolute banging tracks on an album generally overshadowed by other acts. What We Leave Behind might claim to be Brymir's “most sinister album yet”, according to the promo, but I’m still getting my saccharine fix of high-octane full-blast-melody bangers and that’s what I want. I think Brymir and/or their label are largely aware of this, since they usually manage to drop these as advance singles. For your periodic fix of indelible, vanquishing albums akin to “Wings of Fire” and “Voices in the Sky”, look no further than “Tempestbound”, and especially the title track.For those curious as to what a darker Brymir might entail, I’ve found this plan largely successful. “True Darkness” and “Buried Legion” offer a more aggressive take on their established formula, and “The Roaring King” and “Broken Dawn” achieve varying success with a slower approach. While an Aether Realm like grandiosity permeates the tracks, they can be a tad indulgent and fatiguing towards the end of an album that already carries the weight of much bombast. While hilarious, unexpected, and surprisingly apt for their style, the closing cover of Scooter's “How Much is the Fish” (you’ll know it when you hear the melody) is a bit of a contradictory choice for an album that’s supposed to show their serious side. That being said, if you liked their previous album’s I’d bet you’ll like this one too. More Brymir being Brymir is hardly a bad thing, and I’m sure I’ll wake up in a few months with one of their earworms randomly crawling around in my brain.  What We Leave Behind by Brymir What We Leave Behind by Brymir Firtan – HeliosI’ve been following now-German sextet Firtan with intermittently bated breath since my first encounter with 2018s Okeanos. Firtan’s music is firmly rooted in icy black metal, but find sit’s most arresting foothold when the band’s progressive and symphonic leanings join the furious fray. While cuts like “Seegang” and “Uferlos” (2018), “Amor Fati’and “Peraht” (2022) and “Hrenga” (2024) showed glimpses of a ravenous yet poised and grandiose talent on each of their past three albums, Firtan have yet to write an album that sweeps me away as a whole. On their previous three releases, many excellent tracks or movements felt like sweeping vista’s being crammed into the corners of an overcrowded tableau. Arresting and immediately memorable, but ultimately groaning under the weight of overindulgence or less memorable surrounding compositions. Helios, while by no means a stark departure from their established sound, does show Firtan taking steps towards greater consistency and a more measured style of blackened metal. Abandoning some of the slavering hunger and much of the speedy outbursts present on previous albums, they opt for a more doom and death metal inspired soundscape, drawing parallels to particularly Schammasch. While this approach works well to keep songs more focused, it also exposes their sometimes unnecessary length,and makes the album sag under an entirely different but no less noticeable weight at times. Slowing down does allow both acoustic elements  and some of the more death/doom oriented riffing to shine. “Kalika’s Tongue”, “Solis Currus”, “Helios” and “The Hierophant” show the shining promise in Firtan’s new approach, and if they reintroduce some of the wilder aspects from earlier releases and intertwine them with the patience and focus on display on Helios, their next release may very well live up to the expectations that I’ve been quietly carrying around since I first heard that inimitable riff of “Seegang”all those years ago. Helios by Firtan Temic – CeibaIt’s been a while since I’ve written about an album so ingrained in heavy, modern prog (metal) as this one. Those roots come as no surprise when reading of the associated pedigree that comes with this relatively young and unheralded super-group. Featuring (ex or current) members of Devin Townsend, Mike Portnoy’s Shattered Fortress, the Neal Morse Band, Haken, Shining (Nor) and Maraton is a serious endorsement. Prog super-groups, however, are also notoriously prone to writing indulgent if not masturbatory escapades of soulless technicality. Fortunately, Temic manage to avoid this latter pitfall. While the occasional keyboard or guitar solo can test my patience, the album (at least for a prog metal album) is generally well paced and only features one 10-minute-plus song. In terms of influence, it’s mainly (older) Haken that springs to mind, as well as Leprous, Votum, Kingcrow and perhaps Caligula’s Horse. Somewhat ironically, the album’s less than polished vocal delivery might afford it most of its more obvious unique character. Had those rougher, accented edges not been present, I might have given up on the album before reaching its halfway point. That’s not to say it's bad by any means, I’ve just heard too many permutations of this particular style of prog to be easily impressed. Sticking around for the latter half of the album proves more interesting, with longer compositions less focused on generic heavy prog riffs and more of the charming melodicism and sweeping climaxes that elevate Temic above the sum of its well worn parts. “Casting Stone” and “See Myself” get the ball rolling, and momentum carries the album through to “Alone” and obligatory long and ambitious closer “As Long As We Last”, which drifts towards Southern Empire’s criminally underrated Civilisation in tone and mood (if not in song length). Ceiba is a good and occasionally great progressive metal album, just don’t expect to be blown away if you’re familiar with the style.  Ceiba by TEMIC

夜型です。その日の前後の予定にもよりますが、時間が許すなら、ダラダラと夜を過ごしていたいタイプです。「低血圧」というのを言い訳にしているんですけど（笑）、本当に朝は弱いです。 基本的には時差ボケがあっても関係なく夜型ですね。ヨーロッパに行くと、最初はちょっと早起きになるんですよ。ちゃんと眠くなって。でも、だんだん慣れていくと、また夜が長くなっていきます。 新倉瞳（にいくら・ひとみ） 桐朋学園大学音楽学部を首席で卒業し、皇居桃華楽堂新人演奏会に出演して御前演奏を行う。その後スイスに渡り、バーゼル音楽院ソリストコース・教職課程の両修士課程を最高点で修了。これまでに毛利伯郎、堤剛、トーマス・デメンガ、マーティン・ツェラー（バロック・チェロ）の各氏に師事。国内外で数多くの賞を受賞し、2017年に第18回ホテルオークラ音楽賞、2020年度に第19回齋藤秀雄メモリアル基金賞チェロ部門を受賞。桐朋学園大学在学中にEMI Music Japanより『鳥の歌』でCDデビューし、同レーベルから3枚、アールアンフィニからは『11月の夜想曲～委嘱作品集』を含む4枚のソロアルバムをリリース。ほかにも多数のアルバムを発表している。 かつてカメラータ・チューリッヒのソロ首席チェリストとして活躍し、スイスを拠点にヨーロッパや中央アジア、日本でもソリストや室内楽奏者として幅広く活動する。近年はクレズマー音楽や民族音楽にも造詣を深め、音楽祭に招かれワークショップやレクチャーコンサートも行う。カザフスタンの民俗楽器ドンブラも演奏し、2025年にはカザフスタン国営放送で日本人として異例の紹介を受けた。 使用楽器は宗次コレクションより貸与のマッテオ・ゴフリラー（1710年製）。2026年にデビュー20周年を迎えた。 27. 犬派ですか？ 猫派ですか？ 新倉 今、我が家には猫がいるので、猫派です。でも、私、柴犬とかも大好きなんですよね。だから答えづらい（笑）。かわいいんですよね。 新倉さんの愛猫・紬ちゃん 28. 好きな食べ物は何ですか？ 新倉 イケメン好きなんです（笑）。演奏活動でいろいろな土地に伺うと、その土地その土地のイケメン（イケてる麺）探しを常にしております。 海外に長くいるときに一番恋しくなるのはラーメンですね。スイスにもラーメン屋さんは多いですし、最近は海外でも増えてきていますけど、やっぱり日本のラーメンは違います。一番好きなのは豚骨ラーメン。コテコテのものが好きです。 29. 苦手な食べ物はありますか？ 新倉 好き嫌いはないです。パクチーが苦手だったけど、あるとき、レモンとチーズがたっぷりのったパクチーサラダを食べたら、ものすごくおいしくて。それ以来、全然大丈夫になっちゃいました。 疲れていても愛猫が寄り添ってくれると癒される 30. 最近ハマっていることは何ですか？ 新倉 最近ハマっているのは、日本のお祭りです。おととし初めて青森ねぶた祭りに行ったとき、お囃子の音を聞いて、改めて日本のお祭り文化のすばらしさを感じたんです。去年はねぶた祭りに加えて、宮城の七夕祭りにも行きました。 東北では、山形の花笠まつりや盛岡さんさ踊り、福島のわらじまつりにも行ってみたいです。徳島の阿波踊りにも興味がありますし、旅先を選ぶときにも、お祭りがきっかけになることが増えました。夏の終わりには、各地で開催されるお祭りの情報をチェックするのも楽しみです。 31. 最近、一番笑ったことは何ですか？ 新倉 前編で12月3日に上演する「ベートーヴェンの小径」の舞台について、音楽と語りを交えた企画だとお話をしたら、休憩時間にMCの三井さんが「ベルリオーズみたいですね」とおっしゃって（笑）。「私、ベルリオーズだったんだ」みたいな感じで、爆笑しました。一番フレッシュな大爆笑です（笑）。 ベルリオーズは、私もなかなか演奏する機会が少ないので、ちょっと興味が出ました。 新倉瞳 × 南沢奈央「ベートーヴェンの小径」 32. 一番の癒やしは何ですか？ 新倉 やっぱり我が家の紬ですね。猫さまが尊いです。 この間も疲れて帰ったら、玄関に迎えに出てきてくれて。音でわかるみたいで、トントントントンって階段を下りてくるんです。鈴がついているので、リンリンリンリンと音がして。 ぼーっとしていても、私の前に来て、パサッと倒れて甘えてきてくれる。もう、一番の癒やしです。 紬ちゃんと戯れる新倉さん 寝つきがいいし午後まで寝ていることもできる！ 33. ストレス発散法を教えてください。 新倉 私、基本的に「おやすみ3秒」人間なんですよね。ストレスを感じているときって、体も疲れていることが多いですよね。いろんな人に気を使ったり、「何か考えなきゃいけない」と思ったりすると疲れると思うんですけど、寝ないともたないので（笑）、おいしいものを食べて、ぐっと寝る。 そうすると、次の日にまた頑張れる。ストレスに立ち向かえるんです。 34. オフの日はどのように過ごしていますか？ 新倉 放っておけば午後まで寝られる人なので、オフの日はよく寝ています（笑）。睡眠の質を上げるために、アロマスプレーを枕元にシュッとすることもあります。枕元でふわっと香るのは好きです。 35. 今、一番行ってみたい場所はどこですか？ 新倉 屋久島に行ってみたいです。海外にも、ブルガリアなど行きたいところはたくさんあるんですけど、まずは屋久島。国内では、音楽が伴って旅することがどうしても多いので、楽器なしで旅することへの憧れがあります。 36. お気に入りのアイテムや、いつも持ち歩いているものはありますか？ 新倉 あまり外でお化粧直しをしないんですけど、唇が乾燥すると嫌なので、リップクリームは常に持っています。 最近気に入っているのは、KATEの「明後日の水たまり」という名前がついたリップクリームです。保湿力が高くて、発色も自然にほんのり赤くなるところが気に入っています。 ベートーヴェンとコーヒーを飲みながら当時のチェリストの話を聞いてみたい 37. ご自身を動物にたとえるとしたら、何だと思いますか？ 新倉 これは、人に言われてから、すごくそうだなと思っているんですが、アザラシ！ 笑ったときの顔も似ているし、寝ているときの姿というか、ニコニコしてパタパタしている感じが、わりと自分にリンクするなと。 昔、南沢奈央ちゃんが私のコンサートに来てくださったときに、白寿ホールのバックステージで一緒に撮った写真があるんですけど、それがアザラシの写真と完全一致していて。水槽の中からアザラシがふっと笑っている写真と、私がふっと笑っている写真が同じ顔をしていて、「ああ、私はアザラシに似ているんだな」と（笑）。 アザラシに似ていると評判のショット。12月3日に開催される「ベートーヴェンの小径」でも共演する南沢奈央さんと 38. 家族や親しい友人からは、何と呼ばれていますか？ 新倉 「ひーちゃん」とか「ひいたん」とか。小学校の時代は「にいくらくら」と呼ばれていたこともあります。あとは「トミー」。アメリカに住んでいた頃、アメリカの方には「Hitomi」という名前がうまく発音されなくて、「トミー」になっちゃったみたいで。当時仲がよかったマイコちゃんも「マイケル」になって、「マイケル・アンド・トミー」だったんですよね（笑）。 39. 意外だと言われる一面は？ 新倉 ラーメンが好きとか、食べることが好きと言うと、意外と言われますね。クラシックの奏者って、どうしてもお上品な感じに見えるらしくて、そういった意味で「ラーメン」というワードが出てくると、意外みたいですね。 食べることが好きですし、食べるのもけっこう速くて。リハーサルの合間など時間に迫られたときに食べると、誰よりも遅く食べ始めて、誰よりも早く食べ終わっています。 40. 一緒にコーヒーを飲んでみたい歴史上の人物はいますか？ 新倉 いろいろな人と飲んでみたいんですけれども、今はやっぱりベートーヴェンです。 コーヒーは豆の数までこだわって淹れていたそうなので、きっとあまりきれいではなかったであろうベートーヴェンの書斎を訪ねて、火を入れるところから観察して、本当に豆を数えるのか見てみたいです（笑）。 それから、当時交流のあった素晴らしいチェリストの方々からインスピレーションを受けて曲を書いていたと思うので、その話も聞きたい。チェロ・ソナタを人生の長い期間にわたって書いているから、「どういう思いで書いたんですか？」ってインタビューしたいです。 関連記事：ベートーヴェンとコーヒー 民俗音楽に血が騒ぐ！ 41. 超能力を一つ持てるとしたら、どんな力がほしいですか？ 新倉 人の争いやいがみ合いって、たぶん誤解から生まれることが多いと思うんです。本当に悪い人っていなくて、生きていく過程でトゲトゲした気持ちが生まれてしまうんじゃないかなって。だから、そういう気持ちをピッと消せる超能力があったらいいなと思います。誰かが「今、トゲトゲしちゃってるんじゃないかな」と思ったら、ピッてやりたい（笑）。 でも、そういう思いから生まれる音楽もあるので、消せないものだとも思うんです。 あとは、単純にチェロがうまくなる超能力もほしいです（笑）。 42. 好きな映画を一つ挙げるとしたら？ 新倉 ジブリ作品は大好きです。一つ挙げるなら、『風の谷のナウシカ』かな。音楽もいいし、やっぱり自然や、人のいろいろな心が入っていて。あと、テトっていう肩に乗っているかわいいキャラクターも大好きです。ほかには『魔女の宅急便』も好きです。 43. これまでに影響を受けた本はありますか？ 新倉 『シーラという子』（トリイ・ヘイデン著）という本です。幼少期に虐待を受ける女の子の話で、私は幸いそういうことがなく育ってきたので、「ああ、こういう人もいるんだ」ということに、すごく衝撃を受けました。本を読むことで、自分の知らない人生を知ることができたり、まったく違う世界に入れたりするんだ、と感じられた一冊です。読書が好きになったきっかけの本でもあります。 44. 普段、どんな音楽を聴きますか？ 新倉 そのとき、たまたま出会った音楽を聴くことが多いんですが、突き詰めると、自分の血が騒ぐのは、やっぱり民俗音楽だと思います。クラシック音楽でも、民俗音楽に影響を受けているものに、ときめくことが多いかなと。 最近よく聴いていたのは、クリムゾンの「Moonchild」。ジャンルとしてはクラシックとはかなり離れていると思うんですけど、ちょっと民謡のような部分のあとに、即興的な部分が10分くらい続くような曲で、すごく気に入っています。 ベートーヴェンのイメージをアロマスプレーに 45. デビュー20周年を記念して、「天然回帰」とのコラボレーションによるアロマスプレーを発売されますね。なぜアロマスプレーだったのでしょうか？ 新倉 もともと香りに対して特別なものを感じていました。香りで思い出す記憶ってあるじゃないですか。 今回、マネージャーさんのつながりで、ソーシャルフレグランスブランドの天然回帰さんとコラボレーションすることになって。以前、香りを使わせていただいたときに、夜眠るときに枕元にシュッとしたり、朝出かけるときにフレッシュな香りを使ったりすると気分がいいと教えていただきました。自分にとって特別なときに、香りでリフレッシュできるのって素敵だなと思って。そこから、私の中では「朝と夜」がキーワードになりました。 46. 今回のアロマスプレーは、どのような香りをテーマにされたのでしょうか？ 新倉 今回はベートーヴェンの楽曲に合わせて、2つの香りを作りました。朝用は「田園」、夜用は「月光」をテーマにしています。 ベートーヴェンの楽曲を思い出してもらえるようなものを、12月の公演を聴きに来てくださった方に持ち帰っていただきたいと思ったんです。自分の癒やしになっているものと音楽を関連づけていただけたら嬉しいですね。 実際の香りは、天然回帰さんがベートーヴェンの背景などもすごく勉強してくださったうえで、交響曲第6番《田園》とピアノ・ソナタ第14番《月光》を聴いたときのイメージや気分に合うように何パターンか調香してくださって、その中から選びました。香りを嗅いでみて、「あ、これが月光だ」みたいな（笑）。そうやって、新倉瞳のベートーヴェンのイメージと香りがリンクしながら出来上がっていったんだと思います。 香りを選ぶ新倉さん 新倉さんプロデュースのアロマスプレーは、12月3日にサントリーホールブルーローズで開催される「ベートーヴェンの小径」で初めて販売されます！ 47. おすすめの使い方は？ 新倉 朝は、出かけるときにシュッとかけて、ふっと爽やかな気持ちになって、ドアを開ける。そんなタイミングで使っていただくのがおすすめです。夜は、眠る前に枕元にシュッとして、「ああ、今日もいい一日だったな」と、ちょっとしっとり受け止める感じで。あとは、リラックスしたいときには、いつでも自由に楽しんでいただけたらと思います。 ベートーヴェンの二面性を香りに。コラボレーションスプレーの香りが決まりました！ - 天然回帰 新倉瞳さんとつくる「人の持つ二面性のための香り」 聴いてくれる人と一緒に変化を恐れずに楽しんでいきたい 48. 今、一番やってみたいことは何ですか？ 新倉 そのときどきで「今、一番やってみたいこと」を叶えている感じなんです。毎年1回リサイタルをしているので、次のテーマについてもすでに資料を集め始めています。 やってみたいことは常に増えていくんですが、最近は日本の文化に改めて興味が湧いていて、着物に対する知識を増やしたいなと思っています。ひととおりきちんと着られるセットは持っているのですが、まだ知識が深くないので、着物のことをもっと知って、コレクションも増やしたいです。 49. 20周年を迎えた今だからこそ、これから挑戦してみたい音楽はありますか？ 新倉 ちゃんと取り組んでみたいのは、ジャズです。 これまでもジャズのような音楽を演奏したり、ジャズのすごいプレイヤーの方々に助けていただいて演奏したことはあるのですが、ちゃんと和音の勉強などもしないと、私の中では「ジャズをやっている」とは言えないかなと思っています。これからそういった勉強をしていきたいです。 50. これから新倉瞳さんの音楽を聴く方に、伝えたいことを一言お願いします。 新倉 私は興味の対象がどんどん移り変わっていくんですが、結局、それって点と点が線につながっていく、一つの過程だと思っています。そこに一緒に興味を持ってくださって、今の私を楽しみにしてくださっている方がいることは、とても光栄です。そういった変化を、私と一緒に楽しんでくだされば嬉しいです。 でも、その方々にもそれぞれの人生があるから、私の音楽を聴かないタイミングも出てくると思うんですよ。それでもいいと思っています。お互いに変化を恐れずに、一緒に楽しんでいけたら幸せだなと思います。 ポッドキャストの視聴はこちら 新倉瞳さんの出演情報 新倉瞳 × 南沢奈央 ベートーヴェンの小径 日時： 2026年12月3日（木）19：00開演 会場： サントリーホール ブルーローズ 曲目： 語りとともに綴るベートーヴェンの世界 ベートーヴェン／チェロ・ソナタ全曲 構成・脚本・演出： 新倉 瞳 出演： 新倉瞳（チェロ）、南沢奈央（語り）、横山瑠佳（ピアノ） スペシャルゲスト： 大萩 康司（ギター）、佐藤 芳明（アコーディオン）、大渕 愛子（フィドル）、渡辺 庸介（パーカッション） 詳しくはこちら

items.excerpt: 2026.09.30 ONTOMO編集部 東京・神楽坂にある音楽之友社を拠点に、Webマガジン「ONTOMO」の企画・取材・編集をしています。「音楽っていいなぁ、を毎日に。」を掲げ、やさしく・ふかく・おもしろ... 詳しく見る 9月29日、サントリーホール ブルーローズにて、第57回サントリー音楽賞を受賞した佐藤俊介（ヴァイオリン／指揮）と、第25回佐治敬三賞を受賞した「日野浩志郎新作音楽公演『Chronograffiti』」の贈賞式が行なわれた。 サントリー音楽賞は1969年の創設以来、毎年、その前年度においてわが国の洋楽文化の発展にもっとも顕著な功績のあった個人または団体を顕彰し、贈呈している。賞金は700万円。 贈賞理由には、「分断に歪み、混迷を深めるいまの時代において、芸術家にしかできないことをアクチュアルに示し続けている。楽しむだけではなく、思考を突き動かすためにこそ、音楽を。そうした佐藤のビジョンを照らし、クラシック音楽の未来の一翼を担うひとりとして、今後の歩みへの期待を示すもの」ということがあげられている。 ビーバー《ロザリオのソナタ》よりパッサカリアを演奏して喝采を浴び
items.body: 2026.09.30 ONTOMO編集部 東京・神楽坂にある音楽之友社を拠点に、Webマガジン「ONTOMO」の企画・取材・編集をしています。「音楽っていいなぁ、を毎日に。」を掲げ、やさしく・ふかく・おもしろ... 詳しく見る 9月29日、サントリーホール ブルーローズにて、第57回サントリー音楽賞を受賞した佐藤俊介（ヴァイオリン／指揮）と、第25回佐治敬三賞を受賞した「日野浩志郎新作音楽公演『Chronograffiti』」の贈賞式が行なわれた。 サントリー音楽賞は1969年の創設以来、毎年、その前年度においてわが国の洋楽文化の発展にもっとも顕著な功績のあった個人または団体を顕彰し、贈呈している。賞金は700万円。 贈賞理由には、「分断に歪み、混迷を深めるいまの時代において、芸術家にしかできないことをアクチュアルに示し続けている。楽しむだけではなく、思考を突き動かすためにこそ、音楽を。そうした佐藤のビジョンを照らし、クラシック音楽の未来の一翼を担うひとりとして、今後の歩みへの期待を示すもの」ということがあげられている。 ビーバー《ロザリオのソナタ》よりパッサカリアを演奏して喝采を浴びた後、贈賞式でスピーチを行なう佐藤俊介。 ヴァイオリニストであり、指揮者、室内楽奏者である佐藤俊介は、世界各地のピリオド楽器アンサンブルやシンフォニック・オーケストラを指揮し、ソリストとしても出演。2013～23年オランダ・バッハ協会のコンサートマスターを、18年からは音楽監督を兼務し、録音したJ.S.バッハのカンタータや器楽作品の数々は、同協会のYouTubeで見ることができる。2011年からはコンチェルト・ケルンのソリスト、指揮者、コンサートマスターを務め、2013年からアムステルダム音楽院の教授としてヒストリカル・ヴァイオリンを教えている 贈賞式に登壇した佐藤は、「たいへん光栄であると同時に、身の引き締まる思い。ブルーローズは特別な思い入れがある場所で、26年前の2000年、当時16歳だった私は日本で初めてのコンサートを行なうことになり、その会場の1つがここだった。 4歳から19歳までずっとアメリカに住んでいて、当時は日本語の敬語がうまく使えず、アンコールの曲名を伝えるのに、お客様に向かってタメ口で話してしまった（笑）。そんなデビュー当時のとんちんかんな私でさえ、何かのスタート地点に立っているという意識はあったが、まさか26年後にサントリー音楽賞の受賞者として、再びこの同じステージに上がらせていただくとは思っていなかった。 この26年間、多くの方に出会い、ご指導いただき、私の未熟さや失敗を寛容に受け入れてくださり、私の音楽家としての価値を信じてくださった。困難や迷いに遭遇した時もあったが、これらの方々一人ひとりのおかげで、今の自分がここにいることを考えると、今回の賞を受賞したのは自分だけではないということを痛感する。 本日の贈賞式も、今の私にとって新たなスタート地点であるような気がする。これからどんな経験をし、どんな出会いが待っているか、楽しみでならない。これまで私を導いてくださった先生方、共演してくださった音楽家の皆様、演奏の場を作り支えてくださった皆様、そして何より演奏会場で音楽を共にしてくださった聴衆の皆様に、心より感謝申し上げる」と述べた。 最新アルバム『BEE1H0VEN~ベートーヴェン：ヴァイオリン・ソナタ全集』が新レコード・アカデミー賞第1回大賞に輝き、2027年4月からは、東京交響楽団のクリエイティブ・パートナーを3年間務めることになった佐藤。今年5月からは、自身が創設したロマン派以降の音楽を主な対象とする古楽オーケストラ「Past Forward Ensemble」の演奏活動もスタートした。 「強い信念で周囲の音楽家を巻き込みながら、卓越した行動力で新しい音楽の潮流を作っていく。日本の次世代を担う音楽家たちに大きな影響を与え、これからますます存在感を発揮していく」（サントリー音楽財団代表理事 堤剛氏）と讃えられる佐藤が、今後ヴァイオリニストとして、指揮者として、ますます多く日本の聴衆の前に姿を現してくれることを願ってやまない。

items.excerpt: トーキョーアーツアンドスペース本郷にて、国際的な交流を促進し、多文化的な視点で多様なテーマについて思考するプログラム「TOKAS Project」が開催されます。 9回目となる今回は、トーキョーアーツアンドスペース（TOKAS）とソウルとの交流20周年を記念して、過去にレジデンス・プログラムに参加した日韓のアーティストを中心に、知覚や存在の輪郭の揺らぎへの問いと応答をテーマに、5名のアーティストによる展覧会が行なわれます。 本展では、アーティストたちがそれぞれ異なる視点から観察した生の姿を、展示空間に再び立ち上げる行為（＝再演）をとおして、その瞬間の彼らの感覚や視点から新たな解釈を促し、現代における生の本質を見つめ直すことを試みます。 ＜参加アーティスト＞ ウン・ジェピル、キム・ドヒ、ク・ドンヒ、パク・ミンハ、三野新 関連イベント ■アーティスト・トーク ＊日英逐次通訳あり 日時｜2026/10/03（土）15:00〜17:00 会場｜トーキョーアーツアンドスペース本郷 出演｜ウン・ジェピル、キム・ドヒ、ク・ドンヒ、パク・ミンハ 参加費｜無料 ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 ■パフォー

items.excerpt: 今年8月から渋谷のユーロスペースで始まり、現在は全国各地にその上映場所を移している「パフォーマンス・アート：身体と空間をめぐる映画祭」。合計4プログラム5作品のドキュメンタリーからなる特集上映ですが、東京在住の筆者はこの夏、予定の隙間を見つけては劇場に足を運び、なんとか全作コンプリート（それを可能にしてくれた長期間のプログラム編成に感謝）。そのいずれもが観に来てよかったとしみじみ思える作品たちでした。 夏の日差しがもはや懐かしい［筆者撮影］ 折角なら全作観ようと思えるこの「映画祭」のサイズ感も心地良く、作品同士の連関にはっとするだけでなく、そこで観たものが別の場所や次の季節でまた別のものに出会わせてくれる、というおまけのような循環も。例えばプログラムDの『ナム・ジュン・パイク 月は最古のTV』（アマンダ・キム監督、2023）を観た後にワタリウム美術館の「没後20年 ナムジュン・パイク｜じゅげむ展」（11月23日まで）を観ると、彼の作品のなかの音楽やパフォーマンスの部分に自然とフォーカスするようになったりと、また体験が変わります。あるいはピナ・バウシュとヴッパタール舞踊団の欧州ツアーを追

items.album: 杉江あこ｜方丈記に学ぶ　–生きるを編み直す小さな建築–
items.tags: art sound art contemporary music improvisation
items.excerpt: 会期：2026/08/28～2027/01/11 会場：21_21 DESIGN SIGHT ギャラリー1＆2［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://www.2121designsight.jp/program/hojoki/ 人はそんなに小さな建築が好きなのか。確かに超高層ビルやマンションの林立、都心の再開発などが止まない現代社会だからこそ、その反動から自らの身の丈に合った建築を求めたくなるという心理はわからないでもない。近代建築の父であるル・コルビュジエも、地中海を望む南仏カップ・マルタンに休憩小屋を建て、晩年を過ごしたことで知られている。結局、大きな建築は国家繁栄や経済性などのためであり、対して小さな建築は個人のささやかな望みということなのだろう。 会場風景 21_21 DESIGN SIGHTギャラリー2 撮影：木奥恵三 本展は、鴨長明の名随筆『方丈記』に記された「方丈の庵」を起点に、現代における生き方への問いをテーマとした企画展である。方丈の庵とは一丈四方の住まいのことで、現代の面積に置き換えると約9㎡、四畳半程度の空間である。長明は晩年に都から離れ、山に方丈の庵を建てて隠遁
items.body: 会期：2026/08/28～2027/01/11 会場：21_21 DESIGN SIGHT ギャラリー1＆2［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://www.2121designsight.jp/program/hojoki/ 人はそんなに小さな建築が好きなのか。確かに超高層ビルやマンションの林立、都心の再開発などが止まない現代社会だからこそ、その反動から自らの身の丈に合った建築を求めたくなるという心理はわからないでもない。近代建築の父であるル・コルビュジエも、地中海を望む南仏カップ・マルタンに休憩小屋を建て、晩年を過ごしたことで知られている。結局、大きな建築は国家繁栄や経済性などのためであり、対して小さな建築は個人のささやかな望みということなのだろう。 会場風景 21_21 DESIGN SIGHTギャラリー2 撮影：木奥恵三 本展は、鴨長明の名随筆『方丈記』に記された「方丈の庵」を起点に、現代における生き方への問いをテーマとした企画展である。方丈の庵とは一丈四方の住まいのことで、現代の面積に置き換えると約9㎡、四畳半程度の空間である。長明は晩年に都から離れ、山に方丈の庵を建てて隠遁生活を送ったのだが、そこには厭世的な心情が大きく働いていた。隠遁生活は、心は自由でも、孤独と不便が付きものである。つまり暮らしの不自由さをある程度受け入れてでも、世俗から離れたい気持ちが強かったということだ。会場内には長明の方丈の庵の再現を試みた《非実在空間としての方丈の庵》をはじめ、参加作家によるさまざまな解釈の下での方丈の庵が建ち並んでおり、なかなか見応えがあった。中には靴を脱いで内部へ入れる作品もあり、体験型の楽しい内容となっていた。 会場風景 21_21 DESIGN SIGHTギャラリー1 《非実在空間としての方丈の庵》 撮影：木奥恵三 会場風景 21_21 DESIGN SIGHTギャラリー2 左：山口晃《螺庵》 右：2m26《living with》 撮影：木奥恵三 しかし、私自身、小さな建築に憧れるかどうかというと、今のところそうした気持ちはない。というのも、どうしても不便さが目に付いてしまうからだ。広すぎず、狭すぎず、ほどほどの面積で、雨風をしのぐだけでなく温度や湿度をちょうどよく保てて、清潔に快適に暮らしたいというのが希望である。都市から離れた山里で隠遁生活を送る勇気などまったくないのだ。たぶん多くの現代人が同じような考えなのでは……とここまで思案して、ふと浮かんだのはいわゆるミニマリストである。ミニマリストとは必要最低限の物だけで豊かな暮らしを送る人のことをいうが、つまり彼らこそ現代における『方丈記』の精神を体現しているのではないか。方丈の庵という住まいの狭小さばかりに目が向いていたが、自分にとって本当に必要な要素だけに削ぎ落とすという行為は、住まいの狭小さも物の少なさも同じなのでは……という考えに至り、本展のテーマがようやく腑に落ちたのである。 会場風景 21_21 DESIGN SIGHTサンクンコート 正田智樹＋竹中工務店＋veig《蓑庵 マウン庭》 撮影：木奥恵三 鑑賞日：2026/08/29（土）

items.body: Sometimes, the band is the standout performance. What’s up, everyone! Welcome back to yet another installment of the J-Music Exchange/Rate! Your monthly source of Japanese music album reviews brought to you by yours truly and my good friend and fellow Japanese music fan Al from Omunibasu. If you’ve been rocking with us for a while now, then you already know the deal, but if this is your first time here and you’re not entirely sure what the Exchange/Rate is all about, please give the following primer a quick readーThe Exchange/Rate is a tandem album review series conducted every month by yours truly alongside my good friend and fellow Japanese music fan Al (from Omunibasu). Each month we decide on a specific theme with which our reviews would revolve around. We then pick out albums from our respective libraries which we think best coincides with that theme. We will then give the album we chose to the other person and vice versa (exchange), after which we then listen to and subsequently review the album we were given (rate). This project has not only allowed us to explore music beyond our libraries, but it provides an opportunity for us to see our favorite albums from a different point of view. It is our hope that this series is able to do the same for you and that you either find a new artist to try out and/or we offer you a fresh take on one of *your* favorite albums Al and I take turns deciding on a theme for our reviews every month, and for September we’re handing the reins back over to him. And I gotta say, I thought he came up with a pretty interesting one this time around, as we’ll be talking about albums that we feel exemplify an excellent group effort. Now, what exactly do we mean by that? Well, I don’t necessarily think it’s as simple as picking out an album where everyone involved is just really good at what they do. Rather, we’re looking at releases where you can genuinely feel the importance of everyone’s contributions to the finished work. Where the drums, bass, guitars, vocals, keys, production, or whatever else might be involved all feel integral to what makes the album what it is, and where taking any one of those elements away would leave you with something noticeably different. Of course, how that group effort manifests can vary quite a bit from one album to another, which is also what makes this such a fun theme to explore. For my pick, I went ahead and gave Al Fooocus by Aooo, a release that I think demonstrates the concept particularly well with how each of its members gets an opportunity to bring their own musical identity into the fold while still working together as one cohesive unit. You can check out what Al thought of that over at the Omunibasu Substack! Al, meanwhile, decided to send me Mani Mani by CRCK/LCKS, an album made by a group of musicians who, as we’re about to find out, have quite the collective pedigree between them. And perhaps more importantly for today’s discussion, they might just have a thing or two to teach us about what happens when you put that much individual talent in the same room. Let’s get into it! ーー CRCK/LCKS (クラックラックス) is a five-piece Japanese band formed in 2015, consisting of vocalist/keyboardist Oda Tomomi, saxophonist and multi-instrumentalist Konishi Ryo, guitarist Inoue Mei, bassist Ochi Shunsuke, and drummer Ishikawa Shun. Comprised of musicians with backgrounds predominantly rooted in jazz, the group brings together their respective expertise to create a style that freely moves between jazz, pop, R&B, and other contemporary influences, with an emphasis on intricate ensemble work and experimentation. ＜Ｍａｎｉ Ｍａｎｉ (まにまに)＞(＊Spotify link to the full album) CDJapan Affiliate Link(s):Mani Mani / CRCK/LCKS ＜T ｒａｃｋｌｉｓｔ＞ ０１・あらわらわ/arawarawa０２・レンタル神様/rental kamisama０３・真空パック/shinkuu pack０４・Psycho Sky０５・T.I.C.０６・沖に出たら/oki ni detara０７・枝と嵐/eda to arashi０８・バラライカ/balalaika０９・つまらない毎日/tsumaranai mainichi１０・Tiny Mirror１１・7月27日１２・You say goodbye１３・manimani Ａｌ：Ever since I first discovered CRCK/LCKS a few years ago, I’ve always found them to be a pretty fascinating band. It’s possible that I didn’t fully grasp what they were all about at first, but their two Temporary albums were ones I’d always come back to randomly, just because of how avant-garde the songs were and their overall irregular take on pop music. One moment you could be hearing a groovy cacophony of guitar, bass, and even the saxophone going wild, and another moment can have you getting lost in an ethereal soundscape. They may be a group that I have an on-and-off listening relationship with, but their ability to come up with this nutty stuff never fails to catch my attention. And I do feel like that’s why I came to enjoy their most recent album, Manimani, a lot. I’ll admit that the thought process for this month’s theme was based on how much more perceptive I’ve become when I listen to music, with me often trying to mentally separate the instrumental and/or vocal performances in a song, in order to really appreciate everyone’s efforts individually (and thus, understanding how well it all gels together). And with a band like CRCK/LCKS, who seem to display so many different elements in their music, it’s hard not to take interest in the mesmerizing or pleasant oddities they’ve been known for. Especially considering how varied the song selection is on Manimani, as the band showcases a more rambunctious side in the opener’s ending sequence (“arawarawa”), the unbelievably calming jazzy nature of “edatoarashi”, or how the bouncy and weirdly hyper traits in song like “bararaika” made it a standout song during my initial go-through with the album… it’s a record that feels very familiar if you’re an existing fan of the band, yet their efforts still feel super fresh with how surprisingly varied it is, style-wise. Another reason why I might’ve picked this one was because it’s described to be a cool celebration of CRCK/LCKS’ existence as a group, and every single member is featured on its songwriting credits. And after finding that out, it made it clear how much of a collective effort this album was, with everyone being able to chip in with their own ideas. And honestly, it resulted in an even more of an enjoyable experience. ーー Now, I actually thought about doing this one a little bit differently than I normally do for Exchange/Rate album reviews. If you’re a longtime follower of this series and are thus quite familiar with how I structure my end of the reviews, you’ll know that I typically pick out, at minimum, four songs from the album to talk about. These aren’t necessarily always my four favorite tracks either. More often than not, I use them to formulate a framework for how I want to approach the record as a whole; what I find good or intriguing about it, what I think the artist is trying to accomplish, and ultimately what kind of music listening experience I believe the album has to offer. In spending some time with CRCK/LCKS’ Mani Mani, however, I very quickly realized that I can’t really go about doing that here. Or, perhaps more accurately, I don’t think I should. Part of my reasoning for that is ultimately going to be at the heart of my overall thoughts on the album, but I think a good place to start this discussion is by first looking at the individual parts that make up CRCK/LCKS. Because if we’re going to talk about Mani Mani, I think we first have to talk about the people who made it. The band is led by multi-instrumentalist and Berklee College of Music graduate Konishi Ryo, known primarily within Japanese jazz circles for his work on the saxophone. Joining him on keys and vocals is classically trained Oda Tomomi, with jazz guitarist Inoue Mei on guitar, Ochi Shunsuke on bass, and Tokyo University of the Arts graduate and credentialed percussionist Ishikawa Shun behind the drums. For your everyday overseas Japanese music fan, I don’t necessarily expect all of those names to immediately jump off the page. For those more entrenched in the Japanese jazz scene in particular, however, seeing these five musicians come together in service of one collaborative project might read as something closer to a supergroup. Across the five members are numerous accolades and accomplishments within the Japanese music world, with each having established themselves through their own work and collaborations with renowned musicians both within and outside of Japan. All of which is to say that nobody in CRCK/LCKS necessarily needs the band to prove what they’re capable of individually. Everyone involved is already exceptionally accomplished at what they do. Which, naturally, begs a much more interesting question. What happens when you put all five of them together? That’s ultimately where my interest in Mani Mani lies. With this much individual talent packed into one group, it would be incredibly easy to approach the album by pulling everything apart and pointing toward what each member contributes. But I also think doing so would miss what makes CRCK/LCKS so fascinating in the first place. The question I’m more interested in asking isn’t what each of these five musicians can do individually. It’s whether what they create together amounts to something greater than the sum of its parts. Given how skilled everyone in CRCK/LCKS is with their respective instruments, I think it would be perfectly natural to assume that there’d eventually be some sense of one member overpowering another. Put five musicians of this caliber together and surely someone is gonna end up taking over the room, right? Except, as you’ll hear even from the opening stretch with Arawarawa, and subsequently thereafter with songs like Rental kamisama and Shinkuu pack, that never really happens. Instead, there’s this remarkable cohesion to the way CRCK/LCKS perform together where nobody sounds as though they need to tone down their own musicality simply to accommodate the other virtuosos playing alongside them. Everyone is still very clearly doing what they do best, only somehow without any of it coming at the expense of somebody else. You can still hear and appreciate Ishikawa Shun’s impeccable drum work without it ever distracting from Oda Tomomi’s lovely singing. Likewise, Konishi Ryo can bring his saxophone into the arrangement without completely stealing the spotlight away from Inoue Mei and Ochi Shunsuke on guitar and bass respectively. Nobody necessarily has to retreat into the background for somebody else to shine. And I think that’s an important distinction to make when talking about Mani Mani. The impressive thing isn’t simply that five extremely talented musicians are able to play well together. You’d probably expect that much given everyone’s credentials. It’s that they can seemingly play to the full extent of their abilities at the same time and still sound like a band rather than five individually impressive performances happening on top of one another. Part of me wants to simply chalk that up to the members being incredibly compatible with one another. At the very least, you don’t get the impression listening to Mani Mani that anyone feels the need to constantly prove themselves or overshadow everybody else in the room. But I do want to pose another possibility as to why CRCK/LCKS work so well together, and that’s the fact that all five of them come from jazz backgrounds. Obviously, there’s already going to be some preexisting overlap there. Having five musicians who operate within the same general musical space naturally gives them a shared foundation to work from. What I’m more interested in, however, is jazz itself and how the characteristics of the genre might have helped provide CRCK/LCKS with that unifying thread. Jazz is, by nature, a remarkably loose and unrestricted style of music. One of its most defining characteristics is improvisation, which inherently asks musicians to be responsive not only to what they’re playing, but also to what’s happening around them at any given moment. A performance can shift depending on what somebody else decides to do, leaving everyone involved to react and find their place within it. There’s a certain volatility to jazz in that regard, but I also think that’s precisely what makes it so conducive to having this many different elements operating at once. And perhaps that’s part of why CRCK/LCKS never feel overcrowded despite how much musicianship is constantly on display throughout Mani Mani. These aren’t simply five talented musicians who happen to be playing alongside one another. They’re five musicians coming from a musical tradition that, at its core, places a tremendous amount of value on listening and responding to the people playing alongside you. So when Ishikawa changes something on the drums, or Konishi comes through with the saxophone, or Inoue and Ochi start working something between the guitar and bass, everyone else has the musical vocabulary to respond accordingly. Their individual contributions don’t have to be planned around as obstacles; they become opportunities for everybody else to build upon. In that sense, jazz isn’t merely one of the styles that informs CRCK/LCKS’ music. It might very well be the reason all of these moving parts fit together as naturally as they do. In that regard, I do view Mani Mani as something closer to one big jazz jam session between the members of CRCK/LCKS more than anything else, and this is again largely why I decided not to approach this Exchange/Rate the way I normally would. Rather than viewing the album as a collection of individual songs and picking apart specific moments contained within them, I think Mani Mani works better as a showcase of what these five musicians are capable of creating together. It’s less about waiting for any one member to step forward and give you that big standout performance, and more about listening to how everyone continuously interacts with and plays off one another as the album moves along. Though there’s another side to that too, which is that there honestly aren’t that many singular moments throughout Mani Mani that I find myself wanting to isolate in the first place. And I don’t necessarily mean that as a criticism. If anything, part of what made it so difficult for me to pick out four songs to talk about is that the individual tracks themselves don’t really stand out that much over everything else on the album. There are certainly songs I enjoy more than others, with You say goodbye being the one clear exception for me as a song that I absolutely adore and would probably call my favorite track off Mani Mani simply for how beautiful it is. But beyond that, I rarely find myself listening to the album and thinking about one song being the song. Instead, CRCK/LCKS just… play. They create, they experiment, they respond to one another, and then they move on to the next idea. There’s a free-flowing quality to Mani Mani that makes the boundaries between those individual tracks feel considerably less important than the experience of hearing the band perform across the album as a whole. In that sense, listening to Mani Mani reminds me a lot of sitting down at a jazz bar and taking in a live set. You might walk away remembering a particular melody or moment that caught your ear, but that’s not necessarily why you enjoyed yourself. Sometimes the pleasure comes simply from sitting there and watching a group of incredibly capable musicians do their thing, seeing where the music takes them and appreciating how naturally they’re able to find one another along the way. That’s more or less how I find myself listening to Mani Mani. And perhaps that’s the best explanation I can give as to why, for once, I don’t really want to pull the album apart into four songs and tell you what makes each one work. The thing I find most interesting about Mani Mani isn’t any singular moment contained within it. It’s CRCK/LCKS themselves. ＜Ｗｈａｔ Ｉ ｔｈｉｎｋ ｏｆ Ｍａｎｉ Ｍａｎｉ ＞ So, after all of that, I suppose we’re left with the question that I posed at the very beginning: is CRCK/LCKS as a collective greater than the sum of its parts? Well… yes and no. If we’re looking at Mani Mani purely as a showcase of what happens when you put five incredibly accomplished musicians together and let them create, then I do think the answer is a resounding yes. There’s a level of musical understanding between everyone involved that allows each member to perform at an incredibly high level without ever making the album feel like a competition for your attention. Nobody gets lost, but nobody has to overpower everybody else either. Instead, their respective talents continually feed into one another, and I think the jazz background shared between them goes a long way toward explaining why that interaction feels as natural as it does. At the same time, I do think there’s another side to that equation when we start looking at Mani Mani specifically as an album. Going back to my comparison of listening to the record as being akin to sitting through a live set at a jazz bar, there are naturally opportunities for the mind to meander between songs. And I did find myself doing that here. There were a couple of times listening through Mani Mani where I noticed my attention starting to drift, only for the band to pick things back up instrumentally and pull me right back in again. Curiously enough, I almost wonder if that’s somewhat intentional. There are a lot of starts and stops throughout Mani Mani, along with these little interstitial tracks scattered between the more fully realized songs, to the point where it can sometimes feel like you’re supposed to lose track of exactly where you are in the album. One song ends, another idea comes in, the band pauses, something else begins, and eventually you look down and realize you’re three tracks further along than you thought you were. In most cases, I would probably consider that a knock against an album. After all, you’d generally want the songs themselves to leave enough of an impression that you can distinguish one from another. And as I mentioned earlier, outside of something like You say goodbye, there aren’t really many tracks on Mani Mani that I personally came away viewing as these huge individual landmarks. But I’m also not entirely convinced that Mani Mani wants to be experienced that way. The more time I spent with it, the less I found myself approaching the album as thirteen separate tracks and the more I started treating it as one continuous performance. Sometimes you’re completely locked in on what CRCK/LCKS are doing. Other times you let the music play while your mind wanders elsewhere. Then Ishikawa comes crashing back in on the drums, Konishi’s saxophone cuts through, Oda catches your ear with a vocal line, or Inoue and Ochi find another groove together and suddenly you’re paying attention again. And honestly, there’s something kind of pleasant about that. It makes Mani Mani less of an album where I’m constantly waiting for the next song I like to come on, and more of one where I simply enjoy spending time in the presence of the musicians playing it. The individual tracks become less important than the ebb and flow of the performance itself, which I think explains why trying to pick four of them apart for this review never quite felt right to me. So, is the whole greater than the sum of its parts? From a purely musical standpoint, absolutely. CRCK/LCKS are five tremendously accomplished musicians individually, but what makes Mani Mani interesting isn’t simply getting to hear all five of them demonstrate what they’re capable of. It’s hearing what each of them becomes in response to the other four. As an album, though, I think that same collective quality comes with a tradeoff. Mani Mani can be so free-flowing that its songs occasionally lose some of their individual identity along the way. But perhaps that’s also the point. Sometimes you don’t go to a jazz bar because you’re waiting to hear one particular song. Sometimes you go because the band is playing. ＜Ｍｙ Ｒａｔｉｎｇ＞４ ｏｕｔ ｏｆ ５ ＆ ８ ｏｕｔ ｏｆ １０ Mani Mani is, in a lot of ways, both memorable and unremarkable And I realize those two things sound like they shouldn’t be able to coexist, but I think that’s ultimately the best way I can summarize my experience with the album. Outside of something like You say goodbye, I don’t necessarily see myself walking away from Mani Mani remembering a bunch of individual songs or singular moments that completely blew me away. What I will remember, however, is the experience of listening to CRCK/LCKS play together. Because even during the moments where my attention started to drift, I don’t think there was ever a point where I questioned the quality of the musicianship on display. If anything, hearing five musicians this accomplished play alongside one another with seemingly very little interest in individually taking over the spotlight made me appreciate the collective that much more. Perhaps that’s also what makes Mani Mani such a fitting album for this month’s theme. When everyone involved is already this talented individually, it’d be easy for the appeal to simply become the novelty of hearing all of them on the same record. Instead, the most impressive thing about CRCK/LCKS is how quickly you stop thinking about any one member at all. ーー What are your guys’ thoughts on CRCK/LCKS’ Mani Mani? Let us know down in the comments! Likewise, what albums come to mind for you when you think of an excellent group effort? Whether it’s a band where every member feels integral to the music or simply a group of musicians who bring out the best in one another, we’d love to hear your picks! Lastly, before I let you guys go, don’t forget to check out Al’s review of Fooocus by Aooo over at the Omunibasu Substack if you haven’t yet! Happy Listening!

items.album: John Coltrane 100: John Coltrane in Detroit, June 1966
items.excerpt: John Coltrane Memorial in Hamlet, N.C. Photographer unknown. By Stuart Broomer If I can write anything meaningful about the music of John Coltrane, it may be about the context in which I came to experience his work live, in 1966, after listening intently to his work for four years on record and writing reviews of some of it as well. One’s juvenilia is embarrassing almost by definition, but that’s my particular gateway here to a world in which Coltrane was playing live a few feet in front of me.
items.body: John Coltrane Memorial in Hamlet, N.C. Photographer unknown. By Stuart Broomer If I can write anything meaningful about the music of John Coltrane, it may be about the context in which I came to experience his work live, in 1966, after listening intently to his work for four years on record and writing reviews of some of it as well. One’s juvenilia is embarrassing almost by definition, but that’s my particular gateway here to a world in which Coltrane was playing live a few feet in front of me. 13 months later he passed away. I write this hopefully to communicate something of the challenging world in which Coltrane made his music, that ever more intense, more radically free music, as testimony to his courage and vision as a great artist, as large a person as one might be in that world. The John Coltrane Reference (Routledge, 2008) by Chris DeVito, Yasuhiro Fujioka, Wolf Schmaler and David Wild, edited by Lewis Porter (Routledge, 2008) is a monumental work of scholarship. After the introductions, there’s a Chronology of Coltrane’s life and career that runs to 357 large pages of fine print, followed by a Discography of 404 similarly sized pages in identical print, followed by 49 more pages of appendices, index, etc. Very near the Chronology’s conclusion, there’s an entry for the John Coltrane Quintet’s appearance at Detroit’s Drome Lounge from June 17-26, 1966. The personnel, then consistent, is identified as Coltrane, tenor and soprano saxophones; Pharoah Sanders, tenor saxophone; Alice Coltrane, piano; Jimmy Garrison, bass; Rasheid Ali, drums, Friday to Sunday, matinees on Sunday. Reviewed in Coda (“John Coltrane Quintet – Drome Bar—Detroit” by Stu Broomer, Aug-Sept., 1966, pp.32 - 33). The review is represented by just a few of its sentences, but I’ll restrict myself to the Reference editor’s choices and their punctuation as well. “This is probably the most moving working band in America (…) Tenor saxophonist Farrell “Pharoah” Sanders is now the most important soloist in the group. (…) When (Coltrane) first heard Albert Ayler in 1962, Coltrane told him he had heard himself playing like that in a dream once. (…). This band has recorded five times but nothing has been released. Perhaps Bob Thiele is hoping Coltrane will return to his old-time sanity. I for one hope he will not”. (Reprinted by permission of the author. All Rights Reserved). What I’m trying to get at here about John Coltrane is an essential drive for expression and liberation, for liberation from every constraint to discover what’s real or what’s at least possible. If my memories from 60 years ago mean anything, they’re about the value of revolt and the horror of the norm, the judgmental restriction of cultural norms, in some places becoming more restrictive than anything I might have felt 60 years ago (a festival of liberalism by comparison). As a result, I want the music more intense, more personal, more unpredictable and I’ll stand up for it anywhere. But it is not without ambiguities. As a teenager in the 1960s, I became obsessed with free jazz. It was a promise of freedom from restraint as well as constraint, an explosion of mixed emotions from great sorrow to ecstasy, in effect, perhaps, a promise too far. My absorption in jazz had begun in childhood with the 1957 TV special The Sound of Jazz and followed with the eventual LP. More television: I saw the Robert Herridge Presents episode with Miles Davis and John Coltrane in 1960 and loved it. My brief initial puzzlement and rapid-onset rapture with free jazz started when I picked up the September 1961 Metronome at the corner variety store. It included an epic essay on the jazz avantgarde by the then LeRoi Jones (I still have the essay somewhere — stapled together — the issue is gone). The writing was abstract, mannered and strange but also enchanting (I had already read a paperback of Kerouac’s Tristessa ), its subject an arcane revolution. By the time I had purchased Ornette! and Free Jazz a few months later, Metronome had ceased to exist. I had only Down Beat , a magazine at the time sufficiently reactionary to condemn John Coltrane and Eric Dolphy as anti-jazz in a cover story. A few years later, circa 1965, I started writing for Coda, then Canada’s only jazz magazine. If there’s a shock in that original account (in bowdlerized form), it’s likely the ranking of Sanders’ performance over Coltrane’s. Without digging for the original, I recall moments from that night when I was listening to the dense, tumultuous music and focussing on the brilliant screaming mayhem of the two saxophones, only to open my eyes and discover that John Coltrane was intently hitting a cowbell with a drumstick and Pharoah Sanders was the only person playing a saxophone. This isn’t a criticism of Coltrane. He was one of the greatest musicians who ever played jazz, but we all know now that he was seriously ill and still carrying a heavy musical load. Other memories: I already had certain knowledge that Jimmy Garrison’s solos, as memorably powerful as they were, depended heavily on the bass’s tuning in fourths, and the complex, droning solos dependent to a significant degree on the use of open strings (I was a bass player at the time). At one point in the evening, Coltrane spoke quietly to him (I was sitting at a piano-shaped stage, my ear within four feet of their mouths) specifying the key for one of his extended introductions. Garrison then looked upset, arguing for another key. I wasn’t surprised by the issue. I was surprised that it was happening about four years into Garrison’s tenure in the band. Another and crucial surprise goes to the heart of the history of free jazz. My party (myself and three others, young musicians from Toronto, three Caucasian, one Japanese) were, in effect, insiders (however “out” we might feel in the Drome). We arrived early, conveying Rashied to the venue since we were staying in the same place, the Detroit Artists Workshop. Arriving early, we found a strange mix of conviviality and formality. Standing just inside the foyer, Jimmy Garrison was shaking hands with patrons as they entered. Even to a bass player, Garrison’s right hand (the plucking one) came as a shock: it felt like a bundle of sticks. As popular, as great , as John Coltrane was, there was a fundamental divide in the audience about the shape his music was assuming, that was apparent from the time the music began (a shock perhaps influenced by the very music that Impulse was choosing to release). In essence there were two audiences. In the Drome it happened largely along racial lines, generally slightly older blacks on the one hand, and the white audience, many significantly younger, significantly suspended between hip and hippie. One audience looked disgruntled, offering spare, obligatory applause; the other clapped wildly with exclamatory shouts. Late in the evening, Coltrane broke into the opening phrase of his anthem, “My Favorite Things”, its bright coiling phrases instantly recognizable from the first note. It was amazing. With my back to the rest of the audience, I could actually feel the room lift, so strong was the shift in mood, comparable, for a brief instant, to the sun breaching a cloud cover. Within a couple of minutes, the sonic tumult had taken over again, and one could feel, even more intensely, the mood of the room dropping, to frustration and disappointment, perhaps, and most intensely, I felt, the abandonment, the sense of betrayal. In total, (expanding on Coltrane's grimly disappointed Black audience) the trip seemed at times to be about race but things would get much darker, or should I say lighter (toxic metaphors lurk in our tongue) -- I had gone there with three other young Toronto musicians with whom I played. I had an association with John Sinclair (then in jail on drug charges -- not sure how current John's name is, but his greatest moment of celebrity came when imprisoned during Woodstock: Abby Hoffman interrupted the beginning of the Who's performance with a comment to the effect that Woodstock didn't mean shit while John Sinclair was in jail; then Pete Townsend hit Hoffman with his guitar for trying to take over the Who's stage). In John’s absence, his partner Leni Sinclair was running the Workshop. I knew The Detroit Artists Workshop through shared performances between Detroit and Toronto, performances arranged by John Sinclair and the Toronto poet Victor Coleman of the Bohemian Embassy, a Toronto coffee house and performance space. Shared performances had included members of Detroit trumpeter Charles Moore’s MC5 with featured musicians that had included Marion Brown and Andrew Hill (through which I got to play bass with Andrew for a weekend among other playing associations). I had also published a poem and a record review in John's mimeo'd music journal Changes , which I think may have only gone to two (or maybe three) issues. The Workshop was the epicentre of radical culture in Detroit whether the issue was music, race, drugs, economics or language. Later it was the spawning ground of the MC5, of "Up Against the Wall Motherfucker" fame, who John Sinclair managed. He later was a founder of the White Panther Party, a Black Panther support group. When I met the members of [Ahmed] a few years ago in Guelph, talk turned to Detroit. Some members were thinking about visiting Detroit, and Pat Thomas and I found ourselves reminiscing about John, whose poetry Pat had accompanied during an Amsterdam performance. John's contract, Pat recalled, required a private pot smoking loft. A few days before our group arrived in Detroit, a young inter-racial couple from the Workshop had been violently attacked on the street by the sons of a former Mississippi sheriff whose property adjoined the Workshop at the rear. While we were staying there, the sheriff had invited the residents of the Workshop to a get together/ barbecue to make peace. None of the Workshop residents (naturally) wanted to go and Leni Sinclair asked our Toronto group (whom they were temporarily housing, four males sufficiently groomed to get across the border without close scrutiny) to go as their representatives. We accepted with a certain reluctance, though things (barbecue, blanched pleasantries) went civilly enough. An hour later, on the way out of Detroit, we stopped at an ice cream outlet before we hit the border. The sons and their wives and children were there as well. On neutral ground, none of us acknowledged the existence of the other. Charles Tyler, Stuart Broomer + Perry Robinson, 1966 ©2014 Bill Copeland AN AFTERWORD: 60 years on, I frequently listen to John Coltrane recordings, probably more than to any other historical jazz artist. I have the complete runs of the Prestige and Atlantic recordings and most of the Impulses on CD and the recordings with Monk and Miles Davis and isolated one-offs like Blue Train on Blue Note. My usual listening choices run the gamut from the Prestige and Atlantic recordings (especially Olé , the last of them, with Freddie Hubbard, Eric Dolphy and Art Davis added to the working quartet of McCoy Tyner, Reggie Workman and Elvin Jones). My listening range ends with one of my favorites, Meditations , with the “classic” quartet augmented by Rashied Ali and Pharoah Sanders. I hardly ever, if at all, listen to much that came later. Whether that’s because the actual experience of the last quintet live was enough – sufficiently intense -- to satisfy my need for that music, or that the music is so unstable or destabilizing that I don’t feel a need to hear it in its “frozen” form. The sole exception made among recordings of the last stage is Interstellar Space , the recording of four duets with Rashied Ali, recorded in February 1967, though it too is rarely played, singled out perhaps for the relative coherence of the music and the focus of its intensity. © Stuart Broomer, 2026 Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Drone and Hum is not necessarily a new record – it was originally released five years ago, back in 2014, as a digital format. Now, as the year closes, this special album is released as a very limited 12” lathe cut vinyl edition, encased in a handmade sleeve and including a 6-page booklet. Photography from J.M Almqvist and a short story by Andrea Lundgren (which is written in Swedish) completes this delightful package. A stamped box includes the English translation of the story, along with an etched iron ore inside another bag. As if that wasn’t enough, 2 download codes for Drone and Hum and Drone and Hum Reworked are also included. The music is deserving of a beautiful physical release. Now, after a time, it has one. Old Amica’s sound is warm and comforting; wintry, but ultimately merry and bright. Chords are full and deep, resonating into the air and creating a sound that feels satisfied, complete, and whole. The music travels slowly, as if it were trampling through clumps of snow. Light tweaks take place here and there, altering notes, reversing them, and experimenting with the general flow of sound, but this never interferes or overtakes the music. The piano is still at the forefront, even with these subtle genetic mutations. Altered notes surround the main piano completely, not as a hostile act, but as a benevolent form of protection, an extra layer of warm clothing which adds to the sound rather than distracts or subtracts. The ambient sound billows out of ‘Solstrimman’ in a spectacular and utterly gorgeous way, and a place of spaciousness echoes throughout the album, where open, snow-coated fields stay untouched and villages are home to tiny populations. Although only making a brief appearance, a clean electric guitar adds some more colour with a warm, repeating melody. In the background, an ambient soundscape lingers and then covers the guitar’s sound in a gust of wind and dancing snow. The movements are almost balletic. The guitar is eventually lost in the ambient layer, shrouded in it completely. And the closing track ‘Eric’s Dinosaurs’ sees the homely piano return, and a thawing arrives with the birdsong. The piano is old, an elderly being, but it has aged like a fine wine, bringing musical maturity and sprinkling experience all over the record. There’s a lot of breathing space here, and as such, it’s a perfect album to close the year. Old Amica – Drone and Hum by Old Amica www.oscarson.bandcamp.com

items.body: Themes and Variations is the first release on Parenthetical Activities, a sub-label of Dissolving which concentrates on experimentation and documentation, recording and amplifying the moments that live ‘in the spaces between the parentheses’. Thomas Shrubsole’s double cassette promises two hours of experimental discourse and intriguing, unrestricted dialogue, is limited to 85 stamped and numbered copies, and includes twelve intuitive acoustic sound-works which are loosely tied together. Recorded over two years, the diverse and eclectic music is written in a nonlinear language of obtuse, curious shapes and fine, angled lines which, as they gel together, create wandering, off-beat sentences and a range of exotic air-hieroglyphics. The dash-dot-dash percussion and the uninhibited, baggy-clothed melody, atypical of dark, late-summer jazz, reclines in the prime time of its intoxicated youth, while quieter interludes, some straddling the borders of total silence, occupy the gaps between music’s accepted and popular lines. Shrubsole invites us to look beyond, to realise that there are no strict beginnings, middles, or endings in music – music is just edited to either begin or fade out at certain points, until the end of its allocated duration. It still sings in the silence; we just can’t pick up its frequencies. Those lines are imaginary, made up because of our inherent need to organise and categorize. The same is true of genres, or the concept of a nation, or the invisible dividing line which separates one country from another; the borders always contested, the soldiers fighting over a plot of land when one side looks just the same as the other. Shrubsole’s audio exploring takes him into no-man’s-land, venturing into the beyond, transcending what we think is possible, breaking barriers and smashing self-conceived and self-restricting borders. They’re ‘studies for alternative instrumental connections’; things that don’t quite fit into the main body of music’s text. Things that live on the outside of the exchange. And the music’s so much richer for its thorough adventuring. This is a mammoth work and a massive undertaking. Altered states are born out of the music’s intricate patterns, and an army of semi-colons, with their brief percussive codes, litter the stave. Shrubsole’s music as Sub Loam has been featured here before, and his approach to music is a freeing thing. For even though the music can at times feel unstructured, the eternal paradox is that there is a structure of sorts, sitting underneath the surface of sound like the lost city of Atlantis. The architecture of the music is submerged, making it trickier to see. Never does it become a gelatinous mess. Boneless patterns appear in less than obvious places, but the soft, swaying drums and the piano’s gentle repetitions and arpeggios reveal the starkly-lit, underground-dwelling structure. It can also be glimpsed in the inner workings of a staccato-blitzed, blip-bleep rhythm. Structure arises out of accidental clashes, out of incidents, out of the creation of music. As soon as Themes and Variations begins to play, the chances of an accidental collision multiply, an accidental returning to structured music when it had initially begun its life with no real predestination. The limited edition comes with two white, stamped cassettes, and a self-locking card box. That box also contains three posters, a twelve-page booklet, and a postcard avec download code. www.parentheticalactivities.blogspot.com

items.body: Moments Before ‘Moments Before’ casts Matt Bartram on a sea full of low slung shoe gazed waves and anti static walls of noise. I reviewed his fourth record ‘The Dreaming Invisible’ for this site in 2013. Back then I was wondering how he made such a big sound out of small means. Now I imagine I can ride the vapour trails his aqueous soundscapes formulate. It visualises itself in the nature of new wave St. Vincent. Gorgeous liquid harmony, it’s a place with no excess, primarily settled in glazed surf pop, with elements of Caribou also whisked in the mix. The function of Bartrams voice seems to be the instrumental chewing gum that gets stuck to the mouth of the well engineered synths. It wouldn’t be out of place round here on a set of Slowdive demos for the Eno co-produced Souvlaki album. To this extent, Matt can be connected in kindred spirit to the etherealness of that bands front man, Neil Halstead. He’s complimenting the same auto didactic ideal, being comfortable with controlling everything by the end as much by himself as possible. He’ll possibly always be a drifter, but ‘Moments Before’ stakes it’s claim as one of the best recent albums that I own. Go catch a wave, then come to the shore with this gem. www.driftingfalling.com

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.
